pericopes.text: And now I, Mormon, make a record of the things which I have both seen and heard, and call it the Book of Mormon.—

links.text: For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.

provenance.other: “things which we have seen and heard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 4:20. The bare pair “seen and heard” occurs in exactly 5 — Luke 7:22, John 3:32, Acts 4:20, Acts 22:15 and 1 John 1:3 — and every one of them is a formula of eyewitness testimony, so the field is not wide; it is the relative clause that narrows it to one. Mormon's only departures are the person (“I” for “we”) and the inserted “both”.
provenance.significance: Recover Acts 4:20 and it is not a preface but a refusal. Peter and John have been arrested, examined, and “commanded them not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus” (4:18); “we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” is their answer to a prohibition. Fifteen verses later Mormon writes “I did endeavor to preach unto this people, but my mouth was shut, and I were forbidden that I should preach unto them” (1:16) — and unlike the apostles he obeys, because the prohibition is God's rather than a council's. The book therefore opens with the KJV's classic sentence of a witness who will not be silenced and, within the same chapter, silences him. Whether or not that irony was intended, it is the shape the chapter has.

links.note: 'And now I, Mormon, make a record of the things which I have both seen and heard, and call it the Book of Mormon.' The title sentence of the book is built on the KJV's sole occurrence of “things which we have seen and heard”, converted from a plural apostolic protest into a singular editorial warrant. 1 John 1:3 supplies the other half of the same idiom — “That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you” — and is a genuine alternative, but 1 John lacks the relative clause and the noun “things” that Mormon has. Moderate rather than high because six words is short and the formula is the New Testament's standing one for testimony; well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six.

pericopes.text: And about the time that Ammaron hid up the records unto the Lord, he came unto me, (I being about ten years of age; and I began to be learned somewhat after the manner of the learning of my people,) and Ammaron saith unto me, I perceive that thou art a sober child, and art quick to observe;

links.text: The woman saith unto him, Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet.

provenance.other: “perceive that thou art a” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 4:19. Drop the article and “I perceive that thou art” occurs in exactly 2, John 4:19 and Acts 8:23; Acts 8:23 is Peter telling Simon Magus he is in the gall of bitterness, and is filed in the exclusion register at this verse. Only John 4:19 supplies the frame the Book of Mormon actually uses, which is the identification of a person by a character noun — “a prophet”, “a sober child”.
provenance.significance: The KJV has one sentence in which a speaker announces, on a first meeting, what another person is; and it is spoken upward, by a stranger who recognises a prophet. Mormon 1:2 runs it downward. The last living custodian of the national record meets a ten-year-old and tells him what he is, and the announcement is a commission: the next two verses hand the boy the plates and the hill. What John 4:19 supplies is the grammar of naming an office a person has not yet claimed — the Samaritan woman is right about Jesus before he says so, and Ammaron is right about Mormon before Mormon has done anything. The unstated correspondence is what each recognition costs the recogniser: the woman goes and tells her city (John 4:28-29), and the child she prefigures here will be forbidden to tell his (Mormon 1:16).

links.note: 'And Ammaron saith unto me, I perceive that thou art a sober child, and art quick to observe.' Six words of John 4:19 in order, from the only KJV verse that has them, with the predicate noun changed. The 1830 reading carries a second piece of evidence that the modern text has lost: 1830 has Ammaron “saith unto me”, the KJV's historic present and John 4:19's own verb, where 1920 reads “said” (CONVENTIONS §8). Moderate: the run is short, and a writer steeped in the KJV could reach “I perceive that thou art” without John in view. What holds it up is that he did not merely reach the clause, he reached the clause with its article and its following noun.

pericopes.text: therefore when ye are about twenty and four years old, I would that ye should remember the things that ye have observed concerning this people; and when ye are of that age, go to the land of Antum, unto a hill, which shall be called Shim; and there have I deposited unto the Lord, all the sacred engravings concerning this people.

And behold, ye shall take the plates of Nephi unto yourself, and the remainder shall ye leave in the place where they are; and ye shall engrave upon the plates of Nephi, all the things that ye have observed concerning this people.
And I, Mormon, being a descendant of Nephi, (and my father’s name was Mormon,) I remembered the things which Ammaron commanded me.
And it came to pass that I, being eleven years old, was carried by my father into the land southward, even to the land of Zarahemla:
the whole face of the land having become covered with buildings, and the people were as numerous almost, as it were the sand of the sea.

links.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor numbered; and it shall come to pass, that in the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.

provenance.other: “as the sand of the sea” occurs in exactly 7 KJV verses: Genesis 32:12, Genesis 41:49, Psalm 78:27, Isaiah 10:22, Hosea 1:10, Romans 9:27 and Revelation 20:8. Worth noticing that the KJV's similes for a war host — Joshua 11:4, Judges 7:12, 1 Samuel 13:5 — all read “sea shore” or “sea side” instead, so the situation Mormon 1:7-8 is moving into belongs to one KJV family and the words he uses belong to another. Alma 2:27's sand-multitude, adjudicated in this catalogue, is the war-host family and Judges 7:12's.
provenance.significance: Of the seven, four are covenant-census verses about Israel's increase, and two of those — Hosea 1:10 and its quotation at Romans 9:27 — turn the increase into its opposite. Romans 9:27 reads the sand of the sea and concludes “a remnant shall be saved”; Isaiah 10:22, which it is quoting, adds “the consumption decreed shall overflow with righteousness”. Mormon 1:7 is the last sentence in the Book of Mormon in which the Nephites are numerous, and the next verse begins the war that ends at Cumorah with twenty-four survivors. If the phrase is Hosea's, the metalepsis is exact and bleak: the KJV's promise that a countless people will be called the sons of the living God, said of a people about to be counted down to a remnant, by the man who will do the counting (Mormon 6:11-15).

links.note: 'The people were as numerous almost, as it were the sand of the sea.' Recorded as an echo, not an allusion, because the phrase occurs in 7 KJV verses and no single one of them is demonstrable here; the hedge “almost” is Mormon's own and belongs to no source. It earns a row rather than an exclusion for two reasons. The wording is not the KJV's wording for an army — those verses say sea shore — so the choice is not simply the nearest military simile to hand; and the covenant sense of the phrase is the one that fits a narrator whose whole book is about a numerous people becoming a remnant.
links.whyNot: Seven KJV verses share the phrase and the Book of Mormon reproduces nothing else from any of them. A reader who takes “sand of the sea” as ordinary English for an uncountable multitude — which by 1830 it was — can decline this row without difficulty, and nothing in the verse compels Hosea over Genesis 32:12.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass in this year, there began to be a war between the Nephites, which consisted of the Nephites, and the Jacobites, and the Josephites, and the Zoramites: and this war was between the Nephites, and the Lamanites, and the Lemuelites, and the Ishmaelites.
Now the Lamanites, and the Lemuelites, and the Ishmaelites, were called Lamanites, and the two parties were Nephites and Lamanites.
And it came to pass that the war began to be among them, in the borders of Zarahemla, by the waters of Sidon.

And it came to pass that the Nephites had gathered together a great number of men, even to exceed the number of thirty thousand. And it came to pass that they did have in this same year a number of battles, in the which the Nephites did beat the Lamanites, and did slay many of them.
And it came to pass that the Lamanites withdrew their design, and there was peace settled in the land, and peace did remain for the space of about four years, that there were no blood shed.

But wickedness did prevail upon the face of the whole land, insomuch that the Lord did take away his beloved disciples, and the work of miracles and of healing did cease, because of the iniquity of the people.

links.text: To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues:

provenance.route: 1 Corinthians 12:9-10 and 13:8 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “working of miracles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:10; “gifts of healing” occurs in exactly 2, 1 Corinthians 12:9 and 12:30. Those are the only KJV verses that treat miracle and healing as distributed gifts rather than as events, and 1 Corinthians 13:8 is the only KJV verse that says such gifts cease. Mormon 1:13-14 has all three terms — miracles, healing, gifts — and the verb, in two consecutive sentences.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 12-13 is the KJV's only sustained account of spiritual gifts, and its one statement about their end is a consolation: they cease because “that which is perfect is come” (13:10), superseded by charity, which never faileth. Mormon 1:13-14 borrows the chapter's inventory and reverses its reason — the gifts cease not because something better has arrived but because of iniquity and unbelief — and the reversal is the argument of Mormon's own later writing. His son will reproduce Paul's list almost entire at Moroni 10:8-18, and Mormon's letter at Moroni 7:44-47 will end on charity in Paul's words; his own chapter at Mormon 9:7-25 will insist the gifts have not ceased. This verse is where that family argument starts, and it starts by describing the loss in the vocabulary of the chapter that catalogues the things lost.

links.note: 'The work of miracles and of healing did cease' (1:13); 'and there were no gifts from the Lord' (1:14). Three Pauline technical terms in Paul's own pairing: the working of miracles and the gifts of healing stand side by side in 1 Corinthians 12:9-10 and nowhere else in the KJV, and “cease” is 13:8's verb for what happens to them. High rather than certain because no clause is reproduced — the contact is a vocabulary set and a proposition, not a run of words, and Mormon has “work” where Paul has “working”.

pericopes.text: And there were no gifts from the Lord, and the Holy Ghost did not come upon any, because of their wickedness and unbelief.

links.text: And the child Samuel ministered unto the LORD before Eli. And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision.

provenance.route: 1 Samuel 3 → KJV → Book of Mormon (form, not wording)
provenance.other: “no open vision” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 3:1, and the Book of Mormon does not reproduce it or anything else from the chapter. The row is filed as figural for that reason.
provenance.significance: 1 Samuel 3 is the KJV's one narrative in which a dearth of revelation and the call of a child are the same event, told in that order: there was no open vision, and then the LORD called Samuel. Mormon 1:14-15 puts them in the same order in adjacent sentences — no gifts from the Lord, the Holy Ghost came upon none, 'And I, being fifteen years of age … I was visited of the Lord.' The chapter has already laid out the rest of the scene. An aged custodian who is about to pass out of the story hands the sacred things to a boy he has judged fit (1:2-4, and compare Ammaron's 'I perceive that thou art a sober child' with Eli's part in recognising who is speaking to Samuel); the boy is given a charge for a set later age; and the first thing the boy is eventually told to say is a word of judgment on the house he was raised in. What the type supplies that Mormon does not say is the outcome: Samuel's call ends the silence, and Mormon's does not.

links.note: 'And there were no gifts from the Lord, and the Holy Ghost did not come upon any, because of their wickedness and unbelief.' There is no verbal contact with 1 Samuel 3 and none is claimed. What is claimed is that the Book of Mormon has, in nineteen verses, assembled every element of the KJV's boy-called-in-a-time-of-silence scene and assembled them in the KJV's order, and that a reader who knows 1 Samuel 3 reads Mormon 1:15 differently for it. Moderate: the elements are individually unremarkable and the chapter would read much as it does if 1 Samuel 3 did not exist.
links.whyNot: A type-scene argument with no shared wording, in a chapter that already has better-evidenced links. The row would be withdrawn if it turned out that this sequence — a dearth of gifts, then a boy visited — is a standing Book of Mormon pattern with several instances, since a house formula is not an allusion.

pericopes.text: And I, being fifteen years of age, and being somewhat of a sober mind, therfore I was visited of the Lord, and tasted, and knew of the goodness of Jesus.

links.text: If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.

provenance.route: Psalm 34:8 → 1 Peter 2:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “tasted” occurs in exactly 8 KJV verses, of which three are theological rather than literal: Hebrews 6:4-5 and 1 Peter 2:3. Running mediation-check.py on Psalm 34:8 against its New Testament quotation at 1 Peter 2:3 gives one decisive divergence, and the Book of Mormon takes 1 Peter's side of it: the psalm has the imperative 'O taste and see', 1 Peter the finite past 'ye have tasted', and Mormon 'I … tasted, and knew'. The predicate goes the other way — Mormon's 'the goodness of Jesus' is nearer the psalm's 'that the LORD is good' than 1 Peter's 'gracious' — so the verse has 1 Peter's grammar and the psalm's noun.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 2:3 is not a free-standing sentence; it closes the clause that begins 'As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: if so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.' Recover that and the KJV supplies exactly what Mormon 1:15 is describing and does not say — a first taste, in infancy, that is the beginning of growth rather than its end. He is fifteen, in a chapter where the gifts have just been withdrawn from everyone else, and the one verse he sounds like is the verse about beginners. 1 Peter is also written to 'strangers scattered' (1:1) facing a trial, which is the situation of every reader Mormon is writing for.

links.note: 'Therefore I was visited of the Lord, and tasted, and knew of the goodness of Jesus.' The mediation is the finding here rather than the source: this is the psalm's most famous sentence arriving in the grammatical form its New Testament quotation gave it. Moderate, because the shared material is one verb plus a divergence of tense; a reader could reasonably say that 'taste' for religious experience is ordinary devotional English by 1830 and needs no source at all.
links.whyNot: The decisive point the mediation tool returns rests on grammatical form, not on distinctive vocabulary, and its own backbone score is zero shared words. That is thin evidence for a route, even where the route is the interesting part.

links.text: Thou shalt be visited of the LORD of hosts with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with storm and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire.

provenance.route: Isaiah 29:6 → KJV → 2 Nephi 27:2 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “visited of the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:6. The mediation is recorded through the earlier Book of Mormon text because Isaiah 29:6 is already quoted entire at 2 Nephi 27:2, where this catalogue adjudicates it as a certain quotation and where 'Thou shalt be visited' has already been changed to 'they shall be visited' — so the phrase exists inside Mormon's own record, in a third-person form nearer his own, as well as in Isaiah.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29 is the chapter the Book of Mormon reads as being about itself: the vision that becomes 'the words of a book that is sealed', the learned man who cannot read it and the unlearned man who is handed it (29:11-12), the marvellous work and a wonder (29:14). Mormon 1 is the chapter in which the sealing up begins — Ammaron hides the records unto the Lord (1:2), the boy who will finish the burying is chosen, and the boy has just been described as one who 'began to be learned somewhat after the manner of the learning of my people'. Against that, what the KJV's one visitation 'of the LORD' actually consists of is thunder, earthquake, storm and devouring fire on a city under siege. Mormon 1:15 gives the phrase its gracious sense; Mormon 6 gives it Isaiah's. The suggestion that the chapter is deliberately working Isaiah 29 is ours and is offered as a suggestion; the singleton is a fact.

links.note: 'I was visited of the Lord.' Four words, but they are the KJV's only occurrence of the construction, and the Book of Mormon has demonstrably had that verse in front of it before (2 Nephi 27:2). Moderate rather than high because the sense at the point of contact is inverted — see whyNot — and because 'visit' in the sense of a divine coming is not confined to this verse in the KJV; it is the particular passive with 'of the Lord' that is.
links.whyNot: Isaiah 29:6 is a threat. Ariel is besieged and will be visited with thunder and devouring fire; Mormon is visited and tastes the goodness of Jesus. A reader who applies the wrong-sense test that this register uses elsewhere — see the exclusion at Mormon 1:11 — could reasonably reject the row on that ground alone, and would be making the argument the catalogue itself usually makes. It is kept because the phrase is a singleton, because the source verse is one the Book of Mormon has already quoted, and because the judgment Isaiah threatens is the event this book ends with.

pericopes.text: And I did endeavor to preach unto this people, but my mouth was shut, and I were forbidden that I should preach unto them: for behold they had wilfully rebelled against their God, and the beloved disciples were taken away out of the land, because of their iniquity.

links.text: And I will make thy tongue cleave to the roof of thy mouth, that thou shalt be dumb, and shalt not be to them a reprover: for they are a rebellious house.

provenance.other: “my mouth was shut” occurs in no KJV verse, so the contact is not a phrase and the row does not pretend otherwise. “rebellious house”, Ezekiel's standing name for this audience, occurs in exactly 12 KJV verses, every one of them in Ezekiel. “remained there astonished among them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 3:15, against Mormon 1:17's 'But I did remain among them' — suggestive, and no more than that, since only the verb is shared.
provenance.significance: The King James Bible contains exactly one prophet whom God forbids to prophesy, and Ezekiel 3:26-27 is the passage: the tongue cleaves, the mouth is shut, the man is not to be a reprover, and the stated cause is that they are a rebellious house. Two things follow there that matter here. The silence is God's act, not the audience's — a prophet unheard is a commonplace, a prophet gagged by his own commission is not — and it is temporary: 'when I speak with thee, I will open thy mouth' (3:27). Mormon's mouth is opened on exactly those terms at Mormon 3:2, where the Lord says 'Cry unto this people'. The unstated correspondence is Ezekiel 3:15, which is what a silenced prophet does with the interval: he goes and sits where they sit and remains among them. Mormon 1:17 opens 'But I did remain among them', and it is the only reason the record exists.

links.note: 'And I did endeavor to preach unto this people, but my mouth was shut, and I were forbidden that I should preach unto them: for behold they had wilfully rebelled against their God.' Four elements in Ezekiel's order and with Ezekiel's logic: the attempt to speak, the shut mouth, the divine prohibition, and rebellion given as its cause. The vocabulary is not borrowed — 'rebelled' against Ezekiel's 'rebellious house' is the whole of the lexical overlap — which is why this is moderate and not high. Note the 1830 grammar, 'I were forbidden', which 1920 corrected to 'I was'; it is not a KJV reading and does not bear on the source, but it is the reading of the running text.
links.whyNot: No verbal run at all, and the notion of a prophet prevented from preaching is available without Ezekiel — Jeremiah 20:9, Amos 8:11-12 and 1 Samuel 3:1 all supply pieces of it. What confines the field to Ezekiel is the specific detail that God does the silencing and later lifts it, and a reader who thinks that detail is coincidence should decline the row.

pericopes.text: But I did remain among them, but I were forbidden that I should preach unto them, because of the hardness of their hearts; and because of the hardness of their hearts, the land was cursed for their sake.

links.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: “hardness of their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5. Check the pronoun before assuming it: “hardness of your hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is Matthew 19:8, on divorce. Mormon has the third person and therefore Mark. Running mediation-check.py on the two returns no decisive divergence, because they diverge nowhere the Book of Mormon reproduces; the pronoun is the whole test and the tool ignores single common words by design (ADJUDICATING §4).
provenance.significance: The catalogue has recorded this clause ten times before and the phrase itself needs no fresh argument; what is new is where Mormon puts it. In Mark 3:5 hardness of heart is the thing Jesus is grieved by and heals in spite of — the clause is a subordinate one, and the main verb is 'Stretch forth thine hand'. Mark 3:5 is the only KJV verse in which the hardness of their hearts and a healing stand in the same sentence. Mormon 1:13 has just reported that 'the work of miracles and of healing did cease', and four verses later gives the reason in the words of the verse where the healing happened anyway. The suppressed half of Mark 3:5 is the restored hand: the thing that no longer occurs. Ten previous narrators used the clause to explain why someone would not listen; Mormon is the first to use it to explain why the miracles stopped.

links.note: 'Because of the hardness of their hearts; and because of the hardness of their hearts, the land was cursed for their sake.' Five words of Mark 3:5 unaltered and twice over, from the sole KJV home of the phrase, with the pronoun correct. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six, but dependence is not deniable. The clause is by this point a Book of Mormon formula used in nine previous books; per ADJUDICATING §4 the row is written again because Mormon is a new book in a new hand, and the argument for the borrowing itself was made at 1 Nephi 2:18 and is not restated here.

links.text: And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;

provenance.route: Genesis 3:17 → KJV → 2 Nephi 1:7 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “cursed is the ground for thy sake” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:17; “for thy sake” alone occurs in exactly 9 and cannot carry a link. The mediation is through the earlier Book of Mormon text rather than direct: Mormon's 'the land was cursed for their sake' is verbally nearer 2 Nephi 1:7's 'cursed shall be the land for their sakes' — land for ground, plural possessor — than it is to Genesis, and this catalogue adjudicates the Genesis borrowing there and at Jacob 2:29.
provenance.significance: This is the sentence in which the Book of Mormon's central land doctrine is reported as executed. 2 Nephi 1:7 stated it as a condition of tenure, Genesis 3:17 supplied the words, and Samuel the Lamanite announced the curse as imminent at Helaman 13:17-23. Mormon 1:17 is the only place the book says flatly, in the past tense and without qualification, that it has now happened. What Genesis 3:17 contributes that the intervening statements do not is the content of a curse on ground: not destruction but withholding — the earth will no longer yield to the man who works it. The next sentence of Mormon 1 is about exactly that, treasure put into the ground and not given back.

links.note: 'The land was cursed for their sake.' Six words against Genesis 3:17's 'cursed is the ground for thy sake', with the noun and the possessor changed; the shared material is the passive curse plus the 'for … sake' construction, which is why this is moderate rather than high. What earns the row at Mormon 1:17 rather than a silent cross-reference to 2 Nephi 1:7 is the pairing: the same sentence gives Mark 3:5's hardness of heart as the reason the land is cursed, so Eden's formula is being used to say that a people's disposition, not an act, has spoiled the ground under them.

pericopes.text: And these Gaddianton robbers, which were among the Lamanites, did infest the land, insomuch that the inhabitants thereof began to hide up their treasures in the earth; and they became slippery, because the Lord had cursed the land, that they could not hold them, nor retain them again.

links.text: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:

provenance.other: “treasures upon earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 6:19, and so does “break through and steal”. “treasures in the earth” occurs in no KJV verse: the Book of Mormon's preposition is its own, and it is doing different work, since Matthew's treasure is laid up above ground where thieves can reach it and Mormon's is buried to keep them off. The nearest KJV verse for burying is Matthew 25:18, where the unprofitable servant 'digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money'.
provenance.significance: Samuel the Lamanite built the curse of slippery treasures out of Matthew 6:19-20 — adjudicated at Helaman 13:19 — but he used only half the passage. He took the treasure and the losing of it and left the thieves behind, since Matthew's moth, rust and burglars were replaced by the ground itself. Mormon 1:18 is the report of that curse coming to pass, and it restores the missing half in the first clause: the reason anybody is burying treasure at all is that 'these Gaddianton robbers … did infest the land'. So the Sermon's two agents of loss are split across the two passages and the fulfilment supplies what the prophecy dropped. The result is a bleaker sentence than Matthew's. In Matthew you may lose earthly treasure to thieves; here you lose it to the thieves if you keep it and to the ground if you hide it, and the second loss is the Lord's doing.

links.note: 'These Gaddianton robbers … did infest the land, insomuch that the inhabitants thereof began to hide up their treasures in the earth; and they became slippery, because the Lord had cursed the land.' Written as a full link rather than a back-reference because Mormon is a new book and a new narrator (ADJUDICATING §4), and because what is here is not the Helaman 13 borrowing repeated but its other half: the thieves of Matthew 6:19, absent from Samuel's oracle, present in the fulfilment. Moderate, on the same grounds as the Helaman row — the shared material is the noun and the antithesis, not a clause. Note the 1830 spelling 'Gaddianton', which 1920 regularised to 'Gadianton'.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that there were sorceries, and witchcrafts, and magics: and the power of the evil one was wrought upon all the face of the land, even unto the fulfilling of all the words of Abinadi, and also Samuel the Lamanite.—

And it came to pass that in that same year, there began to be a war again between the Nephites and the Lamanites. And notwithstanding I being young, was large in stature, therefore the people of Nephi appointed me that I should be their leader, or the leader of their armies.
Therefore it came to pass that in my sixteenth year, I did go forth at the head of an army of the Nephites, against the Lamanites; therefore three hundred and twenty and six years had passed away.

And it came to pass that in the three hundred and twenty and seventh year, the Lamanites did come upon us with exceeding great power, insomuch that they did frighten my armies; therefore they would not fight, and they began to retreat towards the north countries.

And it came to pass that we did come to the city of Angelah, and we did take possession of the city, and make preparations to defend ourselves against the Lamanites. And it came to pass that we did fortify the city with our mights; but notwithstanding all our fortifications, the Lamanites did come upon us, and did drive us out of the city.
And they did also drive us forth out of the land of David.
And we marched forth, and came to the land of Joshua, which was in the borders west, by the seashore.
And it came to pass that we did gather in our people as fast as it were possible, that we might get them together in one body.

But behold, the land was filled with robbers and with Lamanites; and notwithstanding the great destruction which hung over my people, they did not repent of their evil doings; therefore there was blood and carnage spread throughout all the face of the land, both on the part of the Nephites, and also on the part of the Lamanites; and it was one complete revolution throughout all the face of the land.

provenance.other: “filled with violence” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 6:11 and 6:13, and both are the indictment of the generation of the flood. The n-gram stream offered Exodus 1:7 for the same clause on a five-word run, “the land was filled with”, which is the right string attached to the wrong scene; it is displaced in the register at this verse.
provenance.significance: This is the frame the whole chapter is built in, and it is laid down in three pieces rather than one. Genesis 6 is the King James Bible's single account of an entire population destroyed for having filled the land with violence, and Mormon 2 supplies its three load-bearing clauses in order. At 2:8 the land is filled — “the land was filled with robbers and with Lamanites … there was blood and carnage spread throughout all the face of the land”. At 2:13 the patience runs out in Genesis 6:3's own terms: “the Lord would not always suffer them to take happiness in sin” against “My spirit shall not always strive with man”, and “always strive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. At 2:26 the withdrawal is complete — “the spirit of the Lord did not abide in us”. The Book of Mormon makes the same use of Genesis 6:3 at the other national extinction it narrates, and there it is explicit: Ether 15:19, “the spirit of the Lord had ceased striving with them”. Mormon wrote that sentence too.

links.note: “The land was filled with robbers and with Lamanites; and notwithstanding the great destruction which hung over my people, they did not repent of their evil doings.” No clause is reproduced and the link is proposed on the collocation and the setting: a land filled with violence, a destruction hanging over it, and a people who will not repent. What raises it above a common phrase is that the two other Genesis 6 clauses turn up in the same chapter at 2:13 and 2:26, and that this book has used Genesis 6:3 for exactly this purpose before. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; it is not a quotation and is not offered as one.
links.text: The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence.

pericopes.text: And now the Lamanites had a king, and his name was Aaron; and he came against us with an army of forty and four thousand. And behold, I withstood him, with forty and two thousand. And it came to pass that I beat him with my army, that he fled before me. And behold, all this was done, and three hundred and thirty years had passed away.

And it came to pass that the Nephites began to repent of their iniquity, and began to cry even as had been prophesied by Samuel the prophet: for behold no man could keep that which was his own, for the thieves, and the robbers, and the rumderers, and the magic art, and the witchcraft which was in the land.
Thus there began to be a mourning and a lamentation in all the land, because of these things; and more especially among the people of Nephi.

And it came to pass that when I, Mormon, saw their lamentation, and their mourning, and their sorrowing before the Lord, my heart did begin to rejoice within me: knowing the mercies and the long suffering of the Lord, therefore supposing that he would be merciful unto them, that they would again become a righteous people.

But behold this my joy was vain, for their sorrowing was not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God, but it was rather the sorrowing of the damned, because the Lord would not always suffer them to take happiness in sin.

provenance.other: “goodness of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Psalm 52:1, where it “endureth continually”, and Romans 2:4, where it “leadeth thee to repentance”. Only Romans joins the phrase to repentance, and joining the phrase to repentance is what Mormon 2:13 does. “goodness and forbearance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: Romans 2:4 is a question — “despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?” — and Mormon 2:12-13 answers it in both halves. The triad comes first: at 2:12 Mormon rejoices, “knowing the mercies and the long suffering of the Lord”, which is Paul's second and third terms with “mercies” for “forbearance”. Then the conclusion, negated: their sorrowing was “not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God”. What the transfer does is move Paul's participle. In Romans it is the sinner who does not know; in Mormon 2 the historian knows, and watches the people despise the goodness anyway. Recover the next verse and you have the chapter's plot in advance: “after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath” (Romans 2:5), which is what 2:15's “day of grace was past” records as having happened.

links.note: “Their sorrowing was not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God.” The two content words Romans 2:4 puts together are the two words this clause puts together, and the preceding verse supplies the rest of Paul's triad in Paul's order. Nothing here reaches a reproduced clause, so it is catalogued as an allusion and not a quotation, and it is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold; the case is the collocation and the sequence, not the length. Note that 2:13 carries a second and independent New Testament source in the same sentence — see the 2 Corinthians 7:10 row — and that the two are not rivals: Romans supplies the goodness that ought to have led to repentance, Corinthians the sorrow that failed to be it.
links.text: Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?

provenance.other: “godly sorrow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “sorrow of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them 2 Corinthians 7:10; “sorrowed to repentance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 7:9, the verse before it.
provenance.significance: Paul's antithesis, kept whole and renamed at one term. 2 Corinthians 7:9-10 runs: “Now I rejoice … that ye sorrowed to repentance … For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.” Mormon 2:12-13 runs the same three moves in the same order and inverts each one. He rejoices — “my heart did begin to rejoice within me” — and then withdraws it: “this my joy was vain, for their sorrowing was not unto repentance”. Paul's other member then arrives under a new name: where Paul had “the sorrow of the world”, Mormon has “the sorrowing of the damned”. The renaming is the argument. Paul's world-sorrow “worketh death” as a spiritual outcome; Mormon's damned-sorrow works death in the next sentence and literally, at 2:14, where the sorrowing people “did curse God, and wish to die”. The metalepsis runs the other way too: to read “the sorrowing of the damned” as a considered phrase rather than an insult, a reader has to recover the verse that says what the alternative would have been.

links.note: “Their sorrowing was not unto repentance … but it was rather the sorrowing of the damned.” The sentence is built on the one KJV verse that distinguishes two kinds of sorrow by their outcome, and it keeps the distinction, the order, and the framing rejoicing while substituting for the name of the second kind. Three separate KJV singletons stand behind two verses of Mormon 2. Below Skousen's threshold and not one of his 36; it is an allusion, not a quotation.
links.text: For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.

pericopes.text: And they did not come unto Jesus with broken hearts and contrite spirits, but they did curse God, and wish to die. Nevertheless they would struggle with the sword for their lives.

provenance.route: Job 2:9 (+ Revelation 9:6) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “curse God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 2:9. The neighbouring verses of Job say something else each time — 1:5 has “cursed God in their hearts”, and 1:11 and 2:5 have “curse thee to thy face” — so the bare imperative is Job 2:9's alone. “desire to die” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 9:6.
provenance.significance: The Nephites take the advice Job refused. Job 2:9 is the King James Bible's only “curse God”, it is spoken by Job's wife, it is a two-part counsel — curse God, and die — and the point of the scene is that Job does not take it: “In all this did not Job sin with his lips” (2:10). Mormon 2:14 reports a whole nation doing what one man would not, and preserves the two-part shape: “they did curse God, and wish to die”. Then the sentence refuses to end there. “Nevertheless they would struggle with the sword for their lives” is the paradox of the fifth trumpet, where “men seek death, and shall not find it; and shall desire to die, and death shall flee from them” (Revelation 9:6). The KJV has exactly two places where people want to die and do not get to; Mormon 2:14 has both of them, in one verse, in that order.

links.note: “They did curse God, and wish to die. Nevertheless they would struggle with the sword for their lives.” Two words reproduced from a KJV singleton, with the singleton's own syntax — the imperative pair — carried across intact. The Book of Mormon changes “die” to “wish to die”, and in doing so moves from Job's scene into Revelation's, where wishing to die is precisely what is not granted. Short of a reproduced clause and so catalogued as an allusion, not a quotation; nowhere near Skousen's threshold.
links.text: Then said his wife unto him, Dost thou still retain thine integrity? curse God, and die.

provenance.route: Psalm 34:18 → KJV → Book of Mormon (2 Nephi 2:7 onward) → Mormon 2:14
provenance.other: “broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “contrite spirit” occurs in exactly two, Psalm 34:18 and Isaiah 66:2; only Psalm 34:18 has both, in that order, which is the Book of Mormon's order. Psalm 51:17's pairing is different — “a broken and a contrite heart” — and does not produce the formula. mediation-check.py was run against 1 Peter 3:12, which quotes Psalm 34 in the New Testament, and confirms that is not the route: 1 Peter's quotation stops at Psalm 34:16, two verses short of this one, so no New Testament form of the sentence exists to be followed.
provenance.significance: The proximate model is the book's own, and what Mormon does to it is the finding. “A broken heart and a contrite spirit” is a fixed formula here — five occurrences from 2 Nephi 2:7 to Moroni 6:2 — and Mormon himself is the editor who copied the two occurrences that matter most, where the risen Christ makes the phrase the terms of admission: “whoso cometh unto me with a broken heart and a contrite spirit, him will I baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost” (3 Nephi 9:20), and “come unto me with a broken heart and a contrite spirit” (3 Nephi 12:19). Mormon 2:14 is that invitation negated and pluralised: “they did not come unto Jesus with broken hearts and contrite spirits”. It is the only place in the Book of Mormon where the formula appears in the plural, and the plural is what turns an offer made to a person into a verdict on a nation. The man who transcribed the invitation writes the refusal.

links.note: The wording is the Psalm's and the sentence is the book's. Catalogued at Psalm 34:18 because that is where the two phrases stand together in the KJV, but the route runs through the Book of Mormon's own formula — and specifically through 3 Nephi 9:20 and 12:19, which Mormon abridged, and which this verse contradicts clause for clause. The dependence on the Psalm is not in dispute; the confidence is set at moderate because what Mormon 2:14 is directly answering is 3 Nephi and not the Psalter.
links.text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that my sorrow did return unto me again, and I saw that the day of grace was past with them, both temporally and spiritually: for I saw thousands of them hewn down in open rebellion against their God, and heaped up as dung upon the face of the land. And thus three hundred and forty and four years had passed away.

provenance.other: “dung upon the face of the” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: 2 Kings 9:37 (“of the field”, of Jezebel's carcase), Jeremiah 8:2 and Jeremiah 16:4 (both “of the earth”). Mormon 2:15 reads “as dung upon the face of the land”, and “as dung upon the face” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Kings 9:37 and Jeremiah 16:4. Of those two only Jeremiah 16:4 is about a whole nation's unburied war dead. Jeremiah 25:33 has the image without the phrase — “they shall be dung upon the ground”.
provenance.significance: Take the rest of Jeremiah 16:4 and you have the rest of Mormon 2 and 4: “They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented; neither shall they be buried … and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine; and their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of heaven, and for the beasts of the earth.” Mormon's people die by the sword, unburied, in numbers he counts in thousands. The one substitution is the book's standing one: Jeremiah's “earth” becomes “land”, the word this record uses for its own promised country. And the sentence Jeremiah 16:4 belongs to is a prohibition on mourning — the LORD forbids Jeremiah to lament the dead — which is worth recovering, because mourning is what Mormon has been doing since 2:11 and what he will not stop doing.

links.note: “I saw thousands of them hewn down in open rebellion against their God, and heaped up as dung upon the face of the land.” Six words from a phrase the KJV uses three times, with one noun changed, in the one context where the KJV itself uses it. “hewn down” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and is not decisive on its own (three of them are the axe at the root of the trees, Matthew 3:10, 7:19 and Luke 3:9, which is a different figure); the dung clause is what carries the link. Short of a reproduced clause and so an allusion, not a quotation.
links.text: They shall die of grievous deaths; they shall not be lamented; neither shall they be buried; but they shall be as dung upon the face of the earth: and they shall be consumed by the sword, and by famine; and their carcases shall be meat for the fowls of heaven, and for the beasts of the earth.

provenance.other: “harvest is past” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The phrase Mormon 2:15 actually uses, ‘the day of grace’, is in no KJV verse at all and in no other Book of Mormon verse either — this is its single occurrence in the book, which is why no rarity count can carry the link and the case has to be made from the cluster.
provenance.alternative: The other place the KJV bounds a season of salvation is 2 Corinthians 6:2, ‘now is the day of salvation’, quoting Isaiah 49:8; “day of salvation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. mediation-check.py was run on Mormon 2:15 against Isaiah 49:8 and 2 Corinthians 6:2 and returns nothing usable: its single ‘decisive’ point is the word ‘Thus’, which in this verse belongs to the dating formula ‘And thus three hundred and forty and four years had passed away’ and has no bearing on anything. The Isaiah/Corinthians route is recorded here and declined.
provenance.significance: The argument is a cluster, not a phrase. Three separate points of contact with one short passage of Jeremiah fall inside Mormon 2. Jeremiah 8:2 supplies the dung idiom in this very verse (see the Jeremiah 16:4 row, where 8:2 is one of only three KJV verses with the phrase). Jeremiah 8:20 supplies the figure of a season of rescue that has closed while the people are still alive to notice — ‘The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved’ against ‘the day of grace was past with them’. And Jeremiah 8:19, ‘the voice of the cry of the daughter of my people because of them that dwell in a far country’, is tied for the highest-scoring machine candidate anywhere in this chapter, keyed at 2:27 to ‘my heart did sorrow because of this the great calamity of my people’. Jeremiah 8:18-9:1 is the King James Bible's set piece of a prophet who cannot save his people and will not stop grieving them — ‘When I would comfort myself against sorrow, my heart is faint in me’ — and that is Mormon's posture from 2:12 to 2:27 without interruption.

links.note: ‘The day of grace was past with them, both temporally and spiritually.’ Proposed under the generative posture (CONVENTIONS §0a). The verbal contact with Jeremiah 8:20 alone is one word, ‘past’, and would not be worth recording; what makes it worth recording is that it stands in the same sentence as a phrase drawn from Jeremiah 8:2 and two lines above a machine-found contact with Jeremiah 8:19. The chapter reaches for one page of Jeremiah three times, and this is the middle instance.
links.whyNot: One shared common word. ‘Day of grace’ is a preacher's phrase with a long life in English outside the Bible, and a writer could arrive at ‘the day of grace was past’ with no verse in mind at all. The cluster is the whole case; a reader who thinks the Jeremiah 8:2 contact at the other end of the verse is coincidence should decline this row with it.
links.text: The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that in the three hundred and forty and fifth year, the Nephites did begin to flee before the Lamanites, and they were pursued until they came even to the land of Jashon, before it were possible to stop them in their retreat.

And now the city of Jashon was near the land where Ammaron had deposited the records unto the Lord, that they might not be destroyed. And behold I had gone according to the word of Ammaron, and taken the plates of Nephi, and did make a record according to the words of Ammaron.

And upon the plates of Nephi I did make a full account of all the wickedness and abominations; but upon these plates I did forbear to make a full account of their wickedness and abominations: for behold, a continual scene of wickedness and abominations has been before mine eyes ever since I have been sufficient to behold the ways of man.
And wo is me, because of their wickedness: for my heart has been filled with sorrow because of their wickedness, all my days; nevertheless, I know that I shall be lifted up at the last day.

provenance.other: “Woe is me” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses — Psalm 120:5, Isaiah 6:5, Jeremiah 4:31, 10:19, 15:10 and 45:3, and Micah 7:1 — four of them in Jeremiah. What narrows it to 45:3 is the continuation. Mormon 2:19 goes on ‘my heart has been filled with sorrow … all my days’; Jeremiah 45:3 goes on ‘for the LORD hath added grief to my sorrow; I fainted in my sighing, and I find no rest’. None of the other six pairs the cry with sorrow.
provenance.significance: Recover the speaker and the placement becomes the argument. Jeremiah 45 is a four-verse oracle addressed not to the prophet but to Baruch, the scribe who wrote the book down — the King James Bible's one lament by a professional keeper of a record about the record he has had to keep. It ends with a personal exemption from the general ruin: ‘I will bring evil upon all flesh … but thy life will I give unto thee for a prey in all places whither thou goest’ (45:5). Mormon 2:19 sits two verses after Mormon has described going to the hill Shim, taking up the plates of Nephi and beginning to write (2:17), and one verse after he says what is on them: ‘a continual scene of wickedness and abominations … ever since I have been sufficient to behold the ways of man’ (2:18). Then the lament, and then the same personal exemption in the book's own idiom: ‘nevertheless, I know that I shall be lifted up at the last day’. Scribe, record, grief, exemption — in that order, in both places.

links.note: ‘And wo is me, because of their wickedness: for my heart has been filled with sorrow because of their wickedness, all my days.’ Three common words and a structural coincidence, offered under CONVENTIONS §0a because the coincidence is unusually specific: of the seven KJV verses that say ‘Woe is me’, the one that pairs it with sorrow is also the only one spoken by a record-keeper, and it is placed where the Book of Mormon's own record-keeper has just described taking up his plates. The 1830 spells it ‘wo’, which is the first edition's usual form and not the KJV's; the spelling is not evidence either way here.
links.whyNot: ‘Woe is me’ is a stock cry with seven KJV homes and no distinctive vocabulary beyond it, and grief over a doomed people is the natural thing for Mormon to say at this point whether or not he has read Jeremiah 45. The reading rests entirely on the placement after 2:17-18, and a reader who thinks the placement is accident should decline the row.
links.text: Thou didst say, Woe is me now! for the LORD hath added grief to my sorrow; I fainted in my sighing, and I find no rest.

provenance.route: John 11:24 (+ 6:40, 12:32) → KJV → Book of Mormon (1 Nephi 16:2 onward) → Mormon 2:19
provenance.other: “at the last day” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, and all five are in John: 6:39, 6:40, 6:44, 6:54 and 11:24. Four of them read ‘raise him up at the last day’; only 11:24 puts the phrase after ‘I know that’ — ‘I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day’ — and “I know that he shall rise” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Mormon 2:19 reads ‘I know that I shall be lifted up at the last day’. The verb is from John's other resurrection idiom, 12:32, ‘if I be lifted up from the earth’.
provenance.significance: Two things worth separating. The phrase itself is house style: ‘lifted up at the last day’ occurs nine times in the Book of Mormon, from 1 Nephi 16:2 through Alma to 3 Nephi 27:22, so it reaches Mormon 2:19 as a formula the book had already fixed and not as a fresh reach for John. What is local to this verse is the frame — the confession ‘I know that’ in the mouth of a mourner, which is Martha's at Lazarus's grave and no one else's in the KJV, placed in the mouth of a man who has just said his heart has been filled with sorrow all his days.
provenance.alternative: MEDIATION FLAGGED, and left undecided rather than forced. The schema's `mediation` vocabulary offers `OT-via-earlier-BoM` for a source the book reaches through its own earlier text, but it has no corresponding value for a NEW TESTAMENT source reached that way, which is what this is. `direct-NT` would assert a reach for John that the nine-fold internal formula makes unlikely; `OT-via-earlier-BoM` would misdescribe John as Old Testament. The field is therefore set `uncertain` and this note says what it would otherwise say: NT-via-earlier-BoM. CONVENTIONS §0's rule against inventing a sixth confidence level is taken to apply to the mediation vocabulary too. For Wilson: this will recur wherever a New Testament formula fixed early in the book is reused late, which in Mormon and Moroni is often.

links.note: ‘Nevertheless, I know that I shall be lifted up at the last day.’ The five-word run is John's, exclusively; the sentence around it is the Book of Mormon's own, nine times over. Recorded at moderate confidence because the dependence on John is not in doubt and the directness of it is — the interesting question here is not whether the phrase comes from John but through what, and the answer is the book's own repertoire. See the mediation flag in `provenance.alternative`.
links.text: Martha saith unto him, I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that in this year the people of Nephi again were hunted and driven. And it came to pass that we were driven forth until we had come northward to the land which was called Shem.
And it came to pass that we did fortify the city of Shem, and we did gather in our people as much as it were possible, that perhaps we might save them from destruction.
And it came to pass in the three hundred and forty and sixth year, they began to come upon us again.

And it came to pass that I did speak unto my people, and did urge them with great energy, that they would stand boldly before the Lamanites, and fight for their wives, and their children, and their houses, and their homes.

provenance.route: Nehemiah 4:14 → KJV → Book of Mormon, fused with the book's own war formula from Alma 43:45
provenance.other: “your wives, and your houses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 4:14: ‘fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses’. The n-gram stream proposed 2 Chronicles 20:13 on a five-word run, ‘their wives, and their children’; that verse has the family list and no fighting in it, and it is displaced in the register at this verse.
provenance.significance: The seam is visible in the English. Mormon 2:23 reads ‘fight for their wives, and their children, and their houses, and their homes’ — and houses and homes are the same thing, a redundancy no careful writer produces from a single model. The Book of Mormon's own war formula, set at Alma 43:45, is ‘fighting for their homes, and their liberties, their wives, and their children’: homes, wives, children. Nehemiah 4:14's is wives and houses. Mormon 2:23 contains every term of both lists, and the surplus word is Nehemiah's. The setting agrees at every point: two verses earlier, at 2:21, ‘we did fortify the city of Shem, and we did gather in our people’, which is Nehemiah 4 exactly — a wall going up under threat, a commander who calls the people together and tells them not to be afraid, ‘remember the LORD, which is great and terrible, and fight for’ what is theirs. What the borrowing then measures is a failure. Nehemiah's people finish the wall. Mormon's, at 2:24, are aroused ‘somewhat to vigor’, and the campaign ends four verses later with the strength of the Lord withdrawn.

links.note: ‘And did urge them with great energy, that they would stand boldly before the Lamanites, and fight for their wives, and their children, and their houses, and their homes.’ A KJV singleton phrase, an imperative to fight, and a city being fortified against a besieger, all in three verses. The doublet ‘houses … homes’ is the evidence that this is a fusion rather than a straight borrowing: the Nephite formula and the Nehemiah verse were both in view, and both got written down. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his 36.
links.text: And I looked, and rose up, and said unto the nobles, and to the rulers, and to the rest of the people, Be not ye afraid of them: remember the LORD, which is great and terrible, and fight for your brethren, your sons, and your daughters, your wives, and your houses.

pericopes.text: And my words did arouse them somewhat to vigor, insomuch that they did not flee from before the Lamanites, but did stand with boldness against them.

And it came to pass that we did contend with an army of thirty thousand, against an army of fifty thousand. And it came to pass that we did stand before them with such firmness, that they did flee from before us.

And it came to pass that when they had fled, we did pursue them with our armies, and did meet them again, and did beat them; nevertheless the strength of the Lord was not with us: yea, we were left to ourselves, that the spirit of the Lord did not abide in us; therefore we had become weak, like unto our brethren.

provenance.other: “become weak” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 14:10 and Judges 16:17. Isaiah 14:10 is the one that supplies the comparison as well: “like unto us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “become weak as” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them Isaiah 14:10 — ‘Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?’ Mormon 2:26 has ‘we had become weak, like unto our brethren’, which fuses Isaiah's two clauses into one. Judges 16:17's comparison is different, ‘be like any other man’, and “like any other man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.mt: 2 Nephi 24:10 reproduces Isaiah 14:10 word for word (the only difference is the capital on the second ‘Art’), so the wording itself cannot decide between the KJV and the Book of Mormon's own Isaiah block. The mediation call is made on availability rather than on the text: the book contains this sentence at 2 Nephi 24:10, and Mormon is the abridger of the record that contains it.
provenance.significance: Two sources, doing two different jobs, and both worth having. Isaiah 14:10 gives the words: it is the taunt the dead kings raise over the king of Babylon as he comes down to them, and the whole force of it is a comparison — you are now like us. Mormon 2:26 keeps the comparison and changes its object: ‘we had become weak, like unto our brethren’, and ‘our brethren’ in this book means the Lamanites. What the sentence concedes is that nothing but the strength of the Lord had ever distinguished the two nations from each other, which is the thesis Mormon's abridgement argues from here to chapter 6. Judges 16 gives the situation: Samson is the KJV's one man whose strength is not his own, who loses it and does not notice — ‘he wist not that the LORD was departed from him’ (16:20) — and whose loss is stated as ‘I shall become weak, and be like any other man’ (16:17). Mormon's army wins the battle in the first half of this verse and loses the strength in the second, and does not find out until later. And there is a third layer, internal and pointed: 1 Nephi 4:31 describes Nephi as ‘a man large in stature, and also having received much strength of the Lord’. Both halves of that self-description are in Mormon 2 — ‘I being young, was large in stature’ at 2:1, and the strength of the Lord here, in the negative. ‘Large in stature’ is not a KJV phrase; it occurs three times in the Book of Mormon, twice of Nephi (1 Nephi 2:16, 4:31) and once of Mormon. The chapter gives its last general Nephi's body in verse 1 and takes Nephi's strength away in verse 26.

links.note: ‘Nevertheless the strength of the Lord was not with us: yea, we were left to ourselves, that the spirit of the Lord did not abide in us; therefore we had become weak, like unto our brethren.’ Two KJV singletons and a two-verse phrase, all from one verse of Isaiah, compressed into one clause. Isaiah 14:10 asks its question in two parallel members and Mormon 2:26 answers with both members joined — become weak, like unto — which is the sort of compression that shows a source being used rather than a phrase being remembered. Judges 16 is catalogued as composite rather than as the source because it supplies the story and not the words; the strength that departs unnoticed is Samson's, but ‘like unto’ is Isaiah's. Below Skousen's threshold; an allusion, not a quotation.
links.text: All they shall speak and say unto thee, Art thou also become weak as we? art thou become like unto us?

pericopes.text: And my heart did sorrow because of this the great calamity of my people; because of their wickedness and their abominations. But behold we did go forth against the Lamanites, and the robbers of Gaddianton, until we had again taken possession of the lands of our inheritance.

And the three hundred and forty and ninth year had passed away. And in the three hundred and fiftieth year, we made a treaty with the Lamanites and the robbers of Gaddianton, in the which we did get the lands of our inheritance divided.
And the Lamanites did give unto us the land northward; yea, even to the narrow passage which led into the land southward. And we did give unto the Lamanites all the land southward.

And it came to pass that the Lamanites did not come to battle again until ten years more had passed away. And behold, I had employed my people, the Nephites, in preparing their lands and their arms against the time of battle.
And it came to pass that the Lord did say unto me, Cry unto this people repent ye, and come unto me and be ye baptized, and build up again my church, and ye shall be spared.

And I did cry unto this people, but it was in vain, and they did not realise that it was the Lord that had spared them, and granted unto them a chance for repentance. And behold they did harden their hearts against the Lord their God.

And it came to pass that after this tenth year had passed away, making, in the whole, three hundred and sixty years from the coming of Christ, the king of the Lamanites sent an epistle unto me, which gave unto me to know that they were preparing to come again to battle against us.

And it came to pass that I did cause my people that they should gather themselves together at the land Desolation, to a city which was in the borders, by the narrow pass which lead into the land southward.
And there we did place our armies, that we might stop the armies of the Lamanites, that they might not get possession of any of our lands; therefore we did fortify against them with all our force.

And it came to pass that in the three hundred and sixty and first year, the Lamanites did come down to the city of Desolation to battle, against us. And it came to pass that in that year, we did beat them, insomuch that they did return to their own lands again.
And in the three hundred and sixty and second year, they did come down again to battle. And we did beat them again, and did slay a great number of them, and their dead was cast into the sea.

And now because of this great thing which my people, the Nephites, had done, they began to boast in their own strength, and began to swear before the heavens that they would avenge themselves of the blood of their brethren which had been slain by their enemies.

links.text: Thou sayest, Lo, thou hast smitten the Edomites; and thine heart lifteth thee up to boast: abide now at home; why shouldest thou meddle to thine hurt, that thou shouldest fall, even thou, and Judah with thee?

provenance.other: “boast in their own strength” is in no KJV verse; “in their own strength” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses. The phrase is the Book of Mormon's own, and it occurs in exactly two Book of Mormon verses — Mosiah 11:19 and this one — which is the fact this row rests on. “the blood of their brethren” likewise occurs in no KJV verse, and of its five Book of Mormon occurrences two are Mosiah 11:19 and Mormon 3:9. The KJV end of the chain is the one already catalogued at Mosiah 11:19: “thine heart lifteth thee up to boast”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 25:19.
provenance.significance: This is the clearest case in the chapter of CONVENTIONS §7's `OT-via-earlier-BoM`, and it is available because Mormon is the abridger of Mosiah. Mosiah 11:19 reads: after 'this great victory' Noah's people 'were lifted up in the pride of their hearts; they did boast in their own strength' and 'did delight in blood, and the shedding of the blood of their brethren.' Mormon 3:9 reads: after 'this great thing which my people, the Nephites, had done, they began to boast in their own strength' and swore to 'avenge themselves of the blood of their brethren.' Two rare non-biblical collocations, in the same order, in the only two verses of the book that carry either. Whatever the Bible is doing here, it reaches Mormon 3 through a Book of Mormon page Mormon himself cut down; the narrator is quoting his own abridgement of a wicked king's army against his own. The 2 Chronicles material is what stands behind that page — Amaziah told, after smiting Edom, that his heart lifts him up to boast and that he will fall — and it is the same warning delivered at one further remove.

links.note: The chapter's turn. Two victories (3:7, 3:8) produce the boast, and the boast produces the oath of vengeance that costs Mormon his command four verses later. The verbal case is not with the KJV at all: neither 'boast in their own strength' nor 'the blood of their brethren' is a King James phrase, and the two of them appear together in exactly one other place in the Book of Mormon, Mosiah 11:19, where they describe Noah's soldiers after a victory of their own. The catalogue has already put 2 Chronicles 25:19 behind that verse; this row records that Mormon 3:9 reaches it by way of Mosiah rather than directly, which is why the mediation is `OT-via-earlier-BoM` and why `kjvSpecific` is 'uncertain' — there is no KJV English here to be specific to. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not a candidate for any quotation list.
links.whyNot: The whole weight is on a two-phrase coincidence with one other Book of Mormon verse, and a writer describing a second army boasting after a second victory has reason to reuse his own words without any of it being citation. A reader may take Mosiah 11:19 and Mormon 3:9 as two applications of a house style rather than a chain.

links.text: And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.

provenance.other: “vaunt themselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “mine own hand hath saved me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them Judges 7:2. Not a word of either survives into Mormon 3:9; what survives is the proposition.
provenance.significance: Judges 7:2 is the only verse in the Bible in which God states a policy about the boast of self-sufficiency: he will not give the victory while the army is large enough to claim it. The policy runs one way in Judges — God shrinks Gideon's force to three hundred so that the deliverance cannot be misread — and Mormon 3 runs it the other way and to the end. The Nephites win twice, boast, and are then deprived not of soldiers but of their commander: Mormon resigns at 3:11 for exactly the reason Gideon's army was cut down. Recover Judges 7 and the resignation stops looking like a private moral protest and starts looking like the withdrawal Judges 7:2 threatens.

links.note: No verbal contact, which is why this is an echo and why `kjvSpecific` is 'no'. It earns a row on the strength of the proposition being unique: the KJV says once, and only here, that a victory may be withheld to prevent a people saying that their own hand saved them, and Mormon 3:9 is a people saying it after two victories. The Leviticus 26:8 row at Mosiah 11:19 is the model for this kind of entry — a covenant statement about battlefield arithmetic standing behind a Nephite boast with none of its words surviving.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal at all. Boasting after a victory needs no source, and 'their own strength' is Zeniff's phrase at Mosiah 10:11 before it is anybody's in the KJV.

pericopes.text: And they did swear by the heavens, and also by the throne of God, that they would go up to battle against their enemies, and would cut them off from the face of the land.

links.text: And he that shall swear by heaven, sweareth by the throne of God, and by him that sitteth thereon.

provenance.route: Matthew 23:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the same prohibition also reaches Mormon through his own abridgement at 3 Nephi 12:34-36
provenance.other: “swear by heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “sweareth by the throne” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Matthew 23:22; “the throne of God” occurs in exactly six. Matthew 5:34 has heaven and the throne in apposition — 'neither by heaven; for it is God's throne' — one object of the oath named twice. Matthew 23:22 has them coordinated as two things a man swears by. Mormon 3:10 reads 'swear by the heavens, and also by the throne of God', which is Matthew 23:22's coordination and not Matthew 5:34's apposition. tools/mediation-check.py returns no genuine discrimination between the two verses, because both of its 'decisive' points are places where the Book of Mormon simply has neither continuation; the syntax is the discriminator, not the tool.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 5:34-35, via 3 Nephi 12:34-36, which Mormon abridged himself.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis in Hays's sense, and the Book of Mormon has arranged the recovery for the reader four verses later. 3:14 says the Nephites 'had sworn by all that had been forbidden them' — naming a prohibition without quoting it, which only works if the prohibition can be recovered. It can be recovered twice over: from Matthew, where the two oaths of Mormon 3:10 are the two Jesus singles out, and from the Book of Mormon's own 3 Nephi 12:34-36, where the risen Christ forbids swearing by heaven and by the head in the record Mormon compiled. So the man recording the oath is the man who copied out its prohibition, and the chapter's hinge — his refusal to lead — falls in the verse after the oath. Note also what they swear to do: the oath-taking Matthew 23 attacks is casuistry about which oaths bind, and this oath binds its takers to a war of revenge.

links.note: 'And they did swear by the heavens, and also by the throne of God, that they would go up to battle against their enemies.' Of all the things in the King James Bible a man might swear by, these are the two the New Testament names together in a single verse, and that verse is the only one in the Bible with either phrase: 'he that shall swear by heaven, sweareth by the throne of God'. The Book of Mormon's coordination — by the heavens, *and also* by the throne — follows Matthew 23:22's two-object construction rather than Matthew 5:34's identification of heaven *with* the throne, which is the reason the row is keyed here and not to the Sermon. Well short of a reproduced clause and therefore an allusion, not a quotation; it is nowhere near Skousen's threshold and should not be read alongside his list.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I, Mormon, did utterly refuse from this time forth, to be a commander and a leader of this people, because of their wickedness and abomination.

links.text: Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people.

provenance.other: “commander” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “a leader and commander” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: Isaiah 55:4, which also supplies the third of Mormon's three terms, 'a witness to the people'. Isaiah 55 is not among the chapters transcribed into the Book of Mormon, but it is demonstrably in the book's repertoire: Isaiah 55:1 is quoted at 2 Nephi 9:50 and again at 2 Nephi 26:25.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 55:4 is the everlasting-covenant offer of the Davidic figure: 'I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people.' Three offices, given. Mormon 3 disposes of all three across five verses and in Isaiah's own vocabulary. At 3:11 he 'did utterly refuse from this time forth, to be a commander and a leader of this people' — Isaiah's pair, reversed. At 3:16 he keeps the remaining office and empties it: 'I did stand as an idle witness.' The reversal of order is what a writer does when the phrase is in his ear rather than under his eye, and the retention of 'witness' is what makes the group of three, rather than the pair alone, the thing being answered. Recover Isaiah 55 further and the convergence tightens: the chapter's invitation, 'Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters', is the passage the Book of Mormon quotes at 2 Nephi 26:25 in the form 'Come unto me all ye ends of the earth' — which is the formula framing this very chapter at 3:2 and 3:22. Isaiah 55 supplies both the invitation Mormon repeats and the office he refuses.

links.note: 'I, Mormon, did utterly refuse from this time forth, to be a commander and a leader of this people.' The King James Bible uses the word 'commander' once, in Isaiah 55:4, where it stands beside 'leader' and beside 'witness' — and Mormon uses all three words of himself inside six verses, the first two in the sentence of refusal and the third at 3:16. That is the argument. It is filed at moderate rather than high because of a fact that has to be stated against it: the Book of Mormon has the pair already, at Alma 43:44 ('their chief leader and commander') and Alma 47:19 ('their leader and their chief commander'), as an ordinary Nephite military title. What that shows, though, is that the pair entered the book's vocabulary from the one KJV verse that has it; what is peculiar to Mormon 3 is that the third term arrives too, and arrives attached to the refusal.
links.whyNot: 'Leader and commander' is a standing Book of Mormon title (Alma 43:44, Alma 47:19), so its appearance here may be house vocabulary rather than a reach for Isaiah, and 'witness' at 3:16 is a word Mormon has independent reason to use of a man who has stopped fighting and is still writing. The row withdraws if a reader takes the Alma occurrences to have severed the phrase from Isaiah 55:4 for this writer.

pericopes.text: Behold, I had led them, notwithstanding their wickedness, I had lead them many times to battle, and had loved them, according to the love of God which was in me, with all my heart; and my soul had been poured out in prayer unto my God all the day long, for them; nevertheless, it was without faith, because of the hardness of their hearts.

links.text: Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

provenance.other: “the love of God which” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:39 — 'the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord'. Mormon 3:12 has 'the love of God which was in me'. The relative clause is the whole of the contact: 'the love of God' by itself is common enough (1 John especially), and it is the 'which is in …' that is Pauline and singular.
provenance.significance: Romans 8:35-39 is the passage that lists what cannot separate a believer from the love of God, and ends by locating that love in Christ. Mormon 3:12 relocates it: 'the love of God which was in me', with which he loved a people who would not have it. The verse then does something Romans 8 does not contemplate — it reports the love failing of its object: 'nevertheless, it was without faith, because of the hardness of their hearts.' Read with Romans 8:39 recovered, Mormon's sentence concedes the apostle's point exactly and turns it: nothing separates Mormon from the love of God, and it is his people, not the love, that the separation runs through.

links.note: 'I had loved them, according to the love of God which was in me, with all my heart.' The relative clause is Paul's and no one else's in the King James Bible. The rest of the verse is not: 'with all my heart' is Psalmic and constant, 'all the day long' is Psalmic and constant, and 'the hardness of their hearts' is a Book of Mormon commonplace seventeen verses over (see the register at this verse) even though it happens to be a KJV singleton at Mark 3:5. Filed at moderate because a four-word relative clause is a thin thread to hang a chapter of Romans on, and because 'which was in me' is a natural enough English continuation that a writer could arrive at it without Paul.
links.whyNot: Four words, one of which ('which') is a function word, and the Book of Mormon uses 'the love of God' freely elsewhere. A reader may hold that the phrase is the ordinary way to say the thing in English and that Romans 8 is not in view at all.

pericopes.text: And thrice have I delivered them out of the hands of their enemies, and they have repented not of their sins.

links.text: And when the LORD raised them up judges, then the LORD was with the judge, and delivered them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge: for it repented the LORD because of their groanings by reason of them that oppressed them and vexed them.

provenance.other: “delivered them out of the hand of their enemies” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 2:18. The shorter “delivered them out of the hand” occurs in exactly four (Joshua 9:26, Judges 2:16, Judges 2:18, Ezekiel 34:27), of which only Judges 2:18 continues 'of their enemies'. Mormon 3:13 pluralizes the KJV's singular hand — 'out of the hands of their enemies' — which is the Book of Mormon's usual habit with this idiom and does not disturb the identification.
provenance.significance: Judges 2:16-19 is the Bible's one abstract statement of the judges cycle, written as a summary rather than a story: the LORD raises up a deliverer, delivers them out of the hand of their enemies, and 'when the judge was dead, they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers'. Mormon 3:13 is that summary spoken by the deliverer, in the first person, with the count attached — 'thrice have I delivered them … and they have repented not.' Recover Judges 2 and the shape of the chapter is given: the cycle's only exit, in Judges, is the death of the judge, and Mormon 3 finds the other exit. He does not die; he resigns (3:11) and then declines to fight (3:16), which is a thing no judge in Judges does. The 'thrice' is the counting Judges does across twelve chapters compressed into one clause by a man who can see the end of the series.

links.note: 'And thrice have I delivered them out of the hands of their enemies, and they have repented not of their sins.'
