The phrase is Judges 2:18's and no other verse's in the King James Bible, and it arrives in exactly the setting Judges 2 built it for: a deliverer speaking of repeated deliverances that produced no repentance. What is Mormon's own is the arithmetic. Judges never numbers the cycle; Mormon does, and the number is what makes the following verses possible — a fourth deliverance is not refused in anger but declared to have been earned three times over and spent.

pericopes.text: And when they had sworn by all that had been forbidden them, by our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, that they would go up unto their enemies to battle, and avenge themselves of the blood of their brethren, behold, the voice of the Lord came unto me, saying:

links.text: For so an entrance shall be ministered unto you abundantly into the everlasting kingdom of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.

provenance.other: “our Lord and Saviour” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Peter 1:11 and 2 Peter 3:18; “Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ” occurs in exactly three, those two and 2 Peter 2:20, which lacks the possessive. The title is 2 Peter's alone in the King James Bible — no Gospel, no letter of Paul, no other catholic epistle uses it — and it is a hapax in the Book of Mormon, occurring in exactly one verse of the whole book, this one. The two verses with 'our' cannot be told apart by tools/mediation-check.py, which is expected: the phrase is identical in both. The 1830 spelling 'Saviour' is the KJV's and was changed to 'Savior' by 1920 (CONVENTIONS §8) — the first edition shows the borrowing more plainly than the current text does.
provenance.significance: The interesting context is the one whose wording the Book of Mormon does not quite have. 2 Peter 2:20 uses the same title of people who 'having escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, are again entangled therein and overcome' — and concludes 'the latter end is worse with them than the beginning.' That is Mormon 3 in one sentence: a people delivered three times (3:13), returned to the thing they were delivered from, and cut off (3:15). Whether or not 2 Peter 2 is the verse in the writer's ear, the title he chose for the oath belongs, in the KJV, to the one epistle that uses it chiefly of apostates.

links.note: 'And when they had sworn by all that had been forbidden them, by our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.' The title is 2 Peter's signature and nothing else's in the King James Bible, and this is the only place in the Book of Mormon it appears — a hapax in both corpora at once, which is the strongest form the rarity argument takes. It is worth noting what the sentence uses it for. The Nephites swear by the name; the clause 'by all that had been forbidden them' points back to the prohibition catalogued at 3:10, so the verse names a divine title, the oath it consecrates, and the fact that the oath is forbidden, in that order. Short of a reproduced clause, so an allusion rather than a quotation.

pericopes.text: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay; and because this people repented not after that I had delivered them, behold, they shall be cut off from the face of the earth.

links.text: Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.

provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 32:35 MT: לִָי נָקָם וְשִׁלֵּם — 'vengeance and recompence are mine', which is the KJV's 'To me belongeth vengeance and recompence' and not the Book of Mormon's clause.
provenance.route: Deuteronomy 32:35 → Romans 12:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “vengeance is mine” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “avenge not yourselves” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them Romans 12:19; “belongeth unto me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 10:30. tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point against Deuteronomy 32:35 (the Book of Mormon has Romans's 'is mine, I will repay, saith' where Deuteronomy has 'and recompence, their foot shall slide in due time, for') and two against Hebrews 10:30 (it has 'Vengeance is mine' where Hebrews has 'Vengeance belongeth unto me', and 'repay' where Hebrews has 'recompense'). The Old Testament verse the Lord is quoting is not the form he quotes it in.
provenance.alternative: Hebrews 10:30, which quotes the same Deuteronomy verse in a different English and which the Book of Mormon does reach — but at Mormon 8:20, not here.
provenance.significance: Metalepsis, and the sharpest instance in the book, because the suppressed half of the verse is the half the narrative has spent fourteen verses breaking. Romans 12:19 reads in full: 'Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.' The Lord quotes the proof-text and withholds the commandment it was cited to prove. He does not have to supply it: the Nephites have sworn twice, at 3:9 and again at 3:14, that they would 'avenge themselves of the blood of their brethren', which is the exact thing Romans 12:19 forbids in the words Romans 12:19 forbids it in. So the verse is constructed so that a reader who knows the whole of Romans 12:19 hears the sentence the people are being condemned by, and a reader who does not hears only a promise of divine vengeance — which reads, wrongly, as though God were siding with the oath. The chapter's whole moral turn is in the unquoted clause. Note also that Mormon 8:20, Moroni quoting the same complex, supplies what 3:15 leaves out at the other end: 'Man shall not smite, neither shall he judge: for judgement is mine, saith the Lord; and vengeance is mine also, and I will repay' — the prohibition restored, and with it Hebrews 10:30's second clause, 'The Lord shall judge his people'. Between the two verses the Book of Mormon has the whole of the New Testament's double citation; neither verse has it alone.

links.note: 'Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.' Six words reproduced exactly from Romans 12:19, in a verse where Hardy's apparatus cross-references Deuteronomy 32:35 as well — and the mediation is decidable, which is why this row matters more than its length suggests. Deuteronomy 32:35 in the KJV reads 'To me belongeth vengeance and recompence'; Hebrews 10:30 reads 'Vengeance belongeth unto me, I will recompense'; only Romans 12:19 reads 'Vengeance is mine; I will repay', and that is what the Book of Mormon has, down to the verb. So the Lord, speaking to Mormon in the fourth century, quotes an Old Testament song in the English of a first-century apostle's citation of it, and not in the English of the song. That is the finding, and CONVENTIONS §3a's inverted availability criterion is what makes it a finding rather than an objection. Six words is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and this is not one of his thirty-six; it is catalogued as a quotation on the 1 Nephi 1:14 principle, that a complete clause reproduced from a verse identifiable by absolute rarity is a quotation whatever its length.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that I utterly refused to go up against mine enemies; and I did even as the Lord had commanded me; and I did stand as an idle witness to manifest unto the world the things which I saw and heard, according to the manifestations of the spirit which had testified of things to come.

links.text: For thou shalt be his witness unto all men of what thou hast seen and heard.

provenance.other: “his witness unto all men” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 22:15, which continues 'of what thou hast seen and heard'. The bare pair 'seen and heard' occurs in exactly five KJV verses (Luke 7:22, John 3:32, Acts 4:20, Acts 22:15, 1 John 1:3), of which only Acts 22:15 attaches it to a commission to witness before a universal audience. For the second half of the composite: “here all the day idle” and “stand ye here” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:6, and “standing idle” in exactly two, Matthew 20:3 and 20:6.
provenance.significance: The verse is built out of two New Testament commissions and negates both. Acts 22:15 is Ananias's charge to the newly blinded Paul: 'thou shalt be his witness unto all men of what thou hast seen and heard' — a commission whose whole content is activity, going, speaking. Mormon takes the content entire ('an idle witness to manifest unto the world the things which I saw and heard') and drains it: he is a witness unto all the world of what he saw and heard, and he does it by standing still. The adjective supplies the second text. In the King James Bible, standing idle is what the unhired labourers of Matthew 20 do, and the householder's question to them — 'Why stand ye here all the day idle?' — is the only KJV sentence that puts 'stand', 'here' and 'idle' together, exactly as Mormon does when he says he 'did stand as an idle witness'. Both texts are about being sent, and Mormon 3:16 is the verse in which the Book of Mormon's compiler stops being sent and starts only recording.

links.note: 'I did stand as an idle witness to manifest unto the world the things which I saw and heard.' The clause reproduces the substance of Acts 22:15 with the KJV's singular phrase for it — witness, unto all men or the world, of what was seen and heard — and then inserts a word that belongs, in the King James Bible, to men who have not been hired. This is the counterpart of 3:11: there Mormon refuses the two active offices of Isaiah 55:4, here he keeps the third and qualifies it out of force. 'Manifest unto the world' has no KJV parallel, so the borrowing is at the level of the commission's terms rather than a run of words, which is why this is an allusion.

pericopes.text: Therefore I write unto you, Gentiles, and also unto you, house of Israel, when the work shall commence, that ye shall be about to prepare to return to the land of your inheritance;

links.text: For, lo, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will bring again the captivity of my people Israel and Judah, saith the LORD: and I will cause them to return to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it.

provenance.other: “return to the land” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 30:3 — 'I will cause them to return to the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it.' “land of your inheritance” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses; the possessive is the Book of Mormon's own way of saying what Jeremiah says with a relative clause.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 30 is the Book of Consolation, and 30:3 is its thesis: the days come when the LORD will bring again the captivity of Israel and Judah and cause them to return to the land. Mormon 3:17 addresses the same restoration from the far side of a different dispersion and to a doubled audience — 'unto you, Gentiles, and also unto you, house of Israel' — which is the move the chapter then makes twice more, at 3:18 and 3:19, where a single promise is administered by two sets of twelve. Recover Jeremiah 30:3 and what Mormon has added is visible: Jeremiah's return is a return of the captivity to one land; Mormon's is a work that 'shall commence' among Gentiles who are told to prepare for it.

links.note: 'When the work shall commence, that ye shall be about to prepare to return to the land of your inheritance.' The one KJV verse with 'return to the land' is the one KJV verse whose subject is exactly this — a restoration to an inherited land promised to a scattered people — and the Book of Mormon's substitution of 'of your inheritance' for Jeremiah's 'that I gave to their fathers' says the same thing more briefly. Filed at moderate: four words, of which three are function words, and restoration language is thick enough throughout Isaiah and Jeremiah that a reader may reasonably decline to key it to one verse.
links.whyNot: The shared string is short and largely functional, and 'the land of your inheritance' is a standing Book of Mormon phrase with no KJV original, so the verse may be reaching for the prophetic restoration idiom in general rather than Jeremiah 30:3 in particular.

pericopes.text: yea, behold, I write unto all the ends of the earth; yea, unto you, twelve tribes of Israel, which shall be judged according to your works, by the twelve whom Jesus chose to be his disciples in the land of Jerusalem.

links.text: And Jesus said unto them, Verily I say unto you, That ye which have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.

provenance.route: Matthew 19:28 / Luke 22:30 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the doctrine reaches Mormon already formed at 1 Nephi 12:9-10
provenance.other: “judging the twelve tribes” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 19:28 and Luke 22:30, and there is no third. tools/mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between them: every point at which the two differ — Matthew's 'twelve thrones' and 'in the regeneration', Luke's 'eat and drink at my table' — is a point the Book of Mormon reproduces from neither. Matthew is named as `source` only because it is the fuller of the two; the catalogue cannot choose between them from this verse and does not pretend to.
provenance.alternative: Luke 22:30, indistinguishable on the evidence of this verse.
provenance.significance: 1 Nephi 12:9-10 already has the whole doctrine, and has it in the doubled form Mormon 3:18-19 uses: 'the twelve apostles of the Lamb … shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel; wherefore, the twelve ministers of thy seed, shall be judged of them', and 'these twelve ministers … shall judge thy seed.' Mormon 3:18-19 restates it exactly, two courts, the Nephite twelve judged by the Jerusalem twelve. So the proximate model is not the Gospel but a Book of Mormon page a thousand years earlier in the book's own chronology, and the Gospel verse stands behind that. The schema's `mediation` vocabulary has no value for this — `OT-via-earlier-BoM` names an Old Testament source, and this source is a Gospel — so the field records `direct-NT` and the route is written out here. Flagged rather than fudged (CONVENTIONS, preamble); the same gap recurs at 3:20 and 3:21.

links.note: 'Unto you, twelve tribes of Israel, which shall be judged according to your works, by the twelve whom Jesus chose to be his disciples in the land of Jerusalem.' The promise that the twelve will judge the twelve tribes is made twice in the New Testament and nowhere else in the Bible, and Mormon 3:18 makes it a third time with the referent specified — 'in the land of Jerusalem' — because the next verse needs to distinguish that bench from the other one. Confidence is high on the dependence and `kjvSpecific` is 'uncertain' rather than 'yes' precisely because the Book of Mormon has none of the wording that would identify an English version: it keeps the proposition and drops 'thrones', 'regeneration', 'table' and every other discriminating word. Hardy cross-references both Gospel verses here; the row is his in the sense that the apparatus points at it, and the argument about which of the two, and about the 1 Nephi 12 route, is the catalogue's.

pericopes.text: And I write also unto the remnant of this people, which shall also be judged by the twelve whom Jesus chose in this land; and they shall be judged by the other twelve whom Jesus chose in the land of Jerusalem.

And these things do the spirit manifest unto me; therefore I write unto you all. And for this cause I write unto you, that ye may know that ye must all stand before the judgement seat of Christ, yea, every soul which belong to the whole human family of Adam; and ye must stand to be judged of your works, whether they be good or evil;

links.text: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 5:10 + Romans 14:10 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the composite is already made at 3 Nephi 27:14-15
provenance.other: “judgment seat of Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10, and the Book of Mormon has both of their distinctive halves. tools/mediation-check.py reports divergences pointing both ways, which CONVENTIONS §7 treats as a finding rather than a failure: the Book of Mormon has 2 Corinthians's 'must' against Romans's 'shall', and 2 Corinthians's tail about receiving according to what is done, whether good or bad; but it has Romans's verb 'stand' against 2 Corinthians's 'appear'. “stand before the judgment seat” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 14:10; “we must all appear” occurs in exactly one, 2 Corinthians 5:10. The verse is a fusion of the two and is catalogued as one.
provenance.alternative: Romans 14:10, which supplies the verb and cannot be dropped from the account.
provenance.significance: The chapter's last movement turns from a war to an assize, and it does so in the vocabulary of the two Pauline verses that have a judgment seat in them, plus the Old Testament verse that supplies the final clause — Ecclesiastes 12:14, 'For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.' What makes the row more than a catalogue of parallels is that the Book of Mormon has made this exact composite once already, in the record Mormon himself abridged: 3 Nephi 27:14, where the risen Christ says men shall 'stand before me, to be judged of their works, whether they be good or whether they be evil', and 27:15, 'that they may be judged according to their works.' Mormon 3:20 is that sentence with 'the judgement seat of Christ' substituted for 'before me' — the abridger writing in the third person about the judge who had used the first. As at 3:18, the proximate model is earlier Book of Mormon text and the ultimate sources are New Testament, and the `mediation` enum has no term for that combination. CONVENTIONS §8 in the unusual direction. The KJV spells it 'judgment seat'; the 1830 edition spells it 'judgement seat' here and at 3:22, and the 1920 edition changed it back to 'judgment', i.e. back toward the source. The 1830's spelling is the compositor's British habit overriding the KJV's, which is a useful control on §8's usual argument: first-edition orthography is evidence of the KJV where it agrees with the KJV and evidence of the printing house where it does not.

links.note: 'Ye must all stand before the judgement seat of Christ … and ye must stand to be judged of your works, whether they be good or evil.' Two KJV verses have a judgment seat of Christ and this sentence has something from each: 2 Corinthians's 'must all' and its clause about works and their quality, Romans's verb 'stand'. That is not indecision on our part — mediation-check finds decisive points in both directions, which is what a fusion looks like from underneath. The third element, 'whether they be good or evil', is Ecclesiastes 12:14's formula for the judgment of every work, and the Book of Mormon's own 3 Nephi 27:14 has it in Ecclesiastes's doubled form ('whether they be good or whether they be evil') where Mormon 3:20 contracts it. Filed as allusion and not quotation: no complete clause of either Pauline verse is reproduced. One 1830 point, and it runs the other way from CONVENTIONS §8's usual argument: the KJV spells it 'judgment seat', the first edition spells it 'judgement seat' here and at 3:22, and 1920 changed it back toward the source. First-edition orthography is evidence of the KJV where it agrees with the KJV and evidence of the printing house where it does not.

pericopes.text: and also that ye may believe the Gospel of Jesus Christ, which ye shall have among you; and also that the Jews, the covenant people of the Lord, shall have other witness besides that which they saw and heard, that Jesus, whom they slew, was the very Christ, and the very God;

links.text: But, lo, he speaketh boldly, and they say nothing unto him. Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ?

provenance.other: “the very Christ” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 7:26 — 'Do the rulers know indeed that this is the very Christ?' The nearest other reading is Acts 9:22, 'proving that this is very Christ', without the article. In the Book of Mormon the phrase occurs in exactly two verses, 2 Nephi 26:12 and this one.
provenance.significance: John 7:26 is a question asked in Jerusalem by the crowd about the Jerusalem authorities: do the rulers know that this is the very Christ? It is left unanswered in John, and it is answered here — 'that Jesus, whom they slew, was the very Christ' — by a witness on the other side of the world at the end of his nation. The Book of Mormon has already staked the phrase for this purpose: 2 Nephi 26:12 is about 'the convincing of the Jews, that Jesus is the very Christ', which is Mormon 3:21's subject exactly, so the proximate model is again earlier Book of Mormon text and the KJV verse stands behind it. Mormon then adds a term John's crowd could not have used: 'and the very God'.

links.note: The King James Bible says 'the very Christ' once. Mormon 3:21 says it of the man 'whom they slew', which is the second of the verse's two borrowings (see the Acts 5:30 row). Filed at moderate rather than high because the phrase is short and because 2 Nephi 26:12 has it already in the same application, so a reader may fairly hold that Mormon is reusing his own book's idiom and never touching John. That the idiom got into his book from John 7:26 is the part that is not in doubt.
links.whyNot: Three words, one of them 'the', and the Book of Mormon's own 2 Nephi 26:12 supplies the whole phrase in the same context of convincing the Jews. The row records the KJV origin of a Book of Mormon formula more than a fresh reach for John.

links.text: The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.

provenance.other: “whom ye slew” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Judges 8:18 (Gideon to Zebah and Zalmunna), Matthew 23:35 (Zacharias slain between the temple and the altar) and Acts 5:30. Only Acts 5:30 has Jesus as its object: 'The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom ye slew and hanged on a tree.' Mormon 3:21 turns the pronoun — 'Jesus, whom they slew' — because he is writing to a later audience about the Jews rather than addressing them.
provenance.significance: Acts 5:30 is Peter before the Sanhedrin, and the clause is a charge delivered to the faces of the men charged. Mormon 3:21 keeps the charge and changes its grammatical person, which changes what it is for: 'the Jews, the covenant people of the Lord, shall have other witness besides that which they saw and heard, that Jesus, whom they slew, was the very Christ.' The accusation has become the content of a testimony offered to the accused, and the verse says outright that this record is that other witness. Note the phrase immediately before it — 'the covenant people of the Lord' — which is not an accusation at all, and which the verse holds together with 'whom they slew' in a single clause.

links.note: Three KJV verses have 'whom ye slew' and only one is about Jesus. What Mormon does with it is the argument: Peter's second-person accusation becomes a third-person description inside a sentence whose purpose is to give the accused a further witness, and the same sentence calls them 'the covenant people of the Lord'. Filed at moderate — three words, and the shift of person removes the one feature that made Acts 5:30 an accusation — but the collocation of the slaying with the title 'the very Christ' in the same clause is not a thing English arrives at by itself.
links.whyNot: 'Whom they slew' is a natural English relative clause and the Book of Mormon says elsewhere, without any Acts vocabulary, that the Jews crucified Christ. The row rests on the KJV rarity of the exact string in the second person and on nothing else verbal.

pericopes.text: and I would that I could persuade all ye ends of the earth to repent and prepare to stand before the judgement seat of Christ.

links.text: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.

provenance.route: Isaiah 45:22 (with Isaiah 55:1) → KJV → 2 Nephi 26:25 / Alma 5:50 / 3 Nephi 27:20 → Mormon 3:22
provenance.other: “be ye saved all the ends of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 45:22. The bare “all the ends of the earth” occurs in exactly seven, which is why no rarity argument can be built on the phrase alone — and why this row is keyed on the imperative-plus-vocative construction rather than on the words. In the Book of Mormon the vocative is a formula: 'all ye ends of the earth' occurs in exactly eight verses (2 Nephi 26:25, 33:10, 33:13, 3 Nephi 27:20, Alma 5:50, Ether 4:18, Moroni 7:34 and this one), and 'ends of the earth' in twenty-three. The two that matter here are 2 Nephi 26:25 ('Come unto me all ye ends of the earth') and 3 Nephi 27:20 ('Repent, all ye ends of the earth, and come unto me and be baptized in my name').
provenance.significance: The chapter is bracketed by the two halves of a commandment Mormon transcribed from the risen Christ. At 3:2 the Lord tells him to cry 'repent ye, and come unto me and be ye baptized'; at 3:22 Mormon himself would 'persuade all ye ends of the earth to repent'. 3 Nephi 27:20 has both in one sentence — 'Repent, all ye ends of the earth, and come unto me and be baptized in my name' — and 3 Nephi is the record Mormon abridged. Behind that stands Isaiah 45:22, the KJV's one universal imperative addressed to the ends of the earth, and beside it Isaiah 55:1, which the Book of Mormon fuses with it at 2 Nephi 26:25 ('Come unto me all ye ends of the earth, buy milk and honey without money'). That is the same Isaiah 55 chapter whose fourth verse stands behind Mormon's refusal at 3:11: the prophet who declines to be the people's leader and commander closes by issuing, in his own voice, the invitation from the chapter that named those offices.

links.note: 'I would that I could persuade all ye ends of the earth to repent and prepare to stand before the judgement seat of Christ.' The vocative is Isaiah's and the imperative is Isaiah's, but the route is not: 'all ye ends of the earth' is one of the Book of Mormon's standing formulas, in eight verses across five books, and the version Mormon is closest to is 3 Nephi 27:20, from the pages he abridged himself. This is what CONVENTIONS §7 means by `OT-via-earlier-BoM`, and the mediation is recorded accordingly. `kjvSpecific` is 'no': every English Bible renders Isaiah 45:22's vocative much the same way, and there is no distinctive King James wording here to test.
links.whyNot: The phrase is a Book of Mormon formula in eight other verses — and its Isaianic origin, though not in doubt, was settled long before Mormon 3. A reader may reasonably hold that this verse alludes to nothing and simply uses the book's standing formula for a universal address.

pericopes.text: And now it came to pass that in the three hundred and sixty and third year, the Nephites did go up with their armies to battle against the Lamanites, out of the land Desolation.

And it came to pass that the armies of the Nephites were driven back again to the land of Desolation. And while they were yet weary, a fresh army of the Lamanites did come upon them; and they had a sore battle, insomuch that the Lamanites did take possession of the city Desolation, and did slay many of the Nephites, and did take many prisoners;
and the remainder did flee and join the inhabitants of the city Teancum. Now the city Teancum lay in the borders by the seashore; and it was also near the city Desolation.
And it was because that the armies of the Nephites went up unto the Lamanites, that they began to be smitten: for were it not for that; the Lamanites could have had no power over them.

links.text: Jesus answered, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above: therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin.

provenance.other: “no power at all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 19:11. The Book of Mormon does not reproduce it: “power over” occurs in thirteen KJV verses and is not distinctive.
provenance.alternative: Alma 43:46-47, the Nephite prohibition on offensive war, states the same rule inside the corpus and may be all that Mormon 4:4 is applying.
provenance.significance: John 19:11 is the King James Bible's one sentence on delegated power in a war of the strong against the weak: Pilate holds real authority over Jesus and holds it only on loan, and the sentence ends by assigning the guilt elsewhere — “he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin.” Mormon 4:4 performs the same division of blame in the opposite direction. The Lamanites do the killing; the guilt is the Nephites', because they went up. Recover John's context and the borrowed logic brings its verdict with it: the party that put the victim in the aggressor's hand is the party condemned.

links.note: “And it was because that the armies of the Nephites went up unto the Lamanites, that they began to be smitten: for were it not for that, the Lamanites could have had no power over them.” The sentence states a doctrine of conditional power — the enemy has power over the covenant people only because a condition has been met, and absent it he could have had none. The King James Bible states that doctrine once, at John 19:11, in the same construction: could have + no power + object + an exception clause carrying the whole cause (“except it were given thee from above”). What Mormon changes is the source of the grant. John's power comes from above; Mormon's is forfeited from below, by the Nephites' own aggression, which makes 4:4 a negative form of the same rule.
links.whyNot: The evidence is a sentence shape, not a string. The KJV singleton — “no power at all” — is precisely what the Book of Mormon does not have, and “have power over” is common English and common KJV. The doctrine also has a home inside the corpus at Alma 43:46-47, so Mormon may be citing his own tradition rather than John's sentence. Recorded at low, and recorded at all because the KJV has no other verse where the possession of power over another is made to turn on a stated condition.

pericopes.text: But behold, the judgements of God will overtake the wicked; and it is by the wicked, that the wicked are punished: for it is the wicked that stirreth up the hearts of the children of men unto bloodshed.—

links.text: Moreover all these curses shall come upon thee, and shall pursue thee, and overtake thee, till thou be destroyed; because thou hearkenedst not unto the voice of the LORD thy God, to keep his commandments and his statutes which he commanded thee:

provenance.other: “overtake thee” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Deuteronomy 28:2, 28:15 and 28:45, all of them in the one chapter of covenant sanctions; “the judgments of God” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses, so the noun is the Book of Mormon's and the verb is Deuteronomy's.
provenance.significance: Deuteronomy 28 is the King James Bible's one extended account of what happens to a covenant people that loses its covenant, and its horror is specifically domestic: at 28:53 the besieged “shalt eat the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters.” Mormon 4 reaches that scene nine verses after borrowing the chapter's verb — women and children taken and sacrificed at 4:14, and again at 4:21. The metalepsis is not decorative. Deuteronomy 28 supplies the reason Mormon's narrative never gives in so many words: the destruction of a people's own children is what the curse looks like when it has run its length.

links.note: “But behold, the judgements of God will overtake the wicked.” Overtaking is what the King James curses do, and almost nothing else does: “overtake thee” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Deuteronomy 28:2, 28:15 and 28:45, the blessings that overtake obedience and the curses that overtake disobedience “till thou be destroyed.” The collocation is not natural English — judgments in the KJV are executed, done, made manifest, but never overtake — which makes Deuteronomy 28 the available model. Mormon substitutes his own book's noun for Deuteronomy's “curses” and leaves the verb standing, in the chapter where the Nephite destruction becomes irreversible. The 1830 spelling “judgements”, modernized in 1920, is the KJV's own orthographic register though not its spelling of this word.

links.text: O Assyrian, the rod of mine anger, and the staff in their hand is mine indignation.

provenance.route: Isaiah 10:5-12 → (KJV, or 2 Nephi 20:5-12) → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “rod of mine anger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 10:5. Mormon 4:5 reproduces none of it; the link is entirely at the level of doctrine.
provenance.alternative: Habakkuk 1:6-13 teaches the same thing — the Chaldeans raised up to punish a people “more righteous than he” — and Mormon 4:5 gives nothing that decides between Isaiah and Habakkuk. Isaiah is preferred only because the Book of Mormon has Isaiah 10 inside itself and does not have Habakkuk anywhere.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 10 is a two-stage oracle and Mormon 4:5 is its compression. Assyria is the rod of God's anger, sent against a hypocritical nation (10:6); Assyria is then punished for the arrogance with which it swung (10:12), “howbeit he meaneth not so, neither doth his heart think so” (10:7). The Book of Mormon says both stages in one clause — it is by the wicked that the wicked are punished — and then adds the instrument's own guilt in the next breath: “it is the wicked that stirreth up the hearts of the children of men unto bloodshed.” That is Isaiah's second stage, stated as a general law rather than as a sentence on one empire. It is also, in a chapter where the Lamanites are the rod, a refusal to let the rod be innocent.

links.note: The chapter's one aphorism — “it is by the wicked, that the wicked are punished” — shares no distinctive word with any KJV verse, and it is nonetheless a close paraphrase of one passage: Isaiah 10:5-12, where the wicked nation is the instrument of judgment on the wicked nation and is judged in turn. Mormon needs exactly this doctrine here, because his narrative has just made the Nephites the aggressors (4:4) and is about to make the Lamanites child-killers (4:14): neither side can be the righteous party, and the war has to be theologically legible anyway. Isaiah 10 is the King James Bible's solution to that problem and Mormon 4:5 states it as a maxim. Catalogued as figural because the wording is entirely the Book of Mormon's.
links.whyNot: There is no verbal contact at all — not one shared distinctive word — and doctrines of this kind are recoverable from Isaiah 10, Habakkuk 1, Jeremiah 25:9 and Ezekiel 21 alike. A reader who declines this row is declining it on the strongest possible ground, that the catalogue is meant to record dependence and this records agreement. It is written because the chapter's argument is unintelligible without a precursor of this shape, and because 2 Nephi 20 puts one in the Book of Mormon's own hands.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites did make preparations to come against the city Teancum.
And it came to pass in the three hundred and sixty and fourth year, the Lamanites did come against the city Teancum, that they might take possession of the city Teancum also.

And it came to pass that they were repulsed and driven back by the Nephites. And when the Nephites saw that they had driven the Lamanites, they did again boast of their strength; and they went forth in their own might, and took possession again of the city Desolation.
And now all these things had been done, and there had been thousands slain on both sides, both the Nephites and the Lamanites.

links.text: Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.

provenance.other: “now all these things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 10:11. Within the Book of Mormon, “all these things had been done” occurs only here, so this is not a narrator's formula recurring.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 10:1-11 recites the deaths of a covenant people in the wilderness — overthrown, destroyed of the destroyer — and stops to say why the recital exists: “they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.” The sin the recital is warning against, named at 10:7 out of Exodus 32:6, is idolatry. Mormon 4 is a chapter of idolatry (4:14, 4:21) and of a covenant people overthrown, written by an abridger who has just addressed a future readership directly (Mormon 3:17-22) and told them why he is writing. If the phrase came from Paul, it came with Paul's whole editorial posture attached: this is the one place in the KJV where a writer counts the dead and then explains that the counting is for someone else's benefit.

links.note: “And now all these things had been done, and there had been thousands slain on both sides.” The opening four words are a KJV singleton — “now all these things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the verse is 1 Corinthians 10:11, which makes the same move at the same point in the same kind of recital: a narrator breaking off a list of a covenant people's dead to say what the list is for. Mormon's clause takes the summing gesture without Paul's purpose clause, and then supplies the purpose clause himself in the chapters that follow. The borrowing, if it is one, is of a rhetorical position rather than of a doctrine.
links.whyNot: Four words, all of them among the commonest in English narrative prose; a writer could produce “and now all these things” without ever having read 1 Corinthians. A count of one on a plain phrase is weaker evidence than a count of one on a marked phrase like “shedding of blood”, and the row rests on the coincidence of position — the same words doing the same job at the same seam in a recital — rather than on the count alone.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the three hundred and sixty and sixth year had passed away, and the Lamanites came again upon the Nephites to battle; and yet the Nephites repented not of the evil which they had done, but persisted in their wickedness continually.

And it is impossible for the tongue to describe, or for man to write a perfect description of the horrible scene of the blood and carnage which was among the people, both of the Nephites and of the Lamanites; and every heart was hardened, so that they delighted in the shedding of blood continually.

links.text: And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission.

provenance.other: “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22. Thirteen Book of Mormon verses use it, and the argument for the borrowing was made where the corpus first takes it up; this row exists because Mormon is a new book and a new hand (ADJUDICATING §4).
provenance.significance: Hebrews 9:22 is the sentence that makes bloodshed mean something: without it there is no remission. 3 Nephi 9:19 has already cancelled the sacrificial system in the Book of Mormon's own voice — “ye shall offer up unto me no more the shedding of blood” — so by the time Mormon 4:11 is written the phrase has been formally emptied of its Hebrews sense inside the corpus itself. What is left of it at 4:11 is a people who shed blood and take pleasure in it. Read with 3 Nephi 9:19 in view, the sentence describes the exact condition the atonement was said to end, resumed by a people three hundred years after they were told it had ended.

links.note: “Every heart was hardened, so that they delighted in the shedding of blood continually.” The noun phrase is a King James singleton, and its one home is the mechanism of atonement: “without shedding of blood is no remission.” The Book of Mormon has taken it over as its standard term for homicide and war — from Alma 26:24 through Alma 48:23, where the Nephite ideal is stated as not delighting in it, to Mormon 7:4, where Mormon commands his readers to “delight no more” in it. Mormon 4:11 is where that transfer is completed and inverted: the same verb Alma 48:23 negated and Mormon 7:4 will forbid is here affirmed, of everyone, continually. The row is written rather than filed as a repeat because Mormon is a new book with a new narrator, and because 4:11's collocation with “delighted” is what 48:23 and 7:4 are both measured against.
links.whyNot: “Shedding of blood” is a natural English nominalization of a common KJV idiom — “whoso sheddeth man's blood”, “shed innocent blood” — and its singleton status may be an accident of the King James translators' phrasing rather than evidence that a writer had Hebrews 9:22 in front of him. The strength here is corpus-internal (the Alma 48:23 / Mormon 7:4 frame) more than it is Pauline.

pericopes.text: And there never had been so great wickedness among all the children of Lehi, nor even among all the house of Israel, according to the words of the Lord, as were among this people.

links.text: When Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to them that followed, Verily I say unto you, I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.

provenance.route: Matthew 8:10 (or Luke 7:9) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “no, not in Israel” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 8:10 and Luke 7:9; “so great faith” occurs in exactly two, the same pair. “So great” alone occurs in sixteen, which is why the frame and not the adjective carries the case.
provenance.alternative: tools/mediation-check.py finds no divergence between Matthew 8:10 and Luke 7:9 at any point Mormon 4:12 reproduces — the shared clause is verbatim in both Gospels, and the two differ only in the narrative frame the Book of Mormon does not take. The Gospel cannot be identified from this verse.
provenance.significance: Matthew 8:10 is followed immediately by 8:11-12: many shall come from the east and west and sit down with Abraham, “but the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness.” The centurion pericope is the King James Bible's first scene of a people outside Israel measured against Israel and found greater, and its sequel is the expulsion of the insiders. Mormon 4:12 runs the same measurement on a people outside Israel — the children of Lehi, a branch of the house cut off from it — and finds them greater in wickedness; Mormon 5 and 6 then narrate their expulsion. The verse borrows the frame of Christ's astonishment and fills it with the opposite content, two chapters before the outcome Matthew 8:12 predicts for the children of the kingdom arrives for these ones.

links.note: “And there never had been so great wickedness among all the children of Lehi, nor even among all the house of Israel, according to the words of the Lord, as were among this people.” The sentence is built on a King James frame: a superlative quantity, measured against Israel, and the measurement coming out the surprising way. “No, not in Israel” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 8:10 and its Lucan parallel, where Jesus marvels at a Gentile soldier and says “I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel.” Mormon keeps the superlative, keeps Israel as the standard of comparison, keeps the negative construction — “nor even among all the house of Israel” for “no, not in Israel” — and reverses the quality being measured. The 1830 reading “as were among this people”, corrected to “was” in 1920, is the first edition's looser concord and does not bear on the source.
links.whyNot: The KJV clause is not reproduced verbatim; what recurs is a comparative frame, and comparative frames are cheap. A reader could hold that “never so great X, nor even in Israel” is simply how a Hebraizing English writer would say this, with no Gospel in view. The row is written because the frame is not generic in the KJV itself — the centurion pericope is the only place the King James Bible measures anything against Israel in this construction.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites did take possession of the city Desolation, and this because their number did exceed the number of the Nephites.

And they did also march forward against the city Teancum, and did drive the inhabitants forth out of her, and did take many prisoners of women and of children, and did offer them up as sacrifices unto their idol gods.

And it came to pass that in the three hundred and sixty and seventh year, the Nephites being angry because the Lamanites had sacrificed their women and their children, that they did go against the Lamanites with exceeding great anger, insomuch that they did beat again the Lamanites, and drive them out of their lands;
and the Lamanites did not come again against the Nephites, until the three hundred and seventy and fifth year.
And in this year they did come down against the Nephites with all their powers; and they were not numbered, because of the greatness of their number.
And from this time forth did the Nephites gain no power over the Lamanites, but began to be swept off by them even as a dew before the sun.

links.text: Therefore they shall be as the morning cloud and as the early dew that passeth away, as the chaff that is driven with the whirlwind out of the floor, and as the smoke out of the chimney.

provenance.other: “as the early dew” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hosea 6:4 and Hosea 13:3, and they are the King James Bible's only figure of a people vanishing like dew. The KJV has no phrase “dew before the sun”. Within the Book of Mormon, “as a dew” occurs only at Mormon 4:18.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 16:14-21 is the one other KJV place where dew and sun meet — the dew lifts, the manna is left, and “when the sun waxed hot, it melted.” It supplies the physical picture and none of the theology; Hosea supplies the theology and not the sun.
provenance.significance: Hosea 13 is the chapter in which Ephraim “offended in Baal, and died” and is answered with “I will be thy king: where is any other that may save thee?” Mormon 4 is a chapter in which a covenant people's children are being killed before idols and no deliverer appears. “Swept off” is the Book of Mormon's own covenant term for the removal of a nation from the land of promise (Ether 2:8-10), so the sentence already carries a legal sense; laying Hosea's dew on it supplies the reason the sweeping is happening. Read with Hosea in view, 4:18 is not a report of military attrition. It is the moment the narrator stops describing a war and starts describing an oracle being fulfilled.

links.note: “Began to be swept off by them even as a dew before the sun.” The image is not in the King James Bible in these words, but the figure behind it is, and it belongs to one prophet: “as the early dew” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hosea 6:4 and 13:3, both of them about a covenant people whose goodness or whose existence passes away like dew in the morning. Hosea 13:3 puts the dew in a series of evanescences — morning cloud, early dew, chaff driven with the whirlwind, smoke out of the chimney — which is exactly the register of Mormon's clause. The Book of Mormon substitutes the agent Hosea leaves implicit: Hosea's dew simply “passeth away”, Mormon's goes before the sun.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites did come down against the city Desolation; and there was an exceeding sore battle fought in the land Desolation, in the which they did beat the Nephites.

And they fled again from before them, and they came to the city Beaz; and there they did stand against the Lamanites with exceeding boldness, insomuch that the Lamanites did not beat them until they had come again the second time.
And when they had come the second time, the Nephites were driven and slaughtered with an exceeding great slaughter; their women and their children were again sacrificed unto idols.

links.text: And shed innocent blood, even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan: and the land was polluted with blood.

provenance.other: “sacrificed unto the idols” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 106:38; “polluted with blood” occurs in exactly two, Psalm 106:38 and Hosea 6:8. “Sacrificed unto” alone occurs in ten, so it is the object, not the verb, that identifies the source. Ezekiel 16:20-21 and 2 Kings 17:17 describe the same practice and share none of the wording.
provenance.significance: Psalm 106 is Israel's national confession, and four verses past the one Mormon borrows it states the outcome: “And he gave them into the hand of the heathen; and they that hated them ruled over them” (106:41). That is the plot of Mormon 4 through 6. But the Psalm assigns the child sacrifice to the covenant people themselves, and Mormon assigns it to their enemies — so the borrowing puts the Nephites in the position of the Psalm's murdered children rather than of its idolaters, while leaving the Psalm's verdict standing over them anyway. The land polluted with blood is the same land in both texts, and in both it is the covenant people who lose it. Recovering Psalm 106 is what turns 4:21 from an atrocity report into an indictment of the side being killed.

links.note: “Their women and their children were again sacrificed unto idols.” The King James Bible says this once. “Sacrificed unto the idols” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 106:38, and the sentence there is the fullest biblical statement of what Mormon 4 reports twice: “they sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils, and shed innocent blood, even the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan: and the land was polluted with blood.” Mormon drops the article and keeps everything else. The chapter's other elements come with it — the innocent blood of sons and daughters at 4:14 and 4:21, and at 4:11 a land of “blood and carnage” in which “every heart was hardened”, which is the Psalm's polluted land in the Book of Mormon's own idiom. The first occurrence at 4:14 (“did offer them up as sacrifices unto their idol gods”) is the same event in non-KJV wording; the link is placed here, where the wording is (CONVENTIONS §6a).

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Nephites did again flee from before them, taking all the inhabitants with them, both in towns and villages.
And now I, Mormon, seeing that the Lamanites were about to overthrow the land, therefore I did go to the hill Shim, and did take up all the records which Ammaron had hid up unto the Lord.

And it came to pass that I did go forth among the Nephites, and did repent of the oath which I had made, That I would no more assist them; and they gave me command again of their armies: for they looked upon me as though I could deliver them from their afflictions.

But behold, I was without hopes, for I knew the judgements of the Lord which should come upon them: for they repented not of their iniquities, but did struggle for their lives, without calling upon that Being who had created them.

provenance.other: Ephesians 2:12 strings three privatives in a row: 'without Christ … having no hope, and without God in the world'. The outer two are catalogued at Mormon 5:16, where both are KJV singletons; this entry records the middle one.
provenance.alternative: 'Without hope' is ordinary English and Mormon has just described an army fighting a war it cannot win. Taken by itself the phrase needs no source at all, and this row exists only because of what 5:16 does.
provenance.significance: Mormon 5 has all three of Ephesians 2:12's negations and has them in the verse's own order — no hope at 5:2, without Christ and without God in the world at 5:16. Paul's three describe Gentiles before Christ, outside the commonwealth of Israel; Mormon distributes them across a chapter about the seed of Israel being put outside it. The 1830 reading is the sharper witness in a small way that cuts against the link and is recorded for that reason: 1830 has 'hopes' where Ephesians has the singular 'hope', and 1920 changed it to 'hope'. That is CONVENTIONS §8's pattern of a later edition correcting the text toward the KJV, and here it means the first edition is one letter further from the source than the reading a modern reader sees.

links.note: 'But behold, I was without hopes, for I knew the judgements of the Lord which should come upon them.' On its own this would not be catalogued; three words of common English are not evidence. It is catalogued because fourteen verses later Mormon writes that his people 'are without Christ and God in the world', which fuses the first and third privatives of Ephesians 2:12 — and 'having no hope' is the one standing between them. Once 5:16 is established as certain, the opening of the chapter reads as the first of the three rather than as a coincidence, and a reader who reaches 5:16 will look back at 5:2. Proposed under the generative posture (CONVENTIONS §0a) with the objection recorded alongside it.
links.text: That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lamanites did come against us as we had fled to the city of Jordan; but behold, they were driven back that they did not take the city at that time.

And it came to pass that they came against us again, and we did maintain the city. And there were also other cities which were maintained by the Nephites, which strong holds did cut them off that they could not get into the country which lay before us to destroy the inhabitants of our land.

But it came to pass that whatsoever lands we had passed by, and the inhabitants thereof were not gathered in, were destroyed by the Lamanites, and their towns, and villages, and cities were burned with fire; and thus the three hundred and seventy and nine years passed away.

And it came to pass that in the three hundred and eightieth year, the Lamanites did come again against us to battle, and we did stand against them boldly; but it was all in vain, for so great were their numbers that they did tread the people of the Nephites under their feet.

And it came to pass that we did again take to flight, and they whose flight were swifter than the Lamanites did escape, and they whose flight did not exceed the Lamanites, were swept down and destroyed.

And now behold, I, Mormon, do not desire to harrow up the souls of men in casting before them such an awful scene of blood and carnage as was laid before mine eyes, but I, knowing that these things must surely be made known, and that all things which are hid must be revealed upon the house tops,

provenance.route: Luke 12:2-3 (or Matthew 10:26-27 — see below) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The saying is a couplet and the Book of Mormon has collapsed it. “hid, that shall not be known” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Matthew 10:26, Luke 8:17, Luke 12:2); “shall not be revealed” occurs in exactly two (Matthew 10:26, Luke 12:2); “upon the housetops” occurs in exactly four (Psalm 129:6, Zephaniah 1:5, Matthew 10:27, Luke 12:3). Mormon 5:8 has 'all things which are hid must be revealed upon the house tops', which takes the verb of the first line and the place of the second and puts them in one clause. No KJV verse says anything is revealed upon the housetops: Luke 12:3 has 'proclaimed', Matthew 10:27 has 'preach ye'.
provenance.significance: Which synoptic is undecidable on the wording, and the tool says so. tools/mediation-check.py finds no divergence between Matthew 10:26 and Luke 12:2 that this verse touches — the two differ only in Matthew's opening 'Fear them not therefore' and in 'and' against 'neither', and Mormon has neither element. Between the second halves there is one weak discriminator: Mormon's construction is passive and future ('must be revealed'), which is Luke 12:3's shape ('shall be proclaimed') and not Matthew 10:27's imperative ('preach ye'). That, and Hardy's cross-reference, is why the row is filed on Luke; the Matthean parallel is carried in composite and the case should be read as synoptic rather than Lukan. The metalepsis is worth the recovery. In both gospels the saying is addressed to disciples told not to fear those who kill the body: whatever is whispered under threat of death will be shouted from the roofs. Mormon is a man who has watched his nation killed and is explaining why he will write the record down at all — 'I do not desire to harrow up the souls of men … but I, knowing that these things must surely be made known'. He quotes the fearless-speech saying as the reason he cannot keep silent about a slaughter he would rather not describe.
provenance.mt: 1830 prints 'house tops' as two words where the KJV has 'housetops'; 1920 prints 'house-tops'. The borrowing is not orthographic here and the split spelling is a small argument against a purely visual copy.

links.note: 'And that all things which are hid must be revealed upon the house tops.' Fewer than sixteen words and so below Skousen's threshold for a King James quotation — this is not one of his 36 — but the contact is not in doubt: two distinctive elements of a two-verse synoptic saying are fused into a single clause, and the fusion is not in any Bible. The interest is in the compression. The gospel saying distinguishes what is hidden (which will be revealed) from what is spoken in secret (which will be proclaimed from the housetops); Mormon runs the two together so that the hidden thing itself goes up onto the roof. That is exactly what he is claiming about the record in his hands.
links.text: For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known.

pericopes.text: and also that a knowledge of these things must come unto the remnant of these people, and also unto the Gentiles, which the Lord hath said should scatter this people, and this people should be counted as nought among them, therefore I write a small abridgement, daring not to give a full account of the things which I have seen, because of the commandment which I have received, and also that ye might not have too great sorrow because of the wickedness of this people.
And now behold, this I speak unto their seed, and also to the Gentiles, which hath care for the house of Israel, that realize and know from whence their blessings come:

For I know that such will sorrow for the calamity of the house of Israel; yea, they will sorrow for the destruction of this people; they will sorrow that this people had not repented, that they might have been clasped in the arms of Jesus.

Now these things are written unto the remnant of the house of Jacob; and they are written after this manner, because it is known of God that wickedness will not bring them forth unto them; and they are to be hid up unto the Lord, that they may come forth in his own due time.
And this is the commandment which I have received; and behold they shall come forth according to the commandment of the Lord, when he shall see fit, in his wisdom.

And behold they shall go unto the unbelieving of the Jews; and for this intent shall they go: that they may be persuaded that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God; that the Father may bring about, through his most beloved, his great and eternal purpose, in the restoring the Jews, or all the house of Israel, to the land of their inheritance, which the Lord their God hath given them, unto the fulfilling of his covenant,

provenance.route: John 20:31 (the purpose clause) + Matthew 16:16 (the title) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Jesus is the Christ” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (John 20:31, 1 John 2:22, 1 John 5:1); “the Son of the living God” occurs in exactly two (Matthew 16:16, John 6:69). Mormon 5:14 has both at once — 'that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God' — and that full string is in no KJV verse. John 20:31 reads 'the Son of God'; Matthew 16:16 reads 'Thou art the Christ'. The Book of Mormon has taken the predicate from one and the title from the other.
provenance.significance: The frame is what makes this more than a fused epithet. John 20:31 is the colophon of a gospel, the sentence in which a writer stops narrating and says why he wrote: 'these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ'. Mormon 5:12-14 is the colophon of a record — 'these things are written unto the remnant of the house of Jacob … and for this intent shall they go: that they may be persuaded that Jesus is the Christ' — and it states the Book of Mormon's own purpose in John's terms, two verses after stating that the record is written and hidden up. Recover John 20:31's context and the point of the echo is a claim about genre: this book is asking to be read as a gospel's closing sentence asks to be read. Note also the substitution John will not make: John writes 'the Son of God', and Mormon upgrades it to Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi, the one place in the gospels where the title is given by revelation rather than by a narrator.

links.note: 'That they may be persuaded that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.' Eight words of John's purpose clause with Peter's confession spliced into its second half. The verse is doing the same work John 20:31 does — explaining why a written record exists and what its readers are meant to conclude — and it is doing it in a chapter that has just said the record is 'to be hid up unto the Lord, that they may come forth in his own due time' (5:12). The machine stream reached John 20:31 on its own here, on an eight-word run, which is unusual; most of this chapter's links are invisible to it.
links.text: But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.

pericopes.text: and also that the seed of this people may more fully believe his gospel, which shall go forth unto them from the Gentiles: for this people shall be scattered, and shall become a dark, a filthy, and a loathsome people, beyond the description of that which ever hath been amongst us; yea, even that which hath been among the Lamanites; and this because of their unbelief and idolatry:
For behold, the spirit of the Lord hath already ceased to strive with their fathers, and they are without Christ and God in the world, and they are driven about as chaff before the wind.

provenance.other: “without Christ” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “without God in the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse. Ephesians 2:12 reads 'ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world'. Mormon 5:16 reads 'they are without Christ and God in the world', which is the first phrase and the last with the thirteen intervening words and the second 'without' elided.
provenance.significance: This is metalepsis in Hays's strict sense, and the suppressed material is the argument of the chapter. What Mormon 5:16 deletes from the middle of Ephesians 2:12 is 'aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise' — and Mormon 5 is about nothing else. Four verses later the covenant returns by name: 'then will the Lord remember the covenant which he made unto Abraham, and unto all the house of Israel' (5:20). A reader who recovers the elided clause finds the chapter's thesis sitting inside the verse it was cut out of. The transfer also inverts Paul. Ephesians 2:12 describes Gentiles in their former state, outside a commonwealth that belonged to somebody else; Mormon applies it word for word to the seed of Israel, and gives the blessing they lost to the Gentiles in the very next paragraph (5:19). Paul's next move, 'ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ', is the shape of Mormon's 5:20 — scattering, then remembrance.

links.note: 'They are without Christ and God in the world.' Two King James singletons from a single verse, fused by dropping the thirteen words between them. Dependence is not seriously deniable: either phrase alone occurs once in the Bible, and both occur here in the source's order. The row matters as much for how it was found as for what it says. The n-gram stream did not propose Ephesians 2:12 anywhere in this chapter and could not have: the two phrases are separated in the source by a clause the Book of Mormon does not reproduce, so no contiguous window sees the agreement. This is the failure mode CONVENTIONS §9 records at Psalm 145:9 and it produced the strongest link in the chapter.
links.text: That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world:

provenance.other: “not always strive” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The bare verb “strive with” occurs in six, and none of the other five has a divine subject: Genesis 26:20 is herdsmen quarrelling over a well, Psalm 35:1 and Isaiah 41:11 are human adversaries, Isaiah 45:9 is the potsherd, Hosea 4:4 is striving with the priest. The Spirit of God striving with men, and ceasing to, is Genesis 6:3 alone.
provenance.significance: Genesis 6:3 is the sentence God passes immediately before the Flood: the Spirit is withdrawn, a term of years is set, and then the race is destroyed. Mormon writes it in the perfect tense — 'hath already ceased to strive' — about a people whose destruction he has just finished narrating and will finish burying in the next chapter. The tense is the whole argument. Genesis 6:3 is a countdown; Mormon 5:16 reports that the countdown has already run out. Recover the context and the reader is told what comes next without being told, which is the point of the figure.

links.note: 'For behold, the spirit of the Lord hath already ceased to strive with their fathers.' The idiom is Genesis 6:3's and no other verse's, and Mormon takes it at the exact moment in his narrative where Genesis takes it — after a long account of universal violence and immediately before the extinction of the people described. Note that he moves it back a generation: it is 'their fathers' the Spirit ceased to strive with, so that the destruction of the present generation is already a foregone thing when the chapter opens.
links.text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

provenance.route: Psalm 35:5 (the phrase) + Psalm 1:4 (the verb) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “chaff before the wind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 35:5. The participle Mormon attaches to it is not there: Psalm 35:5 has 'Let them BE as chaff before the wind'. “the wind driveth away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 1:4, 'like the chaff which the wind driveth away'. Mormon 5:16 has 'driven about as chaff before the wind' and 5:18 has 'as chaff is driven before the wind', which is the second psalm's verb inside the first psalm's phrase, twice.
provenance.significance: Psalm 35:5 is a petition, not a description. The psalmist asks God to make his persecutors chaff before the wind and to send the angel of the LORD after them. Mormon reports the petition granted against his own nation, which puts the covenant people in the grammatical position the psalm reserves for its enemies — and Psalm 1:4, which supplies the verb, identifies the chaff as 'the ungodly'. Both psalms are prayers of the righteous about somebody else; Mormon 5:16 is a righteous man saying it of his own.

links.note: 'And they are driven about as chaff before the wind.' A King James singleton, repeated two verses later in a variant form, with a participle drawn from the only other verse in the Bible where chaff and wind are put together this way. The repetition at 5:18 is what raises this above a stock simile: Mormon uses the phrase twice in three verses, in a chapter whose other borrowings are single and precise, and the second use extends it into a second figure — 'or as a vessel is tossed about upon the waves, without sail or anchor'.
links.text: Let them be as chaff before the wind: and let the angel of the LORD chase them.

pericopes.text: They were once a delightsome people, and they had Christ for their Shepherd; yea, they were led even by God, the Father.

But now, behold they are led about by satan, even as chaff is driven before the wind, or as a vessel is tossed about upon the waves, without sail or anchor, or without any thing wherewith to steer her; and even as she is, so are they.

provenance.other: “anchor” in the singular occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:19: 'which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast'. The plural “anchors” occurs in exactly three, all of them in the shipwreck of Acts 27 (27:29, 27:30, 27:40), where they are ship's tackle and nothing else. So the King James Bible has exactly one anchor that means anything, and what it means is hope.
provenance.alternative: A rudderless, anchorless ship is a commonplace figure for a people without direction and needs no scriptural source whatever; Mormon has spent his life on a continent and a page describing flight and drift, and 5:18's sail, anchor and steering are a single sustained image that reads as his own. Acts 27 is the more natural nautical background if one is wanted.
provenance.significance: Read against Hebrews 6:19 the negation becomes an argument rather than a picture. Mormon opened the chapter 'without hopes' (5:2), reported his people 'without Christ and God in the world' at 5:16 from a verse whose third privative is 'having no hope', and here sets them adrift 'without sail or anchor'. In the King James Bible the anchor IS the hope, and it is 'sure and stedfast' precisely because it 'entereth into that within the veil' — it holds because it is fastened to something beyond the storm. A people cut off from the covenant has nothing on the far side to be fastened to. The chain is the reason the row is here; the single word is not.

links.note: 'Or as a vessel is tossed about upon the waves, without sail or anchor, or without any thing wherewith to steer her.' One word of contact, and it is offered as a reading rather than as a demonstration. What makes it worth proposing is that the word is a King James singleton in the singular and that its one occurrence is the metaphor Mormon 5 has already used twice in the negative. Take the three privatives together — no hope, no Christ, no anchor — and the chapter is running one figure, not three. Take them apart and this row is a coincidence about a common noun. Recorded under CONVENTIONS §0a with the objection stated in full.
links.text: Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil;

pericopes.text: And behold, the Lord hath reserved their blessing, which they might have received in the land, for the Gentiles, which shall possess the land.—

provenance.route: Romans 11 → KJV → Book of Mormon (structural, not verbal)
provenance.other: There is almost no shared wording and the row does not claim any. “because of unbelief” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Romans 11:20, Hebrews 3:19, Hebrews 4:6), and Mormon 5:15's 'because of their unbelief and idolatry' is close to Romans 11:20's 'because of unbelief they were broken off' — but the phrase is too ordinary to carry a link on its own and is recorded here only as the one point of verbal contact in the sequence.
provenance.significance: The argument, not the wording, is Paul's. Romans 11 runs: Israel stumbles through unbelief; the blessing passes to the Gentiles for a season; the Gentiles are warned not to boast, because the root bears them and not they the root; and when the fulness of the Gentiles is come in, God remembers his covenant. Mormon 5:15-21 runs the same four steps in the same order — scattered 'because of their unbelief' (5:15), 'the Lord hath reserved their blessing … for the Gentiles' (5:19), 'O ye Gentiles, how can ye stand' with a demand that they 'realize and know from whence their blessings come' (5:10, 5:22), and then 'will the Lord remember the covenant which he made unto Abraham' (5:20). Romans 11:18's 'boast not against the branches' and Mormon 5:10's 'realize and know from whence their blessings come' are the same warning to the same audience for the same reason.

links.note: 'And behold, the Lord hath reserved their blessing, which they might have received in the land, for the Gentiles, which shall possess the land.' Filed as figural because there is no wording to test: the case is that Mormon 5:15-21 reproduces the four-step argument of Romans 11 in Romans's order, including the turn to second-person address of the Gentiles and the warning against forgetting whose root they are standing on. Confidence is moderate rather than high because a covenant book could reach this sequence from Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 without Paul, and 5:20 shows it drawing directly on Leviticus 26:42 for the last step. What Leviticus cannot supply is the middle two steps — the transfer of the blessing to the Gentiles and the reproof of Gentile presumption — and those are Romans 11's contribution to the chapter. Invisible to the machine streams by construction.
links.text: For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.

pericopes.text: But behold, it shall come to pass that they shall be driven and scattered by the Gentiles; and after that they have been driven and scattered by the Gentiles, behold, then will the Lord remember the covenant which he made unto Abraham, and unto all the house of Israel.

provenance.other: “Then will I remember” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 26:42, where it governs the covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham. “remember my covenant” occurs in exactly three (Genesis 9:15, Leviticus 26:42, Ezekiel 16:60); Genesis 9:15 is Noah's rainbow and Ezekiel 16:60 is Jerusalem's youth, so Leviticus 26:42 is the only one where the covenant remembered is the patriarchs'. Mormon 5:20 converts the person — 'then will the Lord remember the covenant which he made unto Abraham' — and keeps the construction and the ordering, Abraham last.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 2:24, 'God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob', is the other place the patriarchal covenant is remembered after affliction, and Luke 1:72's 'to remember his holy covenant' is the New Testament's form of the same idea.
provenance.significance: tools/mediation-check.py was run on Leviticus 26:42 against Exodus 2:24 and Luke 1:72 and returned divergences pointing both ways, which the tool correctly refuses to resolve. Read out, the split is not evenly balanced. The two points favouring Leviticus are positive: Mormon has 'then will … remember' against Exodus's 'And God … remembered', and he has the Abraham-last ordering. The one point favouring Luke 1:72 is that Mormon lacks Leviticus's long triple list of patriarchs — an absence, and an absence explained by the sentence Mormon is writing, which needs one name and not three. Direct-OT is the call. What settles it beyond the phrase is the surrounding chapter: Leviticus 26 is the covenant-curse chapter, and its sequence is Mormon 5's sequence exactly — cities laid waste (26:31, 33), the people scattered among the heathen (26:33), the land enjoying her sabbaths while they are in their enemies' land (26:34), and then, at 26:42, remembrance. Mormon 5:5 burned the towns and cities, 5:20 scatters the people among the Gentiles, and 5:20 remembers the covenant. He is not quoting a verse; he is running a chapter.

links.note: 'And after that they have been driven and scattered by the Gentiles, behold, then will the Lord remember the covenant which he made unto Abraham, and unto all the house of Israel.' A King James singleton construction in a third-person conversion, sitting at exactly the point of Leviticus 26 where the singleton sits — after the scattering and before the restoration. The link is worth more than its four shared words because what is borrowed is the hinge of a chapter, not a phrase from it: the whole force of Leviticus 26:42 is that the remembering comes AFTER the scattering and not instead of it, and Mormon builds his sentence on the same 'after … then'.
links.text: Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob, and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land.

pericopes.text: And also the Lord will remember the prayers of the righteous, which hath been put up unto him for them.
And then, O ye Gentiles, how can ye stand before the power of God, except ye shall repent and turn from your evil ways?

provenance.other: The wording proves nothing by itself: “able to stand” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses and “who can stand” in exactly three (Deuteronomy 9:2, Psalm 147:17, Nahum 1:6). Mormon's 'how can ye stand before the power of God' is the generic form of a question the King James Bible asks in several places, and Nahum 1:6, Malachi 3:2 and 1 Samuel 6:20 are all live alternatives.
provenance.alternative: Nahum 1:6, 'Who can stand before his indignation?', is the closest single verse and would account for the sentence with no help from Revelation.
provenance.significance: The reason to name Revelation 6:17 rather than Nahum is the next verse. Revelation 6:14-17 is the one passage in the Bible where the unanswerable question 'who shall be able to stand?' is set beside the heaven departing 'as a scroll when it is rolled together' — and Mormon 5:22-23 sets those two motifs side by side too, in adjacent sentences addressed to the same audience. The order is reversed (Revelation has the scroll then the question; Mormon has the question then the scroll), which is why this is an echo and not more. But 5:23's scroll is a demonstrable King James borrowing, and mediation-check.py shows its wording is Isaiah 34:4's rather than Revelation 6:14's. So the pair is worth stating precisely: the words at 5:23 come from Isaiah, and the company they keep at 5:22 comes from the chapter of Revelation that quotes Isaiah. That is a real distinction between a source and a setting, and it is the kind of thing the mediation field exists to catch.

links.note: 'And then, O ye Gentiles, how can ye stand before the power of God, except ye shall repent and turn from your evil ways?' Filed at moderate on sequence rather than on vocabulary, and the vocabulary is frankly weak — ten KJV verses ask a version of this question. What is not weak is that the two images of Revelation 6:14-17, the rhetorical question about standing and the heavens rolled up as a scroll, occur in Mormon 5 within one verse of each other, and nowhere else in the book. The inverted order counts against it and is recorded.
links.text: For the great day of his wrath is come; and who shall be able to stand?

pericopes.text: Know ye not that ye are in the hands of God? Know ye not that he hath all power, and at his great command the earth shall be rolled together as a scroll?
