provenance.other: “rolled together as a scroll” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “shall be rolled together” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are Isaiah 34:4. “as a scroll” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 34:4 and Revelation 6:14, which is the New Testament's reuse of it and the reason mediation had to be tested rather than assumed.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 6:14, 'the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together', is the same image in the same Bible and is the passage a reader is likelier to know.
provenance.significance: tools/mediation-check.py returns one decisive point and it is clean: Revelation adds 'when it is rolled together' as a trailing subordinate clause after 'as a scroll', and the Book of Mormon does not have it. Mormon has Isaiah's order — 'shall be rolled together as a scroll' — with the participle before the noun, which is Isaiah's syntax and not John's. So the phrasing is the Old Testament's, taken directly, in a chapter that has otherwise been drawing on the New Testament heavily (Ephesians 2:12 at 5:16, John 20:31 at 5:14, the synoptic saying at 5:8). The one substitution is the interesting residue: Isaiah rolls up THE HEAVENS, and Mormon rolls up THE EARTH. Isaiah 34 is a judgment on Edom in which the sky is dismantled over a land given to desolation; Mormon, standing on a continent that has just been emptied of its people, transfers the dissolution to the ground under it.

links.note: 'Know ye not that he hath all power, and at his great command the earth shall be rolled together as a scroll?' Six words verbatim from a verse whose phrase occurs nowhere else in the Bible, with one noun changed. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and so not one of his King James quotations, but by CONVENTIONS §2 the completeness of the reproduced predicate and the absolute rarity of the phrase make quotation the right category regardless of length. The mediation is the finding here rather than the borrowing: with Revelation 6:14 available and better known, the text takes Isaiah's form.
links.text: And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree.

provenance.other: “Know ye not that ye are” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 3:16, 'Know ye not that ye are the temple of God'. The shorter “Know ye not” occurs in seventeen, and thirteen of the seventeen are Paul's, eleven of those in 1 Corinthians alone (3:16, 5:6, 6:3, 6:9, 6:15, 6:16, 6:19, 9:24 and the rest). The formula is not rare; the completed six-word opening is.
provenance.alternative: Mormon has used interrogative address before this chapter and 'know ye not' is available to any English writer who has read Paul at all — which, on this text's own account of itself, is not available to Mormon, but is the point of the catalogue rather than an argument against the row.
provenance.significance: What is borrowed is a manner of arguing, not a proposition. Paul's 'know ye not' is the hammer of the diatribe: a rapid series of rhetorical questions, each assuming the answer, put to an audience being told it has forgotten what it already knows. Mormon uses it doubled — 'Know ye not that ye are in the hands of God? Know ye not that he hath all power' — in the only place in his book where he turns from narration to address the Gentile reader directly. The predicate is the interesting change. Paul completes the phrase with 'the temple of God'; Mormon completes it with 'in the hands of God', which turns Paul's assurance of indwelling into a warning about being held.

links.note: 'Know ye not that ye are in the hands of God? Know ye not that he hath all power?' The six-word opening is a King James singleton and the doubling is Pauline in a way that a single instance would not be. Offered at moderate because the sense diverges sharply from 1 Corinthians 3:16 — Paul is reassuring the Corinthians that they are God's dwelling; Mormon is telling the Gentiles they are in God's grip — and because the phrase, unlike the chapter's other borrowings, is a piece of rhetorical furniture rather than an image. Its value is that it fixes the register of 5:22-24 as apostolic address rather than prophetic oracle, which is what the second-person turn at 5:24 then confirms.
links.text: Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?

pericopes.text: Therefore repent ye, and humble yourselves before him, lest he shall come out in justice against you; lest a remnant of the seed of Jacob shall go forth among you as a lion, and tear you in pieces, and there is none to deliver.

provenance.route: Micah 5:8 → 3 Nephi 20:16 (Jesus's citation) → Mormon 5:24, fused with Psalm 50:22
provenance.other: Two sources, and the seam between them is visible. From Micah 5:8: “as a lion among the beasts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “none can deliver” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Micah 5:8; “remnant of Jacob” occurs in exactly three (Isaiah 10:21, Micah 5:7, Micah 5:8). From Psalm 50:22: “tear you in pieces” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Mormon 5:24's closing clause is 'and tear you in pieces, and there is none to deliver' — 'tear you', second person, is Psalm 50:22's and cannot be Micah's, which has the third-person 'teareth in pieces'; and 'there is none to deliver' is one auxiliary from Psalm 50:22's 'there be none to deliver' and two words from Micah's 'none can deliver'.
provenance.significance: The mediation is the finding, and it is checkable on one word. Micah 5:8 reads 'the remnant of Jacob shall BE AMONG the Gentiles'. 3 Nephi 20:16, where the risen Jesus recites Micah to the Nephites, reads 'then shall ye which are a remnant of the house of Jacob, GO FORTH AMONG them' — a substitution that belongs to that recitation and to no Bible; “go forth among” occurs in no KJV verse at all. Mormon 5:24 has 'a remnant of the seed of Jacob shall GO FORTH AMONG you'. The proximate model is therefore the Book of Mormon's own earlier citation and not the prophet, which is what mediation 'OT-via-earlier-BoM' is for, and it is the cleanest instance of it the catalogue has had outside 2 Nephi. Note that 3 Nephi 21:12 gives the same passage in Micah's own wording, 'shall be among the Gentiles' — so the book contains both forms and Mormon reproduced the one with the substitution. tools/mediation-check.py, run on Micah 5:8 against Psalm 50:22, returns one decisive point for Micah on the absence of 'there be'; that reading is an artifact of how the segments align, since Mormon's 'there is' is Psalm's construction with one auxiliary changed and not Micah's at all. The tool is right that the verse is composite and wrong about which side the last clause falls on. Recovering Psalm 50:22 pays: it is addressed to 'ye that forget God', and Mormon's demand of the Gentiles fourteen verses earlier was that they 'realize and know from whence their blessings come' (5:10).
provenance.alternative: Micah 5:8 alone, taken direct from the Old Testament, accounts for the lion and the remnant and would be the default reading; it does not account for 'go forth among' or for the second-person 'tear you'.

links.note: 'Lest a remnant of the seed of Jacob shall go forth among you as a lion, and tear you in pieces, and there is none to deliver.' Micah's oracle turned into a threat and aimed at the reader. Three things are happening at once. Micah's remnant is a promise to Israel about the nations; Mormon keeps the lion and the remnant and points them at the Gentiles he is addressing. Psalm 50:22 supplies the second person — 'lest I tear you in pieces' — and with it the psalm's premise, that the people being warned are people who have forgotten God. And the verb of motion is not Micah's but the Book of Mormon's own, taken from the risen Christ's recitation of Micah at 3 Nephi 20:16, which is why the mediation is filed through the earlier Book of Mormon text rather than direct-OT. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Micah 5:8 here; the psalm and the internal route are this catalogue's.
links.text: And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the Gentiles in the midst of many people as a lion among the beasts of the forest, as a young lion among the flocks of sheep: who, if he go through, both treadeth down, and teareth in pieces, and none can deliver.

pericopes.text: And now I finish my record concerning the destruction of my people, the Nephites. And it came to pass that we did march forth before the Lamanites.

And I, Mormon, wrote an epistle unto the king of the Lamanites, and desired of him that he would grant unto us that we might gather together our people unto the land of Camorah, by a hill which was called Camorah, and there we would give them battle.

links.text: That he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear,

provenance.other: “that he would grant unto us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 1:74; “grant unto us” occurs in exactly two, Luke 1:74 and Mark 10:37. The eight-word run “that he would grant unto us that we” is shared by these two sentences and by nothing else in either book: the string occurs nowhere else in the Book of Mormon.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing turns inside out. Luke 1:74 is the middle of the Benedictus, Zacharias's prophecy of what the covenant with Abraham was for: “that he would grant unto us, that we being delivered out of the hand of our enemies might serve him without fear.” Mormon's petition has the same eight words and reverses every term under them. The one who is asked to grant is not God but the king of the Lamanites; what is asked for is not deliverance out of the hand of the enemy but permission to assemble in front of him; and what it secures is not serving God without fear but, five verses later, waiting for him with “that awful fear of death which fills the breasts of all the wicked” (6:7). The Book of Mormon's last Nephite prayer is addressed to the enemy, and it is worded out of the KJV's prayer for rescue from enemies.

links.note: “And I, Mormon, wrote an epistle unto the king of the Lamanites, and desired of him that he would grant unto us that we might gather together our people unto the land of Camorah.” Eight consecutive words of Luke 1:74, in Luke's order, and Luke's construction all the way through: the subordinated “that he would grant unto us” followed by a second “that we … might”. Nothing in the diplomatic situation calls for this phrasing; “asked him to let us gather” would do the same work. The run is well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six, but on the pilot's standard (CONVENTIONS §2) a run this long from a KJV singleton is a link. Note that the machine stream did rank this first in the chapter, at rarity 3.17 — one of the few places in Mormon where the n-gram floor and the reading agree.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the king of the Lamanites did grant unto me the thing which I desired.

And it came to pass that we did march forth to the land of Camorah, and we did pitch our tents round about the hill Camorah; and it was in a land of many waters, rivers and fountains; and here we had hope to gain advantage over the Lamanites.

links.text: And the third angel poured out his vial upon the rivers and fountains of waters; and they became blood.

provenance.other: “rivers and fountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:4. “land of many waters” occurs in no KJV verse; “many waters” is common, and in Revelation 17:1 and 17:15 it is the seat of the whore and is glossed as “peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues”.
provenance.significance: The one place in the King James Bible where rivers and fountains are named together is the third bowl of Revelation 16, where they are turned to blood; twelve verses later, at Revelation 16:16, the kings of the earth are gathered “into a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon” — a battlefield known by a name rather than a description, which is what the hill Camorah is about to become. Mormon's survey of the ground is dated, tactical and flat (“here we had hope to gain advantage over the Lamanites”), and eleven verses later the ground has flesh, bones and blood lying on it (6:15). Whether or not the phrase was chosen, the catalogue records that the Book of Mormon's Armageddon is described in the vocabulary of Revelation's.

links.note: “And it was in a land of many waters, rivers and fountains.” Two words of contact, and they are the two words that occur together in only one KJV verse. Set against that: this is an ordinary English pair for describing well-watered country, the syntax shares nothing with Revelation 16:4, and the Book of Mormon uses “many waters” eleven times without apocalyptic freight. Recorded at moderate because the rarity is real and the setting — the naming of the final battlefield — is where an apocalyptic phrase would matter most if it is one.
links.whyNot: “Rivers and fountains” may simply be the natural English pairing for a watered landscape; its being a KJV singleton is at least partly an accident of how seldom the KJV describes terrain. There is no second point of contact with Revelation 16 anywhere in the chapter, and the Armageddon reading depends on a verse (16:16) that shares no wording with Mormon 6 at all.

pericopes.text: And when three hundred and eighty and four years had passed away, we had gathered in all the remainder of our people unto the land Camorah.

And it came to pass that when we had gathered in all our people in one to the land of Camorah, behold I, Mormon, began to be old; and knowing it to be the last struggle of my people, and having been commanded of the Lord that I should not suffer that the records which had been handed down by our fathers, which were sacred, to fall into the hands of the Lamanites, (for the Lamanites would destroy them,) therefore I made this record out of the plates of Nephi, and hid up in the hill Camorah, all the records which had been entrusted to me by the hand of the Lord, save it were these few plates which I gave unto my son Moroni.

And it came to pass that my people, with their wives and their children, did now behold the armies of the Lamanites a marching towards them; and with that awful fear of death which fills the breasts of all the wicked, did they await to receive them.

links.text: And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.

provenance.other: “fear of death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 2:15. It occurs in exactly two verses of the Book of Mormon: here and Moroni 9:5, in the letter Mormon writes to Moroni about this same war, where the Nephites are so angry that “it seemeth me that they have no fear of death”.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 2:15 does not merely mention the fear of death; it defines it as the condition Christ came to end — “that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death … and deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.” Mormon says of his people that they died in exactly that fear, and ten verses later says why: “how could ye have rejected that Jesus, who stood with open arms to receive you” (6:17). The KJV's only sentence about the fear of death is a sentence about being delivered from it, and Mormon's people are the case in which the deliverance was declined. That reading is what makes the aside “which fills the breasts of all the wicked” more than a moralising interjection: it is the diagnosis Hebrews gives.

links.note: “And with that awful fear of death which fills the breasts of all the wicked, did they await to receive them.” The definite article is the tell — “that awful fear of death”, as though naming something already known. What is already known is Hebrews 2:15, the only KJV verse in which the phrase appears, where the fear of death is a lifelong bondage rather than a battlefield emotion. Mormon generalises it in exactly Hebrews' direction: not fear felt by these men on this morning, but the standing condition of “all the wicked”. Two words is thin contact and the note rests on the singleton and on the theology it carries, not on volume.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that they came to battle against us, and every soul was filled with terror, because of the greatness of their numbers.
And it came to pass that they did fall upon my people with the sword, and with the bow, and with the arrow, and with the axe, and with all manner of weapons of war.
And it came to pass that my men were hewn down, yea, even my ten thousand which were with me, and I fell wounded in the midst; and they passed by me that they did not put an end to my life.

And when they had gone through and hewn down all my people save it were twenty and four of us, (among whom was my son Moroni,) and we having survived the dead of our people, did behold on the morrow, when the Lamanites had returned unto their camps, from the top of the hill Camorah, the ten thousand of my people which were hewn down, being led in the front by me;
and we also beheld the ten thousand of my people which were led by my son Moroni.
And behold, the ten thousand of Gidgiddonah had fallen, and he also in the midst;

links.text: How are the mighty fallen in the midst of the battle! O Jonathan, thou wast slain in thine high places.

provenance.other: “in the midst of the battle” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 1:25, and in no other verse of the Book of Mormon. “how are the mighty fallen” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 2 Samuel 1:19, 1:25 and 1:27 — all three of them this one lament. “the weapons of war” occurs in exactly two, 2 Samuel 1:27 and Jeremiah 21:4.
provenance.significance: David's elegy is the King James Bible's battlefield lament, and Mormon 6 is the Book of Mormon's. The correspondences are of position, not only of wording. David laments from outside a defeat he did not witness; Mormon laments from the top of the hill on the morning after one he survived. 2 Samuel 1:19 and 1:25 place the slain “upon thy high places” and Mormon 6:11 places the surviving twenty-four “from the top of the hill Camorah”, looking down at the ten thousand. David's refrain closes on “the weapons of war perished” and Mormon's roll-call opens with “all manner of weapons of war” (6:9). What the Book of Mormon does with the form is to break it: David names two dead men, Mormon names twenty-three and then, at 6:15, gives up naming and counts.

links.note: “And behold, the ten thousand of Gidgiddonah had fallen, and he also in the midst.” The two distinctive elements of 2 Samuel 1:25 are here, in its order — the falling, then the midst — split across a clause boundary rather than reproduced as a run, which is exactly the shape the n-gram stream cannot see (CONVENTIONS §9) and this candidate was not proposed by it. Three verses earlier Mormon says of himself “I fell wounded in the midst” (6:10), which is the same pairing again in the first person. Then the chapter repeats “had fallen” eleven times in three verses and closes the sequence with “ye are fallen” (6:18) and “how is it that ye could have fallen!” (6:19) — a refrain in the position David's refrain occupies. Adjudicated here rather than at 6:10 because 6:13 holds both elements in the KJV's order; the apostrophe half of the same lament is at 6:19.
links.whyNot: “In the midst” alone is common KJV English and “fallen” is unavoidable in a battle narrative; the case rests on the two appearing together, twice, in a chapter that is generically an elegy, rather than on any reproduced clause. A reader who thinks the elegy form is simply what any lament over a defeat looks like can decline the whole row.

pericopes.text: and Lamah had fallen with his ten thousand; and Gilgal had fallen with his ten thousand; and Limhah had fallen with his ten thousand; and Joneam had fallen with his ten thousand; and Camenihah, and Moronihah, and Antionum, and Shiblom, and Shem, and Josh, had fallen with their ten thousand each.

And it came to pass that there were ten more which did fall by the sword, with their ten thousand each; yea, even all my people, save it were those twenty and four which were with me, and also a few which had escaped into the south countries, and a few which had dissented over unto the Lamanites, had fallen, and their flesh, and bones, and blood lay upon the face of the earth, being left by the hands of those who slew them, to moulder upon the land, and to crumble and to return to their mother earth.

links.text: And the slain of the LORD shall be at that day from one end of the earth even unto the other end of the earth: they shall not be lamented, neither gathered, nor buried; they shall be dung upon the ground.

provenance.other: “dung upon the face of the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 8:2 and Jeremiah 16:4, and Jeremiah 25:33 has the same clause with “ground” for “face of the earth”; the three are one oracle repeated. “mother earth” occurs in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own phrase (2 Nephi 9:7, Mosiah 2:26); the nearest KJV sentence is Genesis 3:19, “dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return”.
provenance.significance: The unburied corpse is not a detail of atrocity in the KJV, it is a covenant sanction — Deuteronomy 28:26 threatens it, and Jeremiah passes the sentence three times in the same words. What Jeremiah's formula holds together is precisely Mormon's list: not lamented, not gathered, not buried. Mormon's people are all three. They cannot be gathered because the twenty-four who could gather them are all that is left; they are not buried because there is no one to bury them; and the lamenting is done by one man, in the next verse, for a nation. Read against Jeremiah, the six verses of names in 6:13-15 are the burial the bodies did not get.

links.note: “Their flesh, and bones, and blood lay upon the face of the earth, being left by the hands of those who slew them, to moulder upon the land, and to crumble and to return to their mother earth.” No clause is reproduced, and the sentence's closing phrase is the Book of Mormon's own, not the KJV's. What is Jeremiah's is the whole configuration: corpses left where they fell, on the face of the earth, unlamented and unburied, as the terminal image of a judgment oracle — and Jeremiah is the prophet the chapter reaches for again in the very next verse (see 6:16). Recorded at moderate: the motif is Jeremiah's and the wording is Mormon's. 1830 reads “moulder”, modernized to “molder” in 1920, and “mouldering” likewise at 6:21 — the first edition keeps the KJV's spelling habits in a sentence that has no KJV wording in it.

pericopes.text: And my soul was rent with anguish, because of the slain of my people: And I cried,

links.text: Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people!

provenance.other: “the slain of” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Isaiah 66:16, Jeremiah 9:1, Jeremiah 25:33 and Jeremiah 51:49 — and Jeremiah 9:1 is the only one that joins it to “my people”. “slain of my people” occurs in no KJV verse and in exactly two Book of Mormon verses: 2 Nephi 26:7 and here. “rent with anguish” occurs in no KJV verse and in exactly two Book of Mormon verses: 1 Nephi 17:47 and here.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's best case for a borrowing that has passed through the Book of Mormon before reaching its user. Jeremiah 9:1 supplies the figure — a prophet weeping over the slain of his own people, in a book that has just finished pronouncing their destruction. But the exact string Mormon uses, “the slain of my people”, is not Jeremiah's (his is “the slain of the daughter of my people”); it is Nephi's, at 2 Nephi 26:7, where it is spoken as prophecy of this very battle: “O the pain, and the anguish of my soul for the loss of the slain of my people! For I, Nephi, hath seen it, and it well nigh consumeth me.” Mormon's cry therefore lands on words already written for it six centuries earlier in the book he is abridging, and “my soul was rent with anguish” carries Nephi's other lament with it, the “rent with anguish” of 1 Nephi 17:47. Mormon's is the only lament in scripture that is a quotation of a vision of itself.

links.note: “And my soul was rent with anguish, because of the slain of my people: And I cried.” Two Book of Mormon strings meet here, both Nephi's, and behind them one KJV verse. The mediation is decidable on the wording: Jeremiah 9:1 reads “the slain of the daughter of my people”, 2 Nephi 26:7 reads “the slain of my people”, and Mormon 6:16 has Nephi's form, not Jeremiah's — so the proximate model is the earlier Book of Mormon verse and the ultimate source is Jeremiah. The pairing of soul, anguish and the slain runs through all three. Note also what follows in both books: Jeremiah 9:1 introduces a chapter of unburied bodies (9:22, “as dung upon the open field”), and Mormon 6:16 follows one (6:15).

pericopes.text: O ye fair ones, how could ye have departed from the ways of the Lord! O ye fair ones, how could ye have rejected that Jesus, who stood with open arms to receive you!

links.text: I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts;

provenance.route: Isaiah 65:2 / Romans 10:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon (route undecided)
provenance.alternative: Matthew 23:37 (and its Book of Mormon reuse at 3 Nephi 10:4-6) is the other candidate for the rejected-gathering figure; 3 Nephi 9:14, “mine arm of mercy is extended towards you, and whosoever will come, him will I receive”, is the nearest Book of Mormon sentence and supplies the verb “receive”.
provenance.other: “with open arms” occurs in no KJV verse, and in exactly one Book of Mormon verse — this one. “spread out my hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezra 9:5 and Isaiah 65:2; “stretched forth my hands” occurs in exactly one, Romans 10:21.
provenance.significance: The image of God standing with arms out toward a people who will not come is, in the King James Bible, Isaiah 65:2 and the verse of Paul that quotes it — and it is an image of rejection sustained over time, “all the day”, “all day long”. Mormon puts it in the past perfect and closes it: the arms were open, and the people who could have come are lying on the field. What the catalogue can say is that the figure is scriptural and the words are not.

links.note: “O ye fair ones, how could ye have rejected that Jesus, who stood with open arms to receive you!” There is no verbal contact to test — “open arms” is in no KJV verse and “fair ones” is in none either. What is here is the KJV's one recurring picture of a rejected embrace, which reaches English readers in two forms, Isaiah 65:2's spread-out hands and Romans 10:21's stretched-forth hands, with Matthew 23:37's hen and chickens as the Gospels' version of the same refusal. Recorded as an echo, and recorded honestly as undecided: see whyNot.
links.whyNot: tools/mediation-check.py on Mormon 6:17 against Isaiah 65:2 and Romans 10:21 returns no decisive divergence — the Book of Mormon reproduces neither “spread out” nor “stretched forth”, neither “all the day” nor “all day long”, and neither “rebellious” nor “disobedient and gainsaying”. It has “open arms”, which is in neither. So the verse cannot settle its own mediation and the field is left uncertain (CONVENTIONS §7). A reader may reasonably hold that the source is not a text at all but a preaching commonplace, or that the proximate model is 3 Nephi 9:14 rather than any biblical verse; the row is kept because the figure is scriptural, not because the wording proves it.

pericopes.text: Behold, if ye had not done this, ye would not have fallen. But behold, ye are fallen, and I mourn your loss.
O ye fair sons and daughters, ye fathers and mothers, ye husbands and wives, ye fair ones, how is it that ye could have fallen!

links.text: Ye daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet, with other delights, who put on ornaments of gold upon your apparel.

provenance.other: “sons and daughters” occurs in 26 KJV verses and carries no weight here; the rarity in this row is all borrowed from 6:13, where “in the midst of the battle” is a KJV singleton.
provenance.significance: David's lament turns, at 1:24, from the dead to the living women who must now be told, and Mormon's turns the same way and finds nobody there. “O ye fair sons and daughters, ye fathers and mothers, ye husbands and wives” is a roll of every relation a survivor could be addressed in, and every one of them is on the ground. The apostrophe is what a lament does; the horror of Mormon 6 is that the apostrophe has no audience, which is also why the chapter's third and last “fallen” is a question — “how is it that ye could have fallen!” — where David's is a declaration.

links.note: The apostrophe half of the elegy adjudicated at 6:13. 2 Samuel 1:24 addresses the survivors by relation and 6:19 does the same at four times the length; the refrain that closes both is “fallen”, three times in David (1:19, 1:25, 1:27) and three times in Mormon (6:18, 6:19, with the roll of 6:13-15 behind them). Given separately from 6:13 rather than folded into it because a reader coming to this verse on its own is otherwise shown nothing, and because the vocative catalogue is where the Book of Mormon most visibly departs from its model. The argument for the elegy as a whole is at 6:13 and is not restated here.
links.whyNot: No distinctive wording is shared with 2 Samuel 1:24 — not one phrase — and vocative laments over the dead are a form, not a text. This row stands or falls with 6:13.

pericopes.text: But behold, ye are gone, and my sorrows cannot bring your return;

and the day soon cometh that your mortal must put on immortality, and these bodies which are now mouldering in corruption, must soon become incorruptible bodies; and then ye must stand before the judgement seat of Christ, to be judged according to your works: and if it so be that ye are righteous, then are ye blessed with your fathers which have gone before you.

links.text: For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.

provenance.other: “mortal must put on” and “must put on immortality” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:53. “stand before the judgment seat” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 14:10; “judgment seat of Christ” in exactly two, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10. “according to your works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 2:23.
provenance.significance: 1 Corinthians 15:53 is the second half of a sentence whose first half Mormon has already paraphrased, and its own next verse is the one the chapter needs: “So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.” Mormon does not quote it. He is standing over a field on which death has swallowed everything, addressing the dead, and he stops one verse short of the line that answers him. Recovering the suppressed verse is what the borrowing is for — this is metalepsis in Hays's sense, and it is the reason the resurrection chapter, of all chapters, is the one Mormon 6 ends on.

links.note: “The day soon cometh that your mortal must put on immortality, and these bodies which are now mouldering in corruption, must soon become incorruptible bodies.” Five words verbatim from 1 Corinthians 15:53 and a paraphrase of its first clause, in Paul's order. The route matters, because “put on immortality” is already a Book of Mormon formula — Enos 1:27, Mosiah 16:10 and Alma 40:2 all have it — and a reader could reasonably suppose Mormon is reusing the book's own phrase rather than the KJV's. The verb decides it. Paul reads “this mortal MUST put on immortality”; Enos and Mosiah read “shall”, Alma reads “does not”; Mormon 6:21 alone reads “must”, and alone restores the KJV's modal. This verse is in fresh contact with 1 Corinthians 15, not with the formula. The rest of the sentence fuses two further singletons: “stand before the judgment seat” is Romans 14:10's alone, and “according to your works”, in the second person plural, is Revelation 2:23's alone — tools/mediation-check.py against Psalm 62:12 (“according to his work”) returns Revelation 2:23 as decisive on exactly that word. Note finally that the judgment-seat formula enters this book at Mormon 3:20, where the catalogue adjudicates it against 2 Corinthians 5:10 — and 3:20's “ye must all stand” does take 2 Corinthians' “must all”. Mormon 6:21 has only “ye must stand”, without the “all”, which is Romans 14:10's clause and not 2 Corinthians'; the two verses of one book reach the same formula from its two KJV halves. What belongs to 6:21 is that fusion, and its welding onto the resurrection clause. 1830 reads “mouldering” and “judgement seat”, both altered in 1920.

pericopes.text: O that ye had repented before that this great destruction had come upon you. But behold, ye are gone, and the Father, yea, the eternal Father of heaven, knoweth your state; and he doeth with you according to his justice and mercy.

And now behold, I would speak somewhat unto the remnant of this people which are spared, if it so be that God may give unto them my words, that they may know of the things of their fathers; yea, I speak unto you, ye remnant of the house of Israel; and this is the words which I speak:

provenance.other: “remnant of the house of Israel” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 46:3. The looser “remnant of Israel” occurs in exactly seven, which is why the fuller string is the one that carries the argument: the Book of Mormon has the six-word form the KJV uses once, not the common prophetic formula.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowed vocative turns into an argument the Book of Mormon does not make out loud. Isaiah 46:3 addresses the remnant as a body God has carried since before it could walk — “which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb” — and 46:4 finishes the sentence: “even to your old age I am he; and even to hoar hairs will I carry you: I have made, and I will bear; even I will carry, and will deliver you.” The whole point of the Isaian oracle is that this remnant is carried rather than carrying, against the Babylonian gods of 46:1-2 who have to be loaded onto beasts. Mormon's addressees are the survivors of a people that has just been annihilated in a single battle he watched, and the one KJV verse that supplies his name for them is the verse that says a remnant is what God has not put down. Nothing in Mormon 7 says this; the borrowing says it.

links.note: “I speak unto you, ye remnant of the house of Israel.” The vocative is the chapter's addressee and it is a KJV singleton: Isaiah 46:3 is the only verse in the King James Bible that reads “the remnant of the house of Israel.” Mormon has just finished a book whose subject is the destruction of a nation, and the noun he reaches for to name the survivors is the noun Isaiah uses in the one oracle where a remnant is told it will be carried to grey hairs. The link is an allusion and not a quotation — six words, far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, and Mormon takes only the vocative — but the rarity is absolute and the setting is exactly the setting Isaiah 46 supposes. The same address returns at 7:10 as “a remnant of the seed of Jacob”, which is Isaiah 46:3's other half: the verse opens “Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel.” Mormon's chapter opens with the second phrase and closes with the first.
links.text: Hearken unto me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, which are borne by me from the belly, which are carried from the womb:

pericopes.text: Know ye that ye are of the house of Israel.
Know ye that ye must come unto repentance, or ye cannot be saved.
Know ye that ye must lay down your weapons of war, and delight no more in the shedding of blood, and take them not again, save it be that God shall command you.

provenance.route: Psalm 68:30 + Hebrews 9:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the composite is already made at Alma 48:23, in this same narrator's hand
provenance.other: “delight in war” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 68:30, “scatter thou the people that delight in war”, and it is the King James Bible's only use of that verb with warfare as its object. “shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22. Mormon 7:4 is the psalm's verb married to Hebrews' noun phrase, which is the identical fusion this catalogue adjudicates at Alma 48:11 and 48:23 — “they did not delight in the shedding of blood”.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3, the swords-into-plowshares oracle, which the Book of Mormon transcribes at 2 Nephi 12:4. That is the passage a reader expects behind a command to lay down weapons, and it is not the one the wording supports: Isaiah 2:4's verbs are beat, lift up and learn, and none of them is here.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is severe and it works against the addressees. Psalm 68:30 is not a description but a petition — it asks God to scatter the people that delight in war — and Mormon is writing to the scattered survivors of a people that did. He has used the collocation before, in Alma 48, as praise of Moroni, the general who did not delight in bloodshed; here the same words become an imperative addressed to the remnant of the nation that destroyed his own. Read with the psalm recovered, verse 4 tells the Lamanites to stop being the people the psalm prays against, and tells them so at the moment the prayer has visibly been answered on the whole land.

links.note: “Know ye that ye must lay down your weapons of war, and delight no more in the shedding of blood, and take them not again, save it be that God shall command you.” Two rare KJV elements, neither reproduced whole, and their combination is not new to this narrator: the verb-plus-object of Psalm 68:30 and the noun phrase of Hebrews 9:22 are fused at Alma 48:23 in exactly this form, and Mormon is the compiler of Alma. Held at echo because “delight no more in the shedding of blood” reproduces no continuous KJV run, and at moderate rather than low because the fusion is demonstrably a formula of this writer's rather than a coincidence of English — a repetition across a book boundary, which CONVENTIONS §4 says to write as a link rather than pass over, with the argument made at Alma 48:11. What is new here is the addressee. The clause that praised Moroni is now a command to the people Moroni fought, and the burial of weapons it asks for is the Anti-Nephi-Lehies' act at Alma 24:17 — the one precedent in the Book of Mormon for a Lamanite people laying down arms permanently, which is precisely what Mormon 7:4 asks its readers to repeat.
links.text: Rebuke the company of spearmen, the multitude of the bulls, with the calves of the people, till every one submit himself with pieces of silver: scatter thou the people that delight in war.

pericopes.text: Know ye that ye must come to the knowledge of your fathers, and repent of all your sins and iniquities, and believe in Jesus Christ, that he is the Son of God, and that he was slain by the Jews, and by the power of the Father he hath risen again, whereby he hath gained the victory over the grave; and also in him is the sting of death swallowed up.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 25:8 (“He will swallow up death in victory”) and Hosea 13:14 (“O death, I will be thy plagues; O grave, I will be thy destruction”) are the two Old Testament verses Paul is quoting at 1 Corinthians 15:54-55.
provenance.route: Isaiah 25:8 + Hosea 13:14 → 1 Corinthians 15:54-55 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sting of death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:56, and “swallowed up in victory” occurs in exactly one, 1 Corinthians 15:54. Both are Paul's, and the Book of Mormon has both in one sentence. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points against each Old Testament candidate: against Isaiah 25:8 the Book of Mormon has Paul's passive (“swallowed up”, not “He will swallow up”) and none of Isaiah's tail about wiping away tears; against Hosea 13:14 it has “sting”, not Hosea's “plagues”, and “victory”, not Hosea's “destruction”. The route through the New Testament is not a judgment call here — it is the only route that accounts for two of the three nouns.
provenance.significance: The decisive evidence is not the vocabulary but the pairing. 1 Corinthians 15:55 asks two questions and assigns one noun to each: “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” Mormon 7:5 keeps both couplings intact and reverses their order — the victory is over the grave, the sting belongs to death — which is a thing a writer working from Paul's verse does and a thing a writer reaching independently for resurrection language has no reason to do. Recover the rest of the paragraph and the Book of Mormon's next two verses turn out to be still inside it: “brought to pass” is 15:54's, and Paul's “thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory” at 15:57 is the sentence Mormon 7:5 compresses into “he hath gained the victory over the grave”.

links.note: The chapter's densest borrowing and the row that carries it. In one clause Mormon 7:5 has “gained the victory over the grave” and “the sting of death swallowed up”, and the King James Bible puts a sting on death in exactly one verse and swallows death up in victory in exactly one, four words apart in the same Pauline paragraph. Crucially the Book of Mormon preserves Paul's assignment of the two nouns — sting to death, victory to the grave — while inverting their order, which is the signature of a writer quarrying a verse rather than sharing a commonplace. Paul is himself quoting the Old Testament at 15:54-55, so the mediation is testable, and it is not close: the wording is the New Testament's at every point the two forms diverge. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as an allusion, not a quotation, because nothing is reproduced as a continuous clause; the strength is rarity and structure, not length. The working of 1 Corinthians 15 does not stop here — see 7:6.
links.text: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?

provenance.other: “he is the Son of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 9:20. The Book of Mormon reproduces the clause with its introductory “that” intact — “believe in Jesus Christ, that he is the Son of God” against “preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God” — a six-word run that the machine stream ranked first for this verse on a seven-word window.
provenance.significance: Acts 9:20 is the KJV's report of the first sermon preached by a man who had spent the preceding chapter destroying the people he now addresses. Mormon 7 is the last address of a general to the nation that destroyed his. Neither text mentions the other, and the formula they share is the formula of a preacher speaking to the party he was lately at war with.

links.note: A short row with an absolute rarity under it. The propositional content — that Jesus Christ is the Son of God — is the most ordinary claim in Christian writing, which is why the row is held at moderate rather than high; what is not ordinary is the King James Bible's phrasing of it, which occurs in this form in one verse only. Mormon 7:5 has that clause with its complementiser, and has it as the content of what is to be believed rather than of what is preached. A reader may reasonably decline this one as a commonplace of the Book of Mormon's own idiom; it is recorded because the count is one, and because CONVENTIONS §0a asks us to propose rather than withhold.
links.text: And straightway he preached Christ in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.

provenance.other: “come to the knowledge” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 3:7, “ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.” The New Testament's other knowledge-of-the-truth verses use different verbs — 1 Timothy 2:4 “come unto the knowledge”, 2 Timothy 2:25 “acknowledging”, Hebrews 10:26 “received the knowledge” — so the Book of Mormon has the one form the KJV prints once. The Book of Mormon uses the collocation elsewhere, at Jacob 7:24 and Helaman 15:7, where this catalogue routes it to 1 Timothy 2:4.
provenance.significance: The interest is the substitution. Every KJV verse in this family completes the phrase with “of the truth”; Mormon 7:5 completes it with “of your fathers”. For a book whose entire apologetic is that the record of the fathers is the truth the Gentiles and the remnant both lack, replacing the one with the other is not a slip of idiom — it is the chapter's thesis compressed into a preposition, and 7:9 spells it out: believe the record and “ye will know concerning your fathers.”

links.note: “Know ye that ye must come to the knowledge of your fathers.” The verb phrase is a KJV singleton and it is here with its full syntax, but with the object swapped: 2 Timothy 3:7's knowledge is of the truth, Mormon's is of the fathers. Moderate rather than high because the phrase is unremarkable English once detached from its verse and because the surrounding context of 2 Timothy 3 — perilous times, silly women laden with sins — has no presence in Mormon 7 at all; the borrowing, if it is one, is of a phrase and not of a passage. What earns the row is that the swap is the argument the chapter goes on to make twice more, at 7:9 and 7:10.
links.text: Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.

pericopes.text: And he bringeth to pass the resurrection of the dead, whereby man must be raised to stand before his judgement seat.

provenance.other: “brought to pass” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezekiel 21:7 and 1 Corinthians 15:54; the second is the verse from which 7:5 has just taken “swallowed up in victory”. “resurrection of the dead” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses, four of them in 1 Corinthians 15, so on its own it cannot name a source — it is the company it keeps here that does.
provenance.significance: Three consecutive verses of Mormon 7 stay inside one Pauline paragraph: 7:5 takes the sting, the victory and the swallowing from 15:54-57; 7:6 takes the paragraph's own idiom for what God does with them, “brought to pass”, and applies it to the resurrection; 7:7 repeats the idiom for the redemption. What is a passive of a written prophecy in Paul — the saying that is written shall be brought to pass — becomes in Mormon an active of Christ himself, who brings the resurrection to pass. The catalogue's finding is the continuity, not any one of the three.

links.note: Taken alone this verse would not support a link: “resurrection of the dead” is in eleven KJV verses and the judgment seat is adjudicated elsewhere in this book (see the exclusion register at 7:6, which sends a reader to Mormon 3:20 for the Romans 14:10 / 2 Corinthians 5:10 composite). It is written as a link because of what stands on either side of it. “brought to pass” is a two-verse KJV phrase, one of which is 1 Corinthians 15:54, and 7:5 has just quarried that same verse for the swallowing of death and 7:7 repeats the phrase for the redemption of the world — so the borrowing being catalogued is a paragraph worked in sequence, not a formula reached for twice. Held at moderate: a reader who declines the sequence argument is left with an ordinary phrase, and should decline the row. One CONVENTIONS §8 point runs the other way from the usual: the 1830 prints “judgement seat” and the KJV prints “judgment”, so here it is the 1920 edition's respelling that moves the text toward its source rather than away from it.
links.text: So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.

pericopes.text: And he hath brought to pass the redemption of the world, whereby he that is found guiltless before him at the judgement day, hath it given unto them to dwell in the presence of God in his kingdom, to sing ceaseless praises with the choirs above, unto the Father, and unto the Son, and unto the Holy Ghost, which is one God, in a state of happiness which hath no end.

provenance.route: Matthew 28:19 + 1 John 5:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon, very probably by way of 2 Nephi 31:21
provenance.other: “in the name of the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” occurs in exactly one, both Matthew 28:19; “these three are one” occurs in exactly one, 1 John 5:7. Mormon 7:7 has Matthew's triad in Matthew's order with the preposition changed from “of” to “unto”, and closes it with the predicate of the Johannine Comma.
provenance.alternative: 2 Nephi 31:21, which reads “the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost, which is one God, without end. Amen.” Mormon 7:7 reads “unto the Father, and unto the Son, and unto the Holy Ghost, which is one God, in a state of happiness which hath no end”, and closes the chapter three verses later with “Amen.” The four-word tag “which is one God” occurs nowhere in the KJV and in only these two places in the Book of Mormon, and the endlessness clause follows it in both. The proximate model for Mormon 7:7 is more likely Nephi's sentence than the two biblical verses behind it.
provenance.significance: The single most KJV-specific thing in the chapter is doing quiet work here. 1 John 5:7 is the Comma Johanneum: it stands in the King James Bible and in no early Greek manuscript, and it is the one verse in the English Bible that states the numerical unity of the three names outright. A Book of Mormon that says “which is one God” immediately after naming the triad has taken its trinitarian predicate from a verse whose presence in the English Bible is itself a sixteenth-century textual accident. The catalogue records this without adjudicating the theology: the row is about where the words come from.

links.whyNot: The triadic naming formula is by 1830 the common property of every English hymn, creed and prayer book, and a writer could produce it without Matthew in front of him; “which is one God” is the sharper element, and its nearest antecedent is not biblical at all but 2 Nephi 31:21. So the row is moderate, and it is offered as much as a pointer to that internal parallel as to the two biblical verses. It also exposes a gap in this catalogue's vocabulary: CONVENTIONS §7 provides `OT-via-earlier-BoM` for an Old Testament source proximately mediated by an earlier Book of Mormon passage, and provides nothing for a New Testament source in the same position, which is what this appears to be. Recorded as `direct-NT` with the qualification here rather than inventing a value.
links.note: “Unto the Father, and unto the Son, and unto the Holy Ghost, which is one God.” The naming formula is Matthew 28:19's, in Matthew's order, with the genitive turned into a dative because the sentence is about praise rather than baptism — and three verses later, at 7:10, the baptismal sense returns and Matthew's setting with it. The predicate attached to the triad is not Matthew's: “which is one God” answers the question Matthew 28:19 leaves open, and the King James Bible answers it in one place, the Johannine Comma at 1 John 5:7, which this catalogue adjudicates at 3 Nephi 11:27 and 11:32. Mormon 7:7 is the same fusion arriving in a different hand. The row is moderate and carries a whyNot, because the more likely proximate source is a Book of Mormon verse — 2 Nephi 31:21 — rather than either biblical one, and because the schema has no mediation value for that case.
links.text: Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:

pericopes.text: Therefore repent, and be baptized in the name of Jesus, and lay hold upon the Gospel of Christ, which shall be set before you, not only in this record, but also in the record which shall come unto the Gentiles from the Jews, which record shall come from the Gentiles unto you.

provenance.other: “Repent, and be baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:38, and the Book of Mormon has it with the prepositional phrase that follows it in the same verse. “in the name of Jesus” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, all in Acts, and Acts 2:38 is the only one of the six that also contains the imperative pair. The Book of Mormon drops Peter's “every one of you” and his “Christ”, so the run is not continuous.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:38 is Peter's answer to a crowd that has just been told it killed the Messiah — “ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain” — and the answer is repentance and baptism. Mormon 7:5 has just said, three verses earlier, that Christ “was slain by the Jews”, and 7:8 answers that with Peter's sentence. The chapter has reconstructed the Pentecost sermon's own sequence, accusation followed by its remedy, and addressed it to a different people.

links.note: The most straightforwardly identifiable borrowing in the chapter. “Repent, and be baptized” is a KJV singleton, and Mormon 7:8 continues into the same verse's “in the name of Jesus”, which the KJV confines to six verses of Acts of which this is the only one carrying the imperative. What Mormon drops is instructive: Peter's “every one of you” and Peter's “Christ”, leaving the shorter Acts formula the book uses throughout. Catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation because nothing survives as a continuous clause of sixteen words or anything near it, and because the Book of Mormon has been using Acts 2:38 as a fixed formula since 2 Nephi 9:23 — this is Mormon's own hand reaching for a phrase his record has carried for a thousand pages. It is written as a link rather than passed to the register because it enters here in a new book and a new voice, per ADJUDICATING §4.
links.text: Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.

provenance.other: “lay hold upon” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Proverbs 3:18 and Hebrews 6:18; “lay hold upon the hope” occurs in exactly one, Hebrews 6:18; “set before us” occurs in exactly three, Daniel 9:10, Hebrews 6:18 and Hebrews 12:1. Hebrews 6:18 is the only verse in the King James Bible that contains both halves of the Book of Mormon's construction — the seizing verb and the thing set before the seizer — and Mormon 7:8 keeps them in Hebrews' order, changing only the object and the person: “lay hold upon the Gospel of Christ, which shall be set before you.”
provenance.significance: Hebrews 6:18 does not describe just anybody laying hold. It describes those “who have fled for refuge” — a phrase whose Old Testament setting is the cities of refuge, the manslayer running for a place where the avenger of blood may not reach him. Mormon 7 is addressed to the survivors of the people who destroyed his own, four verses after they are told to lay down their weapons and delight no more in the shedding of blood. The KJV's one verse about laying hold on what is set before you is a verse about the refuge of a man with blood on his hands, and the catalogue can find no evidence that the Book of Mormon knows this; the recovered context supplies a reading the surface text does not.

links.note: A two-element borrowing whose elements are rare separately and unique together. Mormon 7:8 says to “lay hold upon the Gospel of Christ, which shall be set before you”, and Hebrews 6:18 says to “lay hold upon the hope set before us”; the verb phrase stands in two KJV verses, the fuller “lay hold upon the hope” in one, and no other verse in the Bible joins that verb to a thing set before its subject. The substitution is the same kind the chapter makes at 7:5 — Hebrews' abstract object exchanged for the Book of Mormon's concrete one, hope for gospel, exactly as knowledge of the truth became knowledge of the fathers — and the change of person from “us” to “you” is what an address to outsiders requires. High rather than certain because neither element is long, and because a writer steeped in Hebrews might produce the collocation without copying the verse; but the collocation is not otherwise available in the King James Bible.
links.text: That by two immutable things, in which it was impossible for God to lie, we might have a strong consolation, who have fled for refuge to lay hold upon the hope set before us:

pericopes.text: For behold, this is written for the intent that ye may believe that; and if ye believe that, ye will believe this also; and if ye believe this, ye will know concerning your fathers, and also the marvellous works which were wrought by the power of God among them;

provenance.route: Psalm 105:5-6, doubled at 1 Chronicles 16:12-13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “marvellous works” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: 1 Chronicles 16:12, 1 Chronicles 16:24, Psalm 9:1 and Psalm 105:5. Two of the four are the same sentence, since 1 Chronicles 16:8-22 reproduces Psalm 105:1-15, and that sentence is the one Mormon 7:9 is using: “Remember his marvellous works that he hath done.” CONVENTIONS §8 applies squarely — the 1830 prints “marvellous”, which is the KJV's spelling, and the 1920 edition Americanised it to “marvelous”, a form that appears in no KJV verse. The borrowing is plainer in the first edition than in the current text.
provenance.significance: The argument is not in verse 9 but in the join between verse 9 and verse 10, and it is the same join the source makes. Psalm 105:5 commands a people to remember the marvellous works God did among their fathers; Psalm 105:6 immediately names the people commanded — “O ye seed of Abraham his servant, ye children of Jacob his chosen.” Mormon 7:9 tells the remnant that believing the record will let them know the marvellous works wrought among their fathers, and Mormon 7:10 immediately names them: “ye are a remnant of the seed of Jacob.” Two verses, in order, doing what the psalm's two verses do in order. The chronicler's parallel at 1 Chronicles 16:12-13 makes the same move with “O ye seed of Israel his servant, ye children of Jacob, his chosen ones”, which is why the row carries both.

links.note: “The marvellous works which were wrought by the power of God among them.” Four KJV verses contain “marvellous works”, and two of them are the single sentence Psalm 105:5 shares with 1 Chronicles 16:12 — a command to remember what God did in the time of the fathers, addressed to their descendants. That is exactly the use Mormon 7:9 makes of the phrase, and the sequence carries: the psalm's next verse turns to address the seed of Jacob, and so does Mormon's. Moderate rather than high because two words is a slender verbal base and neither “wrought by the power” nor “the marvellous works” occurs in any KJV verse as a string — the case rests on the collocation plus the shared move into the following verse, not on a run. The 1830 spelling is evidence in its own right: “marvellous” is the KJV's form and the current text's “marvelous” is not.
links.text: Remember his marvellous works that he hath done; his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth;

pericopes.text: and ye will also know that ye are a remnant of the seed of Jacob; therefore ye are numbered among the people of the first covenant; and if it so be that ye believe in Christ, and are baptized, first with water, then with fire and with the Holy Ghost, following the example of our Saviour according to that which he hath commanded us, it shall be well with you in the day of judgement. Amen.

provenance.route: Matthew 3:11 or Luke 3:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the two synoptic forms cannot be separated here
provenance.other: “with the Holy Ghost, and with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, and both also contain the “with water” half of the Book of Mormon's contrast. Mark 1:8 and John 1:33 have the water-and-Spirit antithesis without the fire, so they are ruled out by the wording. tools/mediation-check.py run on Matthew 3:11 against Luke 3:16 reports no decisive divergence: the two Gospels differ only at points the Book of Mormon does not reproduce — Luke's narrative opening, Matthew's “unto repentance”, bear against unloose — and the clause actually shared is word-for-word identical in both. The row therefore names Matthew as source with Luke as composite and states that the choice is undecidable on this verse's evidence.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon reverses the Baptist's order. Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16 both read “with the Holy Ghost, and with fire”; Mormon 7:10 reads “then with fire and with the Holy Ghost.” Elsewhere in the book the reversal is doctrinally loaded — 3 Nephi 9:20 has the Lamanites “baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost, and they knew it not” — and the effect of putting fire first is to make it a stage of the process rather than an intensifier of the Spirit. Against a chapter that has just told its readers to lay down their weapons, the sequence water, fire, Spirit reads as a purgation, which is what fire means in the Baptist's own next verse, Matthew 3:12: “he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

links.note: “Baptized, first with water, then with fire and with the Holy Ghost.” The King James Bible contains the fire-and-Holy-Ghost pairing in two verses only, Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, and both set it against baptism with water exactly as the Book of Mormon does; Mark's and John's versions of the saying lack the fire and are excluded by the wording rather than by preference. Which of the two synoptics stands behind it cannot be decided here, and the catalogue says so rather than picking: the passage is identical in Matthew and Luke at every word the Book of Mormon reproduces. What the Book of Mormon adds is an ordinal — first water, then fire and Spirit — turning John's contrast between two baptisms into one baptism with stages, and reversing the fire and the Ghost while doing it. Two CONVENTIONS §8 readings sit in the same verse: the 1830's “Saviour” and “judgement” against 1920's “Savior” and “judgment”, the first preserving the KJV's spelling and the second departing from it.
links.text: I indeed baptize you with water unto repentance. but he that cometh after me is mightier than I, whose shoes I am not worthy to bear: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost, and with fire:

provenance.route: the Gospel baptism narratives → Book of Mormon, as an appeal to a narrated event rather than to a wording
provenance.other: There is no verbal contact. Mormon 7:10 says only “following the example of our Saviour according to that which he hath commanded us”; it names no river, no descending dove, no voice, and no John. The wording that is present in the verse belongs to Matthew 3:11, adjudicated separately above, five verses earlier in the same chapter of Matthew.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has already built an extended argument out of this scene, at 2 Nephi 31:5-7, where Nephi asks why the Holy One of Israel needed baptism and answers that he did it “to fulfil all righteousness” and to show the children of men the strictness of the way. Mormon 7:10 is the one-clause version of that chapter, offered to readers who will have no access to Nephi's reasoning — the appeal is to the example, and the reasoning is somewhere else in the book.

links.whyNot: No shared wording of any kind, which means the row cannot be tested the way the rest of the chapter's rows can, and a reader who holds that a catalogue of the Bible in the Book of Mormon should catalogue verbal dependence only is entitled to strike it. It is written as a figural link rather than passed over because a cross-reference to the baptism of Jesus at this verse is the natural one and the register would otherwise be silent about it. The row would be withdrawn if the phrase “the example of our Saviour” were shown to be doing work as a formula of some other source rather than as a pointer to the Gospel scene.
links.note: Discharging the one cross-reference Hardy's apparatus keys to this chapter. His study edition cross-references the four Gospel baptism narratives — Matthew 3:13-17, Mark 1:9-11, Luke 3:21-22 and John 1:29-34 — at Mormon 7:10, and the clause that earns them is “following the example of our Saviour”, which appeals to the event without borrowing a word of any of the four accounts. This catalogue's own reading puts the verse's verbal link at Matthew 3:11, five verses before the narrative Hardy points to, and records the narrative reference separately here as figural, per CONVENTIONS §6a: his row is evidence and it is discharged honestly rather than dressed in a verbal case it does not have. Matthew 3:16 is named as the row's single source because this catalogue's references resolve to single verses; the reference is to the scene, not to that verse's wording.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Mormon 7.10 (Matthew 3:13-17; Mark 1:9-11; Luke 3:21-22; John 1:29-34)
links.text: And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:

pericopes.text: Behold I, Moroni, do finish the record of my father Mormon. Behold, I have but few things to write, which things I have been commanded of my father.

And now it came to pass that after the great and tremendous battle at Camorah, behold, the Nephites which had escaped into the country southward, were hunted by the Lamanites, until they were all destroyed;

and my father also was killed by them; and I, even I remaineth alone to write the sad tale of the destruction of my people. But behold, they are gone, and I fulfil the commandment of my father. And whether they will slay me, I know not;

links.text: Then said Elijah unto the people, I, even I only, remain a prophet of the LORD; but Baal’s prophets are four hundred and fifty men.

provenance.other: “I, even I only, remain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 18:22; “I, even I only, am left” occurs in exactly two, 1 Kings 19:10 and 19:14, both Elijah at Horeb. The bare doubling “I, even I” occurs in nineteen verses and is not by itself evidence; what is rare is the doubling followed by a verb of remaining and a word for aloneness, and in the KJV that construction belongs to Elijah alone.
provenance.significance: The 1830 reading is the evidence. Moroni writes “I, even I remaineth alone”, which is Elijah's construction to the letter — pronoun doubled, verb of remaining, word for aloneness — and 1920 deleted the second “I”, so the current text reads “I even remain alone” and the borrowing is no longer visible on the page (CONVENTIONS §8). The 1920 edition simultaneously moved the verb from “remaineth” to “remain”, which is 1 Kings 18:22's form, so a single verse shows the later edition erasing one KJV feature while accidentally restoring another. Recover Elijah's context and the correspondence deepens: 1 Kings 19:10 continues “and they seek my life, to take it away”, and Moroni's next clause is “And whether they will slay me, I know not.” Elijah is wrong about being the last — seven thousand have not bowed to Baal — and the book will not extend Moroni the same consolation.

links.note: “and I, even I remaineth alone to write the sad tale of the destruction of my people … And whether they will slay me, I know not.” The KJV has one speaker who says he alone remains and that his enemies seek his life, and it is Elijah, twice at Horeb and once on Carmel. Moroni opens his own additions in Elijah's words, on the far side of a national extinction that Elijah's Israel was spared. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation, and not one of his thirty-six; the case rests on the construction, not on length.

pericopes.text: therefore I will write and hide up the records in the earth: and whither I go it mattereth not.

Behold, my father hath made this record, and he hath written the intent thereof. And behold, I would write it also, if I had room upon the plates; but I have not. Friends I have none, for I am alone: my father hath been slain in battle, and all my kinsfolks, and I have not friends nor whither to go; and how long that the Lord will suffer that I may live, I know not.

links.text: And ye shall be betrayed both by parents, and brethren, and kinsfolks, and friends; and some of you shall they cause to be put to death.

provenance.other: “kinsfolks” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 1 Kings 16:11, 2 Kings 10:11 and Luke 21:16 — and only Luke 21:16 also has “friends”. The alternative spelling “kinsfolk” occurs in exactly two, Job 19:14 and Luke 2:44, and Job 19:14 also has friends: “My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me.”
provenance.alternative: Job 19:14 is the other KJV verse pairing kinsfolk with friends, and Job's is the register of desolation Moroni is writing in. It is the better thematic fit and the worse verbal one: it has the singular-looking form, no killing, and its friends have forgotten rather than died.
provenance.significance: The 1830 spelling decides it, and the 1920 correction reverses the decision. 1830 reads “all my kinsfolks”, which is Luke's spelling; 1920 normalised it to “kinsfolk”, which is Job's. A reader of the current text who checks a concordance is sent to Job; a reader of the first edition is sent to the Olivet Discourse — and the Olivet Discourse is the passage this whole chapter is built out of (see 8:26 and 8:30). Luke 21:16 promises that kinsfolk and friends will betray, and that some will be put to death; Moroni reports the outcome as a household inventory — father slain, all kinsfolks slain, friends none — and then, three verses on, prophesies the rest of the discourse to the Gentiles.

links.note: “Friends I have none, for I am alone: my father hath been slain in battle, and all my kinsfolks.” Two words that co-occur in one KJV verse of persecution and death, in the 1830 edition's spelling of the rarer of them. The link is not strong on syntax — Moroni is listing losses, Luke is listing betrayers — and it is recorded at moderate confidence for that reason. What raises it above coincidence is that the chapter goes on to quote the same discourse at length.

pericopes.text: Behold, four hundred years have passed away since the coming of our Lord and Saviour.

And behold, the Lamanites have hunted my people, the Nephites, down from city to city, and from place to place, even until they are no more; and great has been their fall; yea, great and marvellous is the destruction of my people, the Nephites.

links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: “great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and Revelation 15:3, and 1830 preserves the KJV's double-l “marvellous” at both 8:7 and 8:34 where 1920 prints “marvelous” (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: Revelation 15:3 is already in this catalogue at 1 Nephi 1:14, where Lehi praises God in six words that Revelation labels the song of Moses. The formula returns at the other end of the book and it has been turned inside out: “great and marvellous is the destruction of my people”. The doxology of the redeemed, sung by those who have gotten the victory over the beast, is applied by the last Nephite to his own people's annihilation — and the immediately preceding words of Revelation 15:1 are “seven angels having the seven last plagues; for in them is filled up the wrath of God.” Moroni's next verse says exactly that: “it is the hand of the Lord which hath done it.”

links.note: A two-word phrase is thin evidence and this is filed as an echo for that reason. It earns its place on three counts: the phrase belongs to one chapter of the KJV; the 1830 spelling is the KJV's; and the same chapter of Revelation is demonstrably in play at the head of the book. Moroni uses the phrase twice, at 8:7 of the destruction and at 8:34 of the things the Lord has shewn him.

pericopes.text: And behold, it is the hand of the Lord which hath done it. And behold also, the Lamanites are at war one with another; and the whole face of this land is one continual round of murder and bloodshed; and no one knoweth the end of the war.

links.text: That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it.

provenance.other: “the hand of the LORD hath done” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Job 12:9 is the near miss and reads “wrought”, not “done”; Moroni has the Isaiah verb.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the sentence is doing something quite deliberate. Isaiah 41:18-20 is the promise of water in the wilderness — pools in the desert, cedar and myrtle planted in the waste — and the clause Moroni borrows is the conclusion drawn from that mercy: they are to see and know that the hand of the LORD hath done this. Moroni draws the identical conclusion from the identical formula about the extermination of his nation. The verse that certifies Israel's restoration certifies the Nephites' end, in the same words, and the fact that Moroni goes straight on to the Lamanite civil war — “no one knoweth the end of the war” — refuses the reader the consolation Isaiah's chapter supplies four verses later.

links.note: “And behold, it is the hand of the Lord which hath done it.” Six words tracking a KJV singleton, with the demonstrative changed from “this” to “it” because Moroni's antecedent is a destruction rather than a garden. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six quotations; it is catalogued as an allusion on the strength of the singleton alone.

pericopes.text: And now behold, I say no more concerning them, for there are none, save it be Lamanites and robbers, that do exist upon the face of the land;

and there are none that do know the true God, save it be the disciples of Jesus, which did tarry in the land until the wickedness of the people were so great, that the Lord would not suffer them to remain with the people; and whether they be upon the face of the land, no man knoweth.
But behold, my father and I have seen them, and they have ministered unto us.

And whoso receiveth this record, and shall not condemn it because of the imperfections which are in it, the same shall know of greater things than these. Behold; I am Moroni; and were it possible, I would make all things known unto you.
Behold, I make an end of speaking concerning this people. I am the son of Mormon, and my father was a descendant of Nephi;

and I am the same which hideth up this record unto the Lord; the plates thereof are of no worth, because of the commandment of the Lord. For he truly saith, That no one shall have them to get gain; but the record thereof is of great worth; and whoso shall bring it to light, him will the Lord bless.

For none can have power to bring it to light, save it be given him of God: for God will that it shall be done with an eye singled to his glory, or the welfare of the ancient and long dispersed covenant people of the Lord.

links.text: The light of the body is the eye: if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light.

provenance.other: “thine eye be single” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The word “single” occurs in exactly two verses in the whole King James Bible, Matthew 6:22 and Luke 11:34, which are the two forms of one saying; there is no other single eye in scripture.
provenance.alternative: Luke 11:34 has the same saying with “when thine eye is single”. Matthew's subjunctive is the commoner form of the tag in English usage and Matthew governs elsewhere in this chapter, but nothing in Moroni's wording chooses between them.
provenance.significance: This is the metalepsis of the chapter's first half. Matthew 6:22 does not stand alone: it is wedged between “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth” (6:19) and “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (6:24), so in Matthew the single eye is specifically an eye that is not on money. Moroni makes it the condition on who may bring the plates to light, one verse after saying that “no one shall have them to get gain” (8:14) — and thirty verses later the chapter closes by indicting churches that sell forgiveness for money. The Sermon's eye supplies the whole moral architecture of the chapter, and Moroni cites only the eye.

links.note: “God will that it shall be done with an eye singled to his glory.” The 1830 participle “singled” is the edition's own, and 1920 changed it to “single”, i.e. corrected it back toward the King James wording it came from — the same direction of change recorded at 1 Nephi 1:20 (CONVENTIONS §8). The later edition makes the borrowing more visible, not less, which is worth having on the record alongside 8:3 and 8:5, where 1920 does the opposite.

pericopes.text: And blessed be him that shall bring this thing to light: for it shall be brought out of darkness unto light, according to the word of God; yea, it shall be brought out of the earth, and it shall shine forth out of darkness, and come unto the knowledge of the people; and it shall be done by the power of God:

links.text: Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.

provenance.other: “come unto the knowledge” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The wider Pastoral idiom is fixed — 2 Timothy 3:7 has “come to the knowledge of the truth”, Hebrews 10:26 “received the knowledge of the truth” — and its object is invariably the truth.
provenance.significance: Moroni keeps the four-word run and swaps the object: the record shall “come unto the knowledge of the people”. In the KJV it is people who come to the knowledge of the truth; here it is the truth, in the form of a buried book, that comes to the knowledge of the people. The direction of the idiom is reversed, which is what a writer does with a phrase he knows rather than one he is copying.

links.note: A four-word run off a KJV singleton, in a verse otherwise made of Moroni's own light-out-of-darkness vocabulary. Recorded as an echo because a fixed idiom with its object changed is weak evidence of dependence on any one verse; recorded at all because the idiom is not common English and the KJV uses it once.

pericopes.text: and if there be faults, they be the faults of a man. But behold, we know no fault. Nevertheless, God knoweth all things; therefore he that condemneth, let him be aware lest he shall be in danger of hell fire.

links.text: But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.

provenance.other: “in danger of hell fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The wider formula “shall be in danger of” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 5:21 and 5:22, which are consecutive verses of the same saying.
provenance.significance: Matthew 5:22 escalates through three courts — the local judgment, the council, hell fire — and each is earned by a harder word said against a brother.
