Moroni transfers the whole apparatus to a reader's verdict on a book: “he that condemneth, let him be aware lest he shall be in danger of hell fire.” The unstated correspondence is that a reader who dismisses the record for its imperfections has said Raca to Moroni. Four verses later he redeploys the same danger idiom — “in danger to be hewn down and cast into the fire” — for those who deny the covenant, so the two halves of his warning to Gentile readers are both built out of the KJV's language of judicial peril.

links.note: Six words reproduced exactly from the only KJV verse that contains them, in the only sense the KJV gives them. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six, so it is catalogued as an allusion rather than a quotation; the confidence is nevertheless certain, because a six-word singleton in a matching context is not a coincidence anyone can construct an alternative to. Note that the verse it sits in is Moroni's apology for the record's imperfections — the chapter's most-quoted line — which means the apology is armed with the Sermon on the Mount.

links.text: For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things.

provenance.other: “knoweth all things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse also contains the verb “condemn”. Moroni's clause has both, in the same order: “God knoweth all things; therefore he that condemneth …”
provenance.significance: The sense is inverted and the inversion is the point. In 1 John the omniscience is consolation — if your own heart condemns you, God knows more than your heart does, so do not despair. In Moroni it is threat — God knows more than you do, so do not condemn the book. The same two facts, God's total knowledge and the act of condemning, are held in the same sentence and turned to face the opposite way. A reader could reasonably decline the link on the ground that both are commonplace theological furniture, which is why the confidence is moderate; what argues for it is that the KJV puts them together exactly once.

links.note: “Nevertheless, God knoweth all things; therefore he that condemneth, let him be aware.” Two clauses of ordinary doctrine that happen to reproduce the pairing of a KJV singleton, in a verse already demonstrably quoting Matthew 5:22. Recurrence of source-density in a single verse is not proof, but it makes the second contact easier to credit than it would be standing alone.

pericopes.text: And he that sayeth, Shew unto me, or ye shall be smitten, let him beware lest he commandeth that which is forbidden of the Lord.
For behold, the same that judgeth rashly, shall be judged rashly again: for according to his works shall his wages be; therefore, he that smiteth, shall be smitten again of the Lord.

links.text: For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.

provenance.other: “with what judgment ye judge” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The reciprocal adverb that Moroni uses twice — judged “again”, smitten “again” — is Matthew's own: “it shall be measured to you again”.
provenance.significance: Moroni does not quote the saying; he runs its grammar. Matthew 7:2 states a rule of reciprocal measure and Moroni conjugates it through three verbs in one verse — judgeth/judged, smiteth/smitten, works/wages — with the KJV's “again” carried through each time. Then, at 8:20, he supplies the scriptural warrant, and it is Paul rather than Jesus. The Sermon governs the form of the sentence and the epistle is cited for its authority, which is a fair description of how the whole chapter uses the New Testament.

links.note: “the same that judgeth rashly, shall be judged rashly again: for according to his works shall his wages be; therefore, he that smiteth, shall be smitten again of the Lord.” The passive-reciprocal construction with “again” is Matthew 7:2's, and the middle clause is the standing KJV formula for recompense (“reward every man according to his works”, Matthew 16:27). Moroni's addition is the adverb “rashly”, which narrows the Sermon's blanket prohibition on judging into a prohibition on judging hastily — a qualification the Sermon does not make and one the chapter needs, since Moroni spends the next twenty verses judging.

pericopes.text: Behold what the Scripture saith: Man shall not smite, neither shall he judge: for judgement is mine, saith the Lord; and vengeance is mine also, and I will repay.

links.text: Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 32:35 → Romans 12:19 (with Hebrews 10:30) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Deuteronomy 32:35, the passage Paul is quoting, reads “To me belongeth vengeance and recompence” — a phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is not the phrase Moroni has. Hebrews 10:30 quotes the same text a third way, “Vengeance belongeth unto me, I will recompense, saith the Lord.” tools/mediation-check.py returns Romans over Deuteronomy on one decisive point and Romans over Hebrews on two: the Book of Mormon has “is mine … I will repay”, not “belongeth” and not “recompense”.
provenance.significance: Moroni writes “Behold what the Scripture saith”, which is a citation formula, and then cites — not the Song of Moses, but Paul's citation of the Song of Moses, in Paul's English, including Paul's “saith the Lord”, a tag Deuteronomy does not have. Romans 12:19 is itself introduced by “for it is written”. So a fourth-century Nephite quoting scripture reproduces a first-century epistle quoting a fourteenth-century-BC song, at one remove, in seventeenth-century English. This is the chapter's clearest instance of the criterion CONVENTIONS §3a says this corpus inverts: availability fails, and the failure is the finding. Hebrews is not displaced by Romans, it is doing separate work. Moroni claims two things for the Lord, judgement and vengeance, and Romans 12:19 supplies only vengeance; the pairing is Hebrews 10:30's, which follows “I will recompense, saith the Lord” with “And again, The Lord shall judge his people.” Moroni's verse is therefore composite in the strict sense: Romans for the words, Hebrews for the two-part claim, Deuteronomy behind both.

links.note: “Behold what the Scripture saith: Man shall not smite, neither shall he judge: for judgement is mine, saith the Lord; and vengeance is mine also, and I will repay.” Every distinctive word of the second half is Romans 12:19's, and the first half — a prohibition on private smiting and judging — is Romans 12:19's opening clause, “avenge not yourselves”, crossed with the Sermon's “judge not” that governed the preceding verse. The 1830 spelling “judgement” is the older English form and 1920 prints “judgment”; the KJV has “judgment” throughout, so here the first edition departs from the source and the later edition returns to it. This discharges all three references Hardy's apparatus cross-references at this verse.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 8.20 (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19; Hebrews 10:30)

pericopes.text: And he that shall breathe out wrath and strifes against the work of the Lord, and against the covenant people of the Lord, which is the house of Israel, and shall say, We will destroy the work of the Lord, and the Lord will not remember his covenant which he hath made unto the house of Israel, the same is in danger to be hewn down and cast into the fire:

links.text: And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.route: Matthew 3:10 (+ Acts 19:27) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “hewn down, and cast into the fire” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9. “in danger to be” occurs in exactly two, Acts 19:27 and Acts 19:40, both from the Ephesus riot, where it is a term of legal exposure.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9 carry the same seven-word run. Luke 3:9 is the Lukan form of the same Baptist sermon; Matthew 7:19 is the Sermon on the Mount's reuse of it. Nothing in the seven words chooses between the three, and the choice is made on context — see significance.
provenance.significance: Context decides the source, and the recovered context is the argument. Moroni's condemned man is the one who says “the Lord will not remember his covenant which he hath made unto the house of Israel”. Matthew 3:9 — the verse immediately before the one Moroni's words come from — is “think not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.” The Baptist is preaching against exactly one error, presumption about the covenant with Israel, and Moroni applies his sentence to exactly one error, presumption that the covenant with Israel has lapsed. The two are mirror images across the same verse, which is why Matthew 3:10 and not Matthew 7:19 is named as the source. Meanwhile the idiom Moroni welds to the front of it — “is in danger to be” — is not the Baptist's at all but the Ephesian town clerk's, the KJV's phrase for standing legally liable. Moroni has taken a courtroom formula from Acts and a fire from Matthew and made one sentence of them.

links.note: “the same is in danger to be hewn down and cast into the fire.” A seven-word run from a three-verse KJV phrase, fronted by a two-verse KJV legalism, and it is the second time in five verses Moroni has reached for the KJV's language of danger — 8:17 has “in danger of hell fire” from Matthew 5:22. Two different “in danger” idioms, from two different books, four verses apart, both put to the same use: warning a Gentile reader what a wrong verdict costs.

pericopes.text: for the eternal purposes of the Lord shall roll on, until all his promises shall be fulfilled.

Search the prophecies of Isaiah. Behold, I cannot write them. Yea, behold I say unto you, That those saints which have gone before me, which have possessed this land, shall cry; yea, even from the dust will they cry unto the Lord; and as the Lord liveth, he will remember the covenant which he hath made with them.

links.text: And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.

provenance.route: Isaiah 29:4 → KJV → 2 Nephi 26:16 / 33:13 → Book of Mormon (Mormon 8:23)
provenance.other: “whisper out of the dust” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni does not have it. He has “from the dust will they cry unto the Lord”, which is nobody's KJV phrase — but it is very close to 2 Nephi 33:13, “as the voice of one crying from the dust”, and 2 Nephi 26:16 renders Isaiah 29:4 nearly whole (“their speech shall be low out of the dust … as one that hath a familiar spirit … whisper out of the dust”).
provenance.alternative: Direct dependence on Isaiah 29:4. Against it: not one of Isaiah's distinctive words survives here — no ground, no whisper, no familiar spirit, no low speech — and Isaiah's voice speaks while Moroni's cries.
provenance.significance: The mediation is the finding, and the verse announces it: “Search the prophecies of Isaiah. Behold, I cannot write them.” Moroni tells the reader where the source is and then declines to reproduce it, which is precisely the condition under which an earlier Book of Mormon rendering, rather than the Bible, becomes the proximate model. What he actually writes is Nephi's phrase, not Isaiah's, and he writes it again at 8:26 (“as if one should speak from the dead”) and once more in his own farewell at Moroni 10:27, where the two halves stand side by side — “like as one crying from the dead? yea, even as one speaking out of the dust”. Isaiah's necromantic image, which in Isaiah is a threat against Ariel, has by this point in the book become the standing Nephite figure for the record itself, and Moroni inherits it already transformed.

links.note: The verbal contact with Isaiah 29:4 is too slight to catalogue as dependence on the KJV, and kjvSpecific is set to 'no' for that reason. What the verse does have is an explicit instruction to go read Isaiah, a phrase that matches Nephi's rendering rather than Isaiah's, and a chain of BoM recurrences that ends in Moroni's own last chapter. This is the pattern CONVENTIONS §7 reserves 'OT-via-earlier-BoM' for, and Mormon 8 is where it can be seen operating on a writer who says out loud that he is not copying the source.

pericopes.text: And he knoweth their prayers, that they were in the behalf of their brethren. And he knoweth their faith: for in his name could they remove mountains; and in his name could they cause the earth to shake; and by the power of his word did they cause prisons to tumble to the earth; yea, even the fiery furnace could not harm them; neither wild beasts, nor poisonous serpents, because of the power of his word.

links.text: And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.

provenance.other: “could remove mountains” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The gospel sayings about faith and mountains do not use the verb: Matthew 17:20 has “ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place”, and Mark 11:23 “Be thou removed, and be thou cast into the sea”. The transitive “remove mountains”, with the mountains as the object of a believer's power, is Paul's formulation and the King James Bible has it once.
provenance.significance: Moroni's clause is “he knoweth their faith: for in his name could they remove mountains”, and Paul's is “though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.” The verb, the modal and the object are all Paul's; what Moroni drops is the whole point of the sentence he took them from. In 1 Corinthians 13 mountain-moving faith is the thing declared worthless without charity. Moroni cites it as proof that the three Nephites' faith was real. Read the two together and the omission is loud, because Moroni is a writer preoccupied with charity — it is what he ends the book on at Moroni 7 and 10 — and here he uses the one verse in scripture that subordinates faith to charity as a straightforward commendation of faith.

links.note: Three words off a KJV singleton, at the head of a roll-call of what faith accomplished. The wording is Paul's rather than the gospels', which is worth establishing because the gospel sayings are the ones a reader expects behind any sentence about faith and mountains, and they are not the ones in play.

links.text: Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

provenance.other: “stopped the mouths of lions” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “quenched the violence of fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; they are consecutive clauses of one sentence. “the foundations of the prison” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 16:26. “take up serpents” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:18. Moroni reproduces none of these strings; he reproduces the list they make.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 11:33-34 is the King James Bible's one catalogue of what faith did, built as a chain of bare participial clauses with no connective — subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword. Moroni writes the same kind of chain, in the same order of escalation, for the three Nephites: mountains removed, the earth shaken, prisons tumbled, the fiery furnace survived, wild beasts and poisonous serpents harmless. Two of his five items are Hebrews' own two — the fire and the beasts — and Hebrews reaches them, as Moroni does, by way of Daniel 3 and Daniel 6 without naming either. The prisons are Acts 16:26 and the serpents are Mark 16:18, which Hardy's apparatus cross-references at Mormon 9:25, one chapter on; Moroni gets to the same promise a chapter early and by a different route.

links.note: A form-level link with almost no shared vocabulary, filed as an allusion rather than a figural link because the form in question is a specific KJV sentence and not a narrative type. kjvSpecific is 'no': nothing here is worded distinctively enough to test against an English version. What is being claimed is that the roll-call of faith's deeds is a genre the King James Bible supplies once, and that Moroni, introducing his list with “he knoweth their faith”, is writing in it.

pericopes.text: And behold, their prayers were also in behalf of him that the Lord should suffer to bring these things forth.

And no one need not say, They shall not come, for they surely shall, for the Lord hath spoken it: for out of the earth shall they come, by the hand of the Lord, and none can stay it; and it shall come in a day when it shall be said that miracles are done away; and it shall come even as if one should speak from the dead.

links.text: The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he looketh not for him, and in an hour that he is not aware of,

provenance.other: “come in a day when” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:50 and Luke 12:46, which are the two forms of one parable. Matthew reads “shall come in a day when”; Luke reads “will come in a day when”. The Book of Mormon reads “it shall come in a day when”, six times over. tools/mediation-check.py declined to call this divergence — its aligner did not lock onto the auxiliary — but the two words are on the page.
provenance.alternative: Luke 12:46 carries the same phrase. It is ruled out by the auxiliary and by the last word of the parable: Luke's servant gets his portion “with the unbelievers”, Matthew's “with the hypocrites” — a phrase that occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and Moroni's arraignment of the latter-day churches is addressed to “ye pollutions, ye hypocrites” at 8:38.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's largest borrowing and it is invisible to a word-count, because what Moroni takes from Matthew 24:50 is a sentence-frame and not a sentence. Six times in seven verses he begins “yea, it shall come in a day when …”, and the phrase he is repeating exists in the King James Bible in two verses only, both of them the parable of the servant whose lord delays. Recover that parable and the whole prophecy is already written: Matthew 24:48-49's wicked servant says “My lord delayeth his coming”, begins to smite his fellowservants and to eat and drink with the drunken; Moroni's day is one in which churches are built up for gain, leaders are lifted up in pride, and the poor and the needy are passed by. Matthew 24:51 sentences that servant to his portion with the hypocrites; Moroni calls them hypocrites outright. The anaphora is not decoration — it is the parable's verdict extended to a church, one clause at a time.

links.note: Filed at 8:26, the first of the six occurrences, and carried through 8:27, 8:28, 8:29, 8:31 and 8:32 in recurrenceRefs rather than repeated as six links. The n-gram stream proposed Matthew 24:50 at five of the six verses and ranked it as ordinary boilerplate, which is exactly the failure CONVENTIONS §9 describes: a two-verse KJV phrase used six times as a structural refrain reads to the machine as noise and to a reader as an argument.

links.text: And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead.

provenance.other: “one rose from the dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the preceding verse has “if one went unto them from the dead”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moroni's clause is “even as if one should speak from the dead” — the same indefinite “one”, the same “from the dead”, the same conditional frame, with a verb of speech where Luke has verbs of going and rising.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 29:4's voice out of the ground, taken through 2 Nephi (see the link at 8:23), accounts for the dust and the speaking. It does not account for “from the dead”, which is Luke's phrase and not Isaiah's.
provenance.significance: The two candidates are not rivals here; Moroni has fused them, and the fusion is what makes the sentence work. Abraham's answer to Dives is that people who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded by a resurrection — and Moroni has just written, three verses earlier, “Search the prophecies of Isaiah”. He tells his readers to hear the prophets, predicts that they will not, and then describes his book arriving in a generation that says miracles are done away, “even as if one should speak from the dead”. Luke's parable supplies the reason the arrival will fail to persuade, in advance, and Moroni's chapter is a long attempt to persuade anyway.

links.note: Recorded as an echo because the verbal overlap is three ordinary words and the construction is common English. What lifts it is placement: the clause stands at the end of a sentence about a book that comes out of the earth to people who deny miracles, four words after a command to search the prophets, and Luke 16:31 is the one KJV verse that joins those two ideas.

pericopes.text: And it shall come in a day when the blood of saints shall cry unto the Lord, because of secret combinations and the works of darkness;

links.text: And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?

provenance.other: “avenge our blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “How long, O Lord” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse. “blood of saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:6, of the martyrs whose blood the harlot has shed. Moroni's “the blood of saints shall cry unto the Lord” welds the noun of one to the appeal of the other.
provenance.significance: Revelation 6:9-10 is the souls under the altar: martyrs who cry with a loud voice for their blood to be avenged and are told to rest a little season until the number of their fellowservants is fulfilled. Moroni is himself the last survivor of a slaughtered people, writing over their graves; the figure of crying, unavenged blood is not one he needed to borrow, and the reason to think he did is that both of Revelation's phrases turn up in the same two verses of his chapter — the cry at 8:27 and the avenging at 8:41 — and that they frame the prophecy exactly as Revelation's seals frame the plagues. The recovered context supplies what Moroni leaves out: the answer to “How long” is that they must wait until the tale of the martyrs is complete.

links.note: “it shall come in a day when the blood of saints shall cry unto the Lord, because of secret combinations and the works of darkness.” Two KJV singletons from one verse of Revelation, split across the chapter — the crying blood here, the avenging of it in the last verse — with Revelation 16:6's exact noun phrase supplying the subject. Machine candidate Isaiah 19:20 (“they shall cry unto the LORD because of the oppressors”) shares a longer contiguous run and is displaced; see the exclusion register.

links.text: The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.

provenance.other: “the works of darkness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ephesians 5:11 has the nearest rival, “the unfruitful works of darkness”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse of its own; the idiom is Pauline generally and the bare four-word form is Romans 13:12's alone.
provenance.significance: Romans 13:12's clause sits under “the day is at hand”, and Moroni's sits inside “it shall come in a day when” — the anaphora he has taken from Matthew 24. Paul's works of darkness are to be cast off because the day is coming; Moroni's are what the coming day will find. The overlap is one phrase and the interest is that it is the eschatological-day frame in both.

links.note: A four-word KJV singleton in a verse whose main business is elsewhere (see the Revelation 6:10 link above). Recorded at moderate confidence and as an echo: the phrase is distinctive in the KJV but not distinctive in English, and 'secret combinations' — the words it is paired with — is the Book of Mormon's own idiom and has no biblical source at all.

pericopes.text: yea, it shall come in a day when the power of God shall be denied, and churches become defiled, and shall be lifted up in the pride of their hearts; yea, even in a day when leaders of churches, and teachers, in the pride of their hearts, even to the envying of them who belong to their churches;
yea, it shall come in a day when there shall be heard of fires, and tempests, and vapors of smoke in foreign lands;

links.text: And I will shew wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath; blood, and fire, and vapour of smoke:

provenance.route: Joel 2:30 → Acts 2:19 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “vapour of smoke” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:19. Joel 2:30, the verse Peter is quoting, reads “pillars of smoke”, a phrase which occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joel 2:30 and Song of Solomon 3:6. The Book of Mormon has “vapors of smoke”. tools/mediation-check.py reported no decisive divergence here, and it is wrong to do so: its tokeniser will not match the 1830 plural “vapors” against the KJV singular “vapour”, so the one word that settles the question was the one word it could not see. By eye the lexeme is decisive — Moroni has Peter's noun, not Joel's.
provenance.significance: The King James translators rendered the same Hebrew word two ways, “pillars of smoke” at Joel 2:30 and “vapour of smoke” where Acts quotes it, and the Book of Mormon follows the New Testament rendering. That is a fact about English translation practice in 1611, not about Hebrew, and it is the kind of evidence this catalogue exists to record: the divergence Moroni reproduces cannot exist in any text older than the KJV's own committee. Note also what he does with it — Joel and Acts list the sign among the wonders that attend the Spirit's outpouring and the day of the Lord; Moroni lists it among the calamities that will attend the record's appearance, alongside wars and earthquakes from the Olivet Discourse in the next verse. Pentecost's signs have become the last days' disasters.

links.note: “there shall be heard of fires, and tempests, and vapors of smoke in foreign lands.” Three words tracking a KJV singleton, and the singleton is one half of a translational doublet whose other half stands in the Old Testament source. This is the clean mediation case in the chapter: the wording is available only from Acts, so the route runs through the New Testament even though the prophecy is Joel's.

pericopes.text: and there shall also be heard of wars, and rumors of wars, and earthquakes in diverse places;

links.text: For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places.

provenance.other: “rumours of wars” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:6 and Mark 13:7. “earthquakes in divers places” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 24:7 and Mark 13:8. Moroni has both, in the biblical order, in one clause.
provenance.alternative: Mark 13:7-8 carries both phrases in the same order and cannot be excluded on wording alone. Matthew is preferred because the anaphora governing this whole passage — “it shall come in a day when” — comes from Matthew 24:50 and not from Mark, who has no parallel to the parable of the delaying lord.
provenance.significance: 1830 prints “earthquakes in diverse places” and 1920 prints “divers”, which is the King James spelling: the later edition moved the text back toward its source (CONVENTIONS §8). The direction matters, because “divers” and “diverse” were still one word in 1830 and had separated by 1920, so what looks like a modernisation is in fact a re-archaising, made to keep the phrase recognisable. That the borrowing had to be protected in this way is itself evidence that it was recognised.

links.note: “there shall also be heard of wars, and rumors of wars, and earthquakes in diverse places.” Two KJV two-verse phrases from consecutive verses of the Olivet Discourse, in sequence, with Matthew's connective structure. Moroni drops the famines and pestilences and keeps the wars and the earthquakes, which is what a writer addressing a people who have just destroyed themselves in war would keep.

pericopes.text: yea, it shall come in a day when there shall be great pollutions upon the face of the earth: there shall be murders, and robbing, and lying, and deceivings, and whoredoms, and all manner of abominations; when there shall be many which will say, Do this, or do that, and it mattereth not, for the Lord will uphold such at the last day. But wo unto such, for they are in the gall of bitterness, and in the bonds of iniquity.

links.text: For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.

provenance.other: “gall of bitterness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “bond of iniquity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and they are the same verse. The Book of Mormon reproduces eleven consecutive words of it, altering only the number of the second noun: “bonds of iniquity” for “bond of iniquity”.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's finest metalepsis and it is completed by the next verse. Acts 8:23 is Peter's sentence on Simon Magus, and what Simon has done — three verses earlier, at Acts 8:20 — is offer the apostles money for the gift of God: “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.” Moroni pronounces Peter's sentence at 8:31 and then, at 8:32, names the crime: “it shall come in a day when there shall be churches built up that shall say, Come unto me, and for your money you shall be forgiven of your sins.” Neither verse says the word simony. The pair does. A reader who does not recover Acts 8 sees an ordinary denunciation of greedy churches; a reader who recovers it finds that the denunciation has been given the apostolic verdict on the first man who tried to buy the Holy Ghost, and that the verdict was pronounced before the charge was read.

links.note: The longest verbatim run in the chapter and the top-ranked machine candidate, at a rarity of 5.00 with an eight-word window — one of the rare cases where the n-gram stream put the strongest link in the chapter at the top of its own list. Eleven words is below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and this is not one of his thirty-six; it is catalogued as a quotation nonetheless, on the CONVENTIONS §2 ground that a complete clause reproduced from an identifiable single source is a quotation whatever its length.

pericopes.text: Yea, it shall come in a day when there shall be churches built up that shall say, Come unto me, and for your money you shall be forgiven of your sins.

O ye wicked, and perverse, and stiffnecked people, why have ye built up churches unto yourselves to get gain? Why have ye transfigured the holy word of God, that ye might bring damnation upon your souls? Behold, look ye unto the revelations of God. For behold, the time cometh at that day when all these things must be fulfilled.
Behold, the Lord hath shewn unto me great and marvellous things concerning that which must shortly come at that day when these things shall come forth among you.
Behold, I speak unto you as if ye were present, and yet ye are not. But behold, Jesus Christ hath shewn you unto me, and I know your doing;

links.text: For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed,

provenance.other: “as though I were present” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “present in spirit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; they are the same verse. Colossians 2:5 has the same manoeuvre in different words — “though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit”.
provenance.significance: Paul's construction lets an absent apostle pass judgment on a congregation he cannot see, and 1 Corinthians 5:3 is where he uses it to deliver a sentence — “I have judged already … concerning him that hath so done this deed”. Moroni inverts the geometry and keeps the function. Paul is the one who is absent; Moroni's readers are. “Jesus Christ hath shewn you unto me, and I know your doing” supplies the vision that makes the absence immaterial, and what follows is a sentence on a congregation: pride, fine apparel, envying, polluted churches. The verse before it says the Lord has shewn him “great and marvellous things”; this one says what he was shewn was the reader.

links.note: “Behold, I speak unto you as if ye were present, and yet ye are not.” A one-verse KJV construction with the persons exchanged. The 1830 spelling “shewn” in the same verse is the King James form, modernised to “shown” in 1920 (CONVENTIONS §8), which is not evidence for this particular source but is evidence that the sentence around it is being written in King James English.

pericopes.text: and I know that ye do walk in the pride of your hearts; and there are none, save a few only, which do not lift themselves up in the pride of their hearts, unto the wearing of very fine apparel, unto envying, and strifes, and malice, and persecutions, and all manner of iniquities; and your churches, yea, even every one, have become polluted because of the pride of your hearts.
For behold, ye do love money, and your substances, and your fine apparel, and the adorning of your churches, more than ye love the poor and the needy, the sick and the afflicted.

O ye pollutions, ye hypocrites, ye teachers, which sell yourselves for that which will canker, why have ye polluted the holy church of God? Why are ye ashamed to take upon you the name of Christ? Why do ye not think that greater is the value of an endless happiness, than that misery which never dies, because of the praise of the world?

links.text: Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you, and shall eat your flesh as it were fire. Ye have heaped treasure together for the last days.

provenance.route: James 5:1-4 (+ 1 Timothy 6:10) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “gold and silver is cankered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The bare noun “canker” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 2:17, where it is a spreading sore and has nothing to do with money; James 5:3 is the only place in the King James Bible where wealth cankers. “the love of money” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 6:10, and Moroni's 8:37 opens “ye do love money”.
provenance.significance: The last five verses of the chapter follow James 5:1-4 point for point, and they follow it in order. James: weep, ye rich men (5:1); your riches are corrupted and your garments motheaten (5:2); your gold and silver is cankered (5:3); the hire of the labourers crieth, and the cries of them are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth (5:4). Moroni: ye do love money and your substances and your fine apparel (8:37); ye sell yourselves for that which will canker (8:38); ye suffer the hungry and the needy to pass by (8:39); widows and orphans mourn and blood cries for vengeance (8:40); he will not suffer their cries any longer (8:41). The one word that will not come from anywhere else is “canker”, and the reason Moroni can use it as a verb of money is that James used it as a participle of gold.

links.note: “ye teachers, which sell yourselves for that which will canker.” Moroni verbs a word the KJV uses only twice, and only once of wealth. The wider dependence — a five-verse peroration tracking James 5:1-4 in sequence — is what makes the single word safe to build on; the link is filed here, where the rare word is, and 8:37 and 8:41 are carried in recurrenceRefs rather than given separate rows for the same argument.

pericopes.text: Why do ye adorn yourselves with that which hath no life, and yet suffer the hungry, and the needy, and the naked, and the sick, and the afflicted to pass by you, and notice them not?

links.text: I was a stranger, and ye took me not in: naked, and ye clothed me not: sick, and in prison, and ye visited me not.

provenance.route: Matthew 25:42-45 (+ Luke 10:31) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “naked, and ye clothed me not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “sick, and in prison” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — the same verse. Moroni shares the nouns and not the clauses: hungry, needy, naked, sick, afflicted. “passed by on the other side” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 10:31 and 10:32, the priest and the Levite.
provenance.significance: The sheep-and-goats indictment is a list of omissions in the second person plural addressed to people about to be sentenced, and Moroni's is the same list, in the same grammar, addressed to the same kind of defendant — with one change that is worth noticing. In Matthew the failure is not to come to the destitute; in Moroni it is to let them come past you: “suffer the hungry, and the needy, and the naked, and the sick, and the afflicted to pass by you, and notice them not.” The direction of the passing-by is reversed from the Good Samaritan's, where it is the priest who passes by the wounded man. Moroni's rich do not travel; the poor file past their churches while they are adorning them.

links.note: Catalogued as an allusion at moderate confidence, and the confidence is honest: three of the five nouns are the commonest words in the Bible for the destitute, and neither of the two KJV singletons the source verse contains survives in Moroni's sentence. What carries it is the form — a numbered catalogue of neglected persons, in the second person, at a judgment — which the King James Bible supplies exactly once.

pericopes.text: Yea, why do ye build up your secret abominations to get gain, and cause that widows should mourn before the Lord, and also orphans to mourn before the Lord; and also the blood of their fathers and their husbands to cry unto the Lord from the ground, for vengeance upon your heads?

links.text: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.

provenance.other: “crieth unto me from the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. tools/mediation-check.py against Hebrews 12:24, the New Testament's only other treatment of Abel's speaking blood, returns Genesis decisively: Hebrews has “the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel” and shares none of the words Moroni reproduces.
provenance.significance: Moroni does not put the blood in a murdered brother's mouth but in the fathers' and husbands' of the widows and orphans he has just named, and he changes the addressee: in Genesis the blood cries unto God unprompted and God asks the question; here the blood cries “for vengeance upon your heads”, and the question — “why do ye build up your secret abominations to get gain?” — is Moroni's, put to the living. The recovered context makes the accusation specific rather than general. Cain's answer to God was that he did not know where his brother was; the latter-day churches' answer, at 8:39, is that they did not notice the poor going past.

links.note: “the blood of their fathers and their husbands to cry unto the Lord from the ground, for vengeance upon your heads.” The KJV joins crying blood to the ground in one verse only, and Moroni has it with the preposition changed from “unto me” to “unto the Lord” because he is speaking about God rather than as him. The verse also carries Exodus 22:22-24 in its widows and orphans; that strand is adjudicated at 8:41, where the sword arrives.

pericopes.text: Behold, the sword of vengeance hangeth over you; and the time soon cometh that he avengeth the blood of the saints upon you, for he will not suffer their cries any longer.

links.text: If thou afflict them in any wise, and they cry at all unto me, I will surely hear their cry;

provenance.route: Exodus 22:22-24 → KJV → Book of Mormon, with Revelation 6:10, James 5:4 and Deuteronomy 32:41-43 all in contact and none of them isolable
provenance.other: “cry at all unto me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “your wives shall be widows” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the verse following. “the cries of them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 5:4. “avenge the blood of his servants” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 32:43; Moroni's noun is not “servants” but “saints”, and “blood of saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 16:6.
provenance.alternative: James 5:4 for the cries and Revelation 6:10 / 16:6 for the avenged blood of saints; Deuteronomy 32:41-43 for the sword and the vengeance. Each accounts for part of the verse and none for all of it.
provenance.significance: The mediation here is genuinely undecided and is recorded as such rather than defaulted. The sequence of the verse is Exodus 22:22-24's exactly — afflict the widow and the fatherless, they cry unto me, I will surely hear their cry, my wrath shall wax hot and I will kill you with the sword — and Moroni runs it in that order across 8:40-41, ending on a sword. But his cry is “the blood of the saints”, which is Revelation's phrase and not Exodus's, and his verb is “avengeth”, which puts Deuteronomy 32:43 in play; and Deuteronomy 32 is already the ultimate source of the quotation at 8:20, so the chapter would then open its judgment section on Deuteronomy 32:35 and close it on Deuteronomy 32:43, which is a satisfying frame and may be a wholly accidental one. tools/mediation-check.py reports Deuteronomy 32:43 over Revelation 19:2 as decisive; that verdict should not be relied on. It counted “servants” as a shared backbone word when Moroni reads “saints”, and it matched the “vengeance” of “sword of vengeance” against Deuteronomy's tail clause. This is the row a later pass should revisit.

links.note: “Behold, the sword of vengeance hangeth over you; and the time soon cometh that he avengeth the blood of the saints upon you, for he will not suffer their cries any longer.” Four sources are in contact with twenty-four words and the verse will not be assigned to one of them. Exodus 22:22-24 is named as the source because it alone supplies the whole sequence — oppressed widows, a cry, a hearing, a sword — and because Moroni has just spent 8:40 on the widows and the orphans. The wording of the cry is James's and the wording of the blood is Revelation's. Confidence is moderate and mediation is 'uncertain' on the CONVENTIONS §7 principle that a decision not actually made should not be written down as one.

pericopes.text: And now, I speak also concerning those who do not believe in Christ.

Behold, will ye believe in the day of your visitation, behold, when the Lord shall come; yea, even that great day when the earth shall be rolled together as a scroll, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat; yea, in that great day when ye shall be brought to stand before the Lamb of God, then will ye say that there is no God?

provenance.other: “the elements shall melt with fervent heat” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Peter 3:10 and 3:12, and nowhere else in either Testament; the seven-word run is reproduced without a change. Two further elements of the same verse are present in the same sentence: 2 Peter 3:10 opens “the day of the Lord will come” against Moroni's “when the Lord shall come … that great day”, and closes with “the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up” — “the works that are therein” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — against Moroni's transfer of the burning to the earth. “day of visitation” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 10:3 and 1 Peter 2:12, and Moroni's “the day of your visitation” inflects the Petrine one.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 3 is the New Testament's answer to people who say that nothing is going to happen — “Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation” (3:4). Mormon 9 is Moroni's answer to people who say that nothing happens any longer, that revelation and miracle are done away. He opens the argument by taking the scoffers' chapter whole: the fire that will find the elements, the day that comes as a thief, the burning of the works in the earth. Recover the context and the borrowing does the arguing — the epistle Moroni reaches for is the one written against exactly his opponents' premise, and its scoffers are refuted by a delay that is patience rather than absence. The chapter will return to the same page at 9:6.

links.note: 'That great day when the earth shall be rolled together as a scroll, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat.' Seven words verbatim from a two-verse KJV phrase, joined to a seven-word run from Isaiah 34:4 in the same clause and both of them handed to a question — 'then will ye say that there is no God?' The verse is a fusion, not a citation, and it is the densest single sentence of borrowed apocalyptic in the book of Mormon's own colophon. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold taken phrase by phrase, though the whole sentence is longer than it; category is quotation on CONVENTIONS §2's grounds — a complete predicate, absolutely rare, reproduced.
links.text: But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.

provenance.route: Isaiah 34:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon (second occurrence; see Mormon 5:23)
provenance.other: “rolled together as a scroll” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 34:4; “as a scroll” occurs in exactly two, Isaiah 34:4 and Revelation 6:14. Revelation's syntax puts the participle after the noun (“as a scroll when it is rolled together”); Mormon 9:2 has Isaiah's order, as Mormon 5:23 does.
provenance.alternative: Revelation 6:14 is the same image in the same Bible and the better-known verse; the word order rules it out here for the same reason it was ruled out at 5:23.
provenance.significance: The book uses this phrase exactly twice, at Mormon 5:23 and here, and both times with Isaiah's word order and with Isaiah's noun changed from the heavens to the earth. That consistency is worth more than either occurrence alone: it shows the substitution is the text's own settled reading rather than a slip. What changes between the two is the addressee. At 5:23 the rolled-up earth is a threat held over the Lamanites — 'know ye not that ye are in the hands of God?' At 9:2 it is put to the deniers of God as a date: on the day the earth is rolled up you will be standing in front of the Lamb, and the question is whether you will still say there is no God.

links.note: Six words verbatim, one noun changed, in a verse that also reproduces seven words of 2 Peter 3:10. The two apocalypses are welded at the conjunction — Isaiah's scroll and Peter's elements share a single 'yea' — and neither source is named. Recorded separately from the 2 Peter row because the mediation differs: Isaiah reaches this verse in the Old Testament's own form while the rest of the sentence is New Testament, and a verse that draws on both Testaments in one breath is exactly the kind of thing the catalogue exists to make visible.
links.text: And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll: and all their host shall fall down, as the leaf falleth off from the vine, and as a falling fig from the fig tree.

pericopes.text: Then will ye longer deny the Christ, or can ye behold the Lamb of God? Do ye suppose that ye shall dwell with him under a consciousness of your guilt? Do ye suppose that ye could be happy to dwell with that holy Being, when your souls are racked with a consciousness of your guilt that ye have ever abused his laws?
Behold I say unto you, that ye would be more miserable to dwell with a holy and just God, under a consciousness of your filthiness before him, than ye would to dwell with the damned souls in hell?
For behold, when ye shall be brought to see your nakedness before God, and also the glory of God, and the holiness of Jesus Christ, it will kindle a flame of unquenchable fire upon you.

provenance.other: “unquenchable fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 3:12. Luke's parallel at 3:17 inverts it to 'fire unquenchable' and Mark 9:43 paraphrases it as 'the fire that never shall be quenched', so the compound adjective standing before its noun is Matthew's alone.
provenance.significance: John the Baptist's unquenchable fire burns chaff — the separated, worthless part of a harvest. Moroni's kindles on a man who has been made to see his own nakedness in the presence of the glory and holiness he denied. The transfer moves the fire from outside the person to inside him: what ignites is not a heap of chaff but the sight of oneself, and the fuel is the contrast between the nakedness and the holiness. It is the same move the chapter makes at 9:3-4, where hell is redescribed as a state of being unable to bear the company one is in.

links.note: 'It will kindle a flame of unquenchable fire upon you.' Two words, but the compound is a King James singleton in Matthew's word order, and it lands in a sequence (nakedness seen, glory seen, holiness seen, fire kindled) that has no equivalent in the Baptist's threshing floor. Filed moderate: the phrase is rare enough to name a source and short enough that a writer steeped in the KJV could produce it without reaching for one.
links.text: Whose fan is in his hand, and he will throughly purge his floor, and gather his wheat into the garner; but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.

pericopes.text: O then ye unbelieving, turn ye unto the Lord; cry mightily unto the Father in the name of Jesus, that perhaps ye may be found spotless, pure, fair, and white, having been cleansed by the blood of the Lamb, at that great and last day.

provenance.other: “blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 7:14 and 12:11. Only 7:14 attaches it to washing and to whiteness — 'washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb' — and Moroni has both, 'pure, fair, and white, having been cleansed by the blood of the Lamb'.
provenance.significance: Revelation 7:14 answers the question of Revelation 7:13, 'What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they?' — and the answer is that they came out of great tribulation. Moroni is writing at the end of a book whose people have just been destroyed, to readers he cannot see, and the verse he reaches for is the one that identifies the white-robed as survivors of a catastrophe. Note also what he does not take: Revelation washes robes, Moroni cleanses persons. The garment drops out, and with it the last screen between the man and the blood.

links.note: 'That perhaps ye may be found spotless, pure, fair, and white, having been cleansed by the blood of the Lamb, at that great and last day.' The paradox is the KJV's and Moroni keeps it whole: blood is the agent of whiteness. The chapter has been running on the Lamb since 9:2 ('brought to stand before the Lamb of God'), and this is where the Lamb stops being the judge one stands before and becomes the means of standing.
links.text: And I said unto him, Sir, thou knowest. And he said to me, These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.

provenance.other: “may be found of him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “found of him in peace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both 2 Peter 3:14. The bare “without spot” occurs in exactly eleven, so the rarity here is in the construction — being FOUND in a certain condition on the day — not in the adjective.
provenance.significance: This row exists because of where it sits. Mormon 9:2 reproduces seven words of 2 Peter 3:10 and gestures at 3:12 and the burning of 3:10's close; four verses later the exhortation arrives in the shape of 2 Peter 3:14, which is the verse that draws the practical conclusion from exactly those verses — 'seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.' Moroni's 'that perhaps ye may be found spotless … at that great and last day' is the same sentence-shape with the same verb in the same voice, and it follows its source's own order: dissolution first, then the charge to be found unspotted. If 9:2 is a quotation of 2 Peter 3, 9:6 is the evidence that the whole chapter of it was open.

links.note: A weaker verbal case than 9:2's and it is not offered on its own. What makes it worth a row is sequence: the two verses of Mormon 9 that draw on 2 Peter 3 draw on it in its own order, four verses apart, and the second takes the very verse in which the epistle turns its apocalypse into a moral demand. Filed moderate because 'found spotless' is a phrase the Book of Mormon can produce unaided (compare Jacob 1:19, 'we would not be found spotless at the last day'), which is the reading a cautious editor should prefer.
links.whyNot: 'Spotless' is not the KJV's word here at all — 2 Peter has 'without spot' — and 'found … at the last day' is already Book of Mormon idiom by Jacob 1:19, three centuries of narrative time before Moroni. The row rests on the passive verb, the sequence and the neighbouring 9:2 rather than on any distinctive string.
links.text: Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.

pericopes.text: And again I speak unto you, who deny the revelations of God, and say that they are done away, that there is no revelations, nor prophecies, nor gifts, nor healing, nor speaking with tongues, and the interpretation of tongues.

provenance.other: “interpretation of tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 12:10; “kinds of tongues” occurs in exactly one; “working of miracles” occurs in exactly one; all three are that verse. “gifts of healing” occurs in exactly two, 1 Corinthians 12:9 and 12:30. Moroni's list — prophecies, gifts, healing, speaking with tongues, the interpretation of tongues — runs the Pauline items in the Pauline order, 12:9 before 12:10, and closes on the phrase that exists nowhere else in the English Bible.
provenance.significance: The metalepsis is in the verb Moroni gives his opponents. They 'say that they are done away' — and “shall be done away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:10, 'when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away', which stands eleven verses after the gift-list and is the sentence on which every argument that the gifts have ceased has ever been built. Two verses earlier, 1 Corinthians 13:8 says of the same list that 'whether there be tongues, they shall cease' — and “they shall cease” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, of which that is one. So the position Moroni is refuting is not a position he has invented for the purpose: it is 1 Corinthians 13:8-10 read as a timetable, and he answers it by putting Paul's own list back in Paul's own words and asking, at 9:15, 'Has the end come yet?' The whole of Mormon 9:7-20 is an argument conducted inside one chapter-pair of one epistle, and Moroni's answer to cessation is Paul's other verb: God 'has not ceased', 'he ceaseth not'.

links.note: 'They are done away, that there is no revelations, nor prophecies, nor gifts, nor healing, nor speaking with tongues, and the interpretation of tongues.' Three King James singletons from a single verse, taken in that verse's order, with a fourth from the neighbouring 12:9 — and the denial they are put in the mouth of is phrased with the verb of 1 Corinthians 13:10. This is the structural link of the chapter: everything from 9:7 to 9:20 argues the cessation question on 1 Corinthians 12-13's ground, and 9:15's 'Has the end come yet?' is a direct challenge to 13:10's 'when that which is perfect is come'. Moroni will make the same list again, and at greater length, at Moroni 10:8-18.
links.text: To another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues:

pericopes.text: Behold I say unto you, He that denieth these things, knoweth not the Gospel of Christ; yea, they have not read the Scriptures; if so, they do not understand them.

provenance.other: “ye know not the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 12:24; Matthew's parallel reads “not knowing the scriptures”, which also occurs in exactly one. Both are the same rebuke of the Sadducees and both pair scripture-ignorance with 'the power of God' — the phrase Moroni's chapter turns into its refrain from 9:17 onward.
provenance.significance: Read Mormon 9:8-11 straight through and it reproduces the shape of Mark 12:24-26 clause by clause. Mark: you err because you know not the scriptures, neither the power of God (12:24) … have ye not READ in the book of Moses (12:26) … I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. Mormon: he 'knoweth not the Gospel of Christ; yea, they have not read the Scriptures' (9:8) … 'For do we not READ that God is the same yesterday' (9:9) … 'the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' (9:11). Three steps in three verses in the same order, and the third of them carries the New Testament's own punctuation of the divine title rather than Exodus's (see the row at 9:11). Recover the source and the polemic acquires a target it does not name: in Mark the people who cannot read their own scriptures are the party that denies the resurrection, and in Mormon 9 they are the party that denies revelation and miracle. The argument Moroni makes at 9:13 — that Christ's death brings the resurrection to pass — is the argument Mark 12 is about.

links.note: 'He that denieth these things, knoweth not the Gospel of Christ; yea, they have not read the Scriptures; if so, they do not understand them.' No clause is reproduced, which is why this is an allusion rather than a quotation, and the case rests on sequence rather than volume: the rebuke, the not-having-read, and the God of Abraham arrive in Mark's order across four verses, and the middle term is unnecessary to Moroni's argument unless the pattern is being followed. Note the 1830 grammar the 1920 edition tidied away — 'he that denieth … they have not read … they do not understand' — which is worth keeping in view because the plural is what makes the sentence a rebuke of a party rather than of a man.
links.text: And Jesus answering said unto them, Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?

pericopes.text: For do we not read that God is the same yesterday, to-day, and forever: and in him there is no variableness, neither shadow of changing.

provenance.other: “the same yesterday” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 13:8, 'Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.' The 1830 prints 'to-day', hyphenated, against the modern edition's 'today' — the King James spacing survives in the first edition and was normalised later (CONVENTIONS §8). Malachi 3:6, 'I am the LORD, I change not', is the Old Testament's statement of the same doctrine and shares not one word of the formula; Moroni will paraphrase it separately at 9:19, 'He changeth not'.
provenance.significance: This is the only place in Mormon 9 where the borrowing is announced as a borrowing. 'For do we not READ that God is the same yesterday, to-day, and forever' is a citation formula, and it is the second step of the Mark 12:24-26 sequence identified at 9:8: the man who has not read the scriptures is now told what the scriptures say. What he is told is a fusion of two epistles neither of which is named, and the fusion is doing doctrinal work — Hebrews 13:8 predicates immutability of Jesus Christ, James 1:17 of the Father of lights, and Moroni's subject is simply 'God', so the seam between the two verses is exactly where the chapter's Father-and-Son identification at 9:12 will sit.

links.note: Six words reproduced without variation from a KJV singleton, and spliced in the same sentence to a second singleton from James 1:17. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold as a single run and so not one of his King James quotations, but the composite sentence is longer than it and reproduces two whole predicates from two different epistles. Hardy's apparatus cross-references both verses here, which is one of the few rows in this chapter that is not ours alone.
links.text: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.

provenance.other: “no variableness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “shadow of turning” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both James 1:17. Moroni reproduces the first exactly and alters the second by a single noun: 'neither shadow of changing' for 'neither shadow of turning'.
provenance.significance: The substituted noun is not neutral. 'Turning' in James is an astronomical figure — the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation caused by the turning of the heavens — and 'changing' drops the figure to state the doctrine flat. Moroni then builds the next verse on the word he substituted: 'if ye have imagined up unto yourselves a god which doth vary, and in him there is shadow of changing, then have ye imagined up unto yourselves a god which is not a God of miracles' (9:10). The whole argument of 9:9-19 turns on the identity of immutability with continuing miracle: a God who has stopped working miracles has changed, and a God who changes is not God. That inference is Moroni's, not James's, and it is made possible by the one word he moved.

links.note: 'And in him there is no variableness, neither shadow of changing.' Nine words, of which eight are verbatim from a verse containing two King James singletons, and the ninth is a deliberate substitution that the next verse then quotes back. Hardy cross-references James 1:17 at this verse alongside Hebrews 13:8; the two are catalogued separately here because they are two sources fused in one sentence and the argument treats them differently — Hebrews supplies the citation formula's content, James supplies the vocabulary the chapter goes on to use.
links.text: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

pericopes.text: And now, if ye have imagined up unto yourselves a god which doth vary, and in him there is shadow of changing, then have ye imagined up unto yourselves a god which is not a God of miracles.

But behold, I will shew unto you a God of miracles, even the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob; and it is that same God which created the heavens and the earth, and all things that in them is.

provenance.route: Exodus 3:6 → the Synoptic resurrection controversy (Matthew 22:32 / Mark 12:26 / Luke 20:37) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Exodus 3:6 — 'I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.'
provenance.other: The punctuation of the triple decides this and the counts are absolute. “God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” — with the conjunction after Abraham — occurs in exactly four KJV verses, Matthew 22:32, Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37 and Acts 7:32, every one of them New Testament. “God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” — without it — occurs in exactly three, Exodus 3:6, 3:15 and 4:5, every one of them Old Testament. Mormon 9:11 has the first. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points for Matthew 22:32 over Exodus 3:6 and none the other way.
provenance.significance: A one-word difference settles a route, which is why the count is given in full. But the finding is larger than the conjunction. Of the four New Testament verses that carry this form, three are the same pericope — Jesus answering the Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, by pointing out that God calls himself the God of the patriarchs and 'is not the God of the dead, but of the living'. Moroni has been inside that pericope since 9:8 ('they have not read the Scriptures' = Mark 12:24; 'do we not read' = Mark 12:26's 'have ye not read'), and he arrives at its punchline in its New Testament wording. What he does with it is his own: where the Synoptics use the title to prove the resurrection, Moroni uses it to prove that God still works miracles, and then extends it — 'and it is that same God which created the heavens and the earth' — so that the God who spoke at the bush is identified with the creator and the argument from the fathers becomes an argument from creation.

links.note: 'Even the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' Fourteen words shared with four New Testament verses and with no Old Testament verse, on the strength of one conjunction. This is the chapter's cleanest mediation finding: the formula is Exodus's, the wording is the Gospels', and the surrounding argument has been tracking Mark 12:24-26 for three verses. Not a quotation — the clause is a title, not a predicate — but the reproduction is exact and the discrimination is decisive.
links.text: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.

provenance.route: Exodus 20:11 or Acts 4:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon; the two cannot be separated on this verse's evidence
provenance.other: “all that in them is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:11 (the sabbath commandment's creation clause) and Acts 4:24 (the apostles' prayer after the release of Peter and John). The two read identically at every point Mormon 9:11 reproduces, so tools/mediation-check.py can return nothing decisive; both differ from Moroni in supplying 'the sea', which he omits, and Acts 14:15's variant 'all things that are therein' is a third, further-off possibility.
provenance.significance: The 1830 reading is the evidence here, and it is a clean instance of CONVENTIONS §8. The first edition prints 'all things that in them IS' — the King James's own singular verb after a plural subject, which is what makes 'all that in them is' recognisable as a quotation rather than a paraphrase — and the 1920 edition corrected it to 'are'. The correction is grammatically right and it erases the borrowing: the modern text no longer contains the KJV's clause. So the 1830 shows a dependence the current edition has silently removed, and it shows it in the direction opposite to the usual editorial drift, since here the later edition moves AWAY from the source rather than toward it. Compare 1 Nephi 1:20, where the 1920 moved the other way.

links.note: 'And it is that same God which created the heavens and the earth, and all things that in them is.' Five words, but they are five words in an ungrammatical arrangement that no writer produces by accident and that occurs in exactly two KJV verses. Mediation is recorded as uncertain and this is a real undecidedness rather than a shrug: Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24 are word-for-word identical across the whole of what Moroni reproduces, so the verse cannot settle its own route. Context pulls both ways — the chapter's stratum is heavily New Testament, which favours Acts, but the immediately preceding clause is the God of the burning bush, which favours the Decalogue's creation formula. Filed moderate on that account, not on the verbal evidence, which is strong.
links.text: For in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that in them is, and rested the seventh day: wherefore the LORD blessed the sabbath day, and hallowed it.

pericopes.text: Behold, he created Adam; and by Adam came the fall of man. And because of the fall of man, came Jesus Christ, even the Father and the Son; and because of Jesus Christ, came the redemption of man.

And because of the redemption of man, which came by Jesus Christ, they are brought back into the presence of the Lord; yea, this is wherein all men are redeemed, because the death of Christ bringeth to pass the resurrection, which bringeth to pass a redemption from an endless sleep, from which sleep all men shall be awoke by the power of God, when the trump shall sound; and they shall come forth, both small and great, and all shall stand before his bar, being redeemed and loosed from this eternal band of death, which death is a temporal death;

provenance.route: Revelation 20:12, with 1 Corinthians 15:52 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “stand before God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:12, 'And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God' — the bare 'small and great' is common, occurring in exactly thirteen verses, so it is the collocation with standing and with the dead that identifies the source. “the trumpet shall sound” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 15:52, where it is likewise followed immediately by the raising of the dead. The Book of Mormon reads 'the trump shall sound', which is 1 Thessalonians 4:16's noun in 1 Corinthians 15:52's clause.
provenance.significance: Moroni changes one word and the change is the doctrine: Revelation's dead stand before God, Moroni's stand before his BAR. The judicial furniture is the Book of Mormon's own — the phrase recurs across the book — and importing it here converts John's vision of opened books into a courtroom. What survives untouched is the pairing that made Revelation 20:12 worth taking: everyone rises, and the small rise with the great. Moroni is arguing against people who deny that God still acts, and the resurrection he offers as proof is one in which no one is exempted by insignificance.

links.note: 'All men shall be awoke by the power of God, when the trump shall sound; and they shall come forth, both small and great, and all shall stand before his bar.' Two New Testament resurrection texts fused in one clause, each identified by a King James singleton, and the seam is visible: the trumpet is Paul's, the small-and-great standing is John's. The 1830's 'awoke' for the modern 'awakened' is worth noting as a first-edition reading, though nothing in the judgment turns on it.
links.text: And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.

pericopes.text: and then cometh the judgement of the Holy One upon them; and then cometh the time that he that is filthy, shall be filthy still; and he that is righteous, shall be righteous still: he that is happy, shall be happy still; and he that is unhappy, shall be unhappy still.

provenance.other: “filthy still” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “righteous still” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Revelation 22:11. The Book of Mormon uses the pair twice and only twice, at 2 Nephi 9:16 and here.
provenance.significance: Moroni keeps two of John's four terms and replaces the other two. Revelation runs unjust / filthy / righteous / holy — a legal term, a cultic term, and two more of each — and its logic is that the door has closed and no one changes category any more. Moroni runs filthy / righteous / happy / unhappy, and the substitution of the last pair is the whole point of his version: it converts a statement about verdicts into a statement about states, and it is the same move he made at 9:3-4, where the misery of the damned is being unable to bear the company of a holy God rather than a sentence pronounced on them. Note too where the pair drops out of the Book of Mormon: Jacob quotes John's own terms at 2 Nephi 9:16 and follows them with the lake of fire, which is Revelation's furniture; Moroni quotes them and follows them with unhappiness, which is not.

links.note: 'He that is filthy, shall be filthy still; and he that is righteous, shall be righteous still: he that is happy, shall be happy still; and he that is unhappy, shall be unhappy still.' Two complete predicates reproduced from a verse containing two King James singletons, with the KJV's jussive ('let him be') flattened to a plain future — and then extended by two clauses of Moroni's own built on the borrowed frame. Category is quotation on the reproduced predicates; the extension is what makes the row interesting, since the borrowed syntax is being used to say something the source does not say. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold taken run by run.
links.text: He that is unjust, let him be unjust still: and he which is filthy, let him be filthy still: and he that is righteous, let him be righteous still: and he that is holy, let him be holy still.

pericopes.text: And now, O all ye that have imagined up unto yourselves a god which can do no miracles, I would ask of you, have all these things past, of which I have spoken? Has the end come yet? Behold I say unto you, Nay; and God has not ceased to be a God of miracles.
Behold, are not the things that God hath wrought, marvellous in our eyes? Yea, and who can comprehend the marvellous works of God?

provenance.route: Psalm 118:23, or Psalm 118:23 as quoted at Matthew 21:42 / Mark 12:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon; undecidable on this verse
provenance.mt: Psalm 118:23 — 'This is the LORD's doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.'
provenance.other: “marvellous in our eyes” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 118:23 and its two Synoptic quotations at Matthew 21:42 and Mark 12:11. The KJV renders the Greek of the Gospels with the identical English it gives the Hebrew of the Psalm, so tools/mediation-check.py finds no divergence at any point Mormon 9:16 reproduces and reports that the verse cannot settle its own mediation. The 1830 spells 'marvellous' twice, with the King James's double l, where the modern edition prints 'marvelous' (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: What the Psalm calls marvellous in our eyes is a rejection reversed — the stone the builders refused becoming the head of the corner — and the Synoptics quote it at the end of the parable of the wicked husbandmen, addressed to authorities who are about to reject the son. Moroni asks 'are not the things that God hath wrought, marvellous in our eyes?' of people who have decided that God works nothing. Recover the context and the question sharpens: the one thing the Psalm identifies as marvellous is precisely a work of God that its own witnesses failed to recognise. That is the accusation of Mormon 9 in a phrase, and it comes with the Synoptic setting attached — the same pericope-neighbourhood the chapter has been in since 9:8 (Mark 12:24-26 stands fourteen verses after Mark 12:11).

links.note: 'Behold, are not the things that God hath wrought, marvellous in our eyes?' Four words verbatim from a phrase that occurs in exactly three KJV verses, one Psalm and its two quotations, and the borrowed clause is turned from a statement into a rhetorical question — which is the grammatical move the whole of 9:15-19 runs on. Mediation is `uncertain` and honestly so: the KJV's English is identical in all three, so nothing in the words can decide it. The context argument favours the Synoptics, because Mormon 9:8-11 has demonstrably been working in Mark 12, but a context argument is not a verbal one and the field is left open.
links.text: This is the LORD’s doing; it is marvellous in our eyes.

pericopes.text: Who shall say that it was not a miracle, that by his word the heaven and the earth should be; and by the power of his word, man was created of the dust of the earth; and by the power of his word, hath miracles been wrought?
And who shall say that Jesus Christ did not do many mighty miracles? And there was many mighty miracles wrought by the hands of the apostles.

provenance.other: “by the hands of the apostles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 5:12, 'And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people'. Acts 2:43 has the same fact in different words ('many wonders and signs were done by the apostles') and Acts 19:11 the same construction for one man ('God wrought special miracles by the hands of Paul'), so the six-word phrase with the plural is Acts 5:12's alone. Mormon 9:18 keeps the phrase, the adjective 'many' and the participle 'wrought'.
provenance.significance: The verse Moroni takes is the one that says apostolic miracles were public and continuous — 'among the people', in Solomon's porch, in the temple, where anyone could see them. That is exactly the property his opponents deny is available any longer. And the immediate context of Acts 5 is the sequel: the apostles are arrested for it, and Gamaliel tells the council that a work of God cannot be overthrown. Mormon 9:26, 'who can stand against the works of the Lord?', is Gamaliel's question.

links.note: 'And there was many mighty miracles wrought by the hands of the apostles.' A King James singleton kept whole, with 'many' and 'wrought' from the same clause and only Luke's 'signs and wonders' exchanged for the chapter's own keyword, 'miracles'. The exchange matters: Moroni is not narrating Acts but arguing from it, and the substitution converts an account of what happened into an instance of the category under dispute. The 1830's 'there was many' for the modern 'there were many' is a first-edition reading with no bearing on the source.
links.text: And by the hands of the apostles were many signs and wonders wrought among the people; (and they were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch.

pericopes.text: And if there was miracles wrought, then why has God ceased to be a God of miracles, and yet be an unchangeable being. And behold I say unto you, He changeth not: if so, he would cease to be God; and he ceaseth not to be God, and is a God of miracles.
And the reason why he ceaseth to do miracles among the children of men, is because that they dwindle in unbelief, and depart from the right way, and know not the God in whom they should trust.

provenance.route: Matthew 13:58 (with Mark 6:5-6) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “many mighty works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:58, 'And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief'; “because of their unbelief” occurs in exactly two, that verse and Mark 6:6. Mormon 9:18 has 'many mighty miracles' two verses earlier and Mormon 9:20 has the unbelief, so Matthew's single sentence is distributed across Moroni's argument in Matthew's own terms.
provenance.significance: This is the pivot of the chapter's answer and it is built on the one Gospel verse that reports miracles NOT happening. Moroni's opponents infer from the absence of miracles that God has changed; Matthew 13:58 supplies the alternative inference, that the absence is caused at the other end. Mark 6:5 makes the concession sharper still — 'he could there do no mighty work, save that he laid his hands upon a few sick folk, and healed them' — which is the very act Mormon 9:24 will quote from Mark 16:18, so the one thing unbelief could not stop in Nazareth is the sign Moroni promises will follow believers.
