And Mark 16:14, two verses before the commission Moroni reproduces at 9:22, has the risen Christ upbraiding the eleven 'with their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they believed not'. The stratum is consistent: everywhere Moroni touches the Gospels in this chapter, unbelief is the thing that stops the work.

links.note: 'And the reason why he ceaseth to do miracles among the children of men, is because that they dwindle in unbelief.' No clause is reproduced — 'dwindle in unbelief' is the Book of Mormon's own idiom, used from 1 Nephi onward — which is why this is filed as conceptual allusion rather than verbal. What earns the row is that the proposition is a King James singleton's proposition, that Moroni has supplied its other half two verses earlier in the singleton's own words ('many mighty' + 'wrought'), and that he is three verses away from quoting the chapter of Mark in which the same charge is laid against the apostles themselves.
links.text: And he did not many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

pericopes.text: Behold I say unto you, That whoso believeth in Christ, doubting nothing, whatsoever he shall ask the Father in the name of Christ, it shall be granted them: and this promise is unto all, even unto the ends of the earth.

provenance.route: John 16:23, with Acts 10:20 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “shall ask the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “ask the Father in my name” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both John 16:23; John 15:16's nearest rival reads 'ask OF the Father in my name'. Separately, “doubting nothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 10:20, and its inversion “nothing doubting” occurs in exactly one, Acts 11:12 — the two halves of Peter's account of being sent to Cornelius. Mark 11:23's 'shall not doubt in his heart' and James 1:6's 'ask in faith, nothing wavering' are the doctrinally nearer verses and neither supplies the phrase.
provenance.significance: The two singletons come from opposite ends of the New Testament and the join is the argument. John 16:23 is a promise made to disciples in the upper room, on the night before the crucifixion, about what will be possible after the resurrection; Acts 10:20 is the moment the promise is extended past Israel, when the Spirit tells Peter to go with Cornelius's men 'doubting nothing'. Moroni's sentence closes 'and this promise is unto all, even unto the ends of the earth' — his own generalising clause, made out of the two verses that most exactly mark the promise and its extension. He repeats 'doubting nothing' four verses later at 9:25, where it governs the promise Christ makes to whoever believes in his name, which makes the phrase the hinge of the chapter's closing pair of promises.

links.note: 'Whatsoever he shall ask the Father in the name of Christ, it shall be granted them.' Five words verbatim from a King James singleton with the possessive changed from Christ's first person to Moroni's third, and 'doubting nothing' — a second singleton, from Acts — set in front of it. The 1830's 'it shall be granted THEM' after a singular subject was regularised to 'him' in 1920; the plural is the first edition's and it is the reading that matches the sentence's next clause, 'this promise is unto all'.
links.text: And in that day ye shall ask me nothing. Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you.

pericopes.text: For behold, thus saith Jesus Christ, the Son of God, unto his disciples which should tarry; yea, and also to all his disciples, in the hearing of the multitude, Go ye into all the world, and preach the Gospel to every creature;

provenance.other: “go ye into all the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “and preach the gospel to every creature” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Mark 16:15. Matthew's Great Commission (28:19) shares not one of these words; Mark's longer ending is the only place in the English Bible where this sentence exists.
provenance.significance: Everything about this quotation is decided by which Mark is being quoted. Mark 16:9-20 — the 'longer ending' — is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, the two oldest complete Greek witnesses to the Gospel, and is marked as doubtful or bracketed in essentially every critical edition since Tischendorf. A modern reader meets it in a footnote. The King James Bible prints it as scripture without qualification, and Mormon 9:22-24 reproduces roughly fifty consecutive words of it. Moroni introduces them with 'thus saith Jesus Christ, the Son of God, unto his disciples which should tarry' — an attribution to the risen Christ of words that the manuscript tradition does not place in his mouth. Whatever one concludes from that, it is the strongest single instance of `kjvSpecific: yes` in the book: not merely the KJV's English but the KJV's canon.

links.note: Thirteen words reproduced without a variant from a verse containing two King James singletons, introduced by an explicit speech formula naming the speaker and the audience. This is the first of three consecutive verses (9:22-24) that quote Mark 16:15-18 continuously; taken together they run to about fifty words and comfortably exceed Skousen's sixteen-word threshold, though nothing here should be read as a claim about which passages are on his list, which this project does not hold (PLAN §4.1). Hardy's apparatus records the whole span with the note that the wording exactly matches Mark 16:15-18, keying it — as his convention is — at the last verse of the span, 9:25; the link is filed here, where the wording is, and the register at 9:25 sends a reader back.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 9.25 (Mark 16:15-18, cross-referenced at the end of the quoted span)
links.text: And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.

pericopes.text: and he that believeth and is baptized, shall be saved, but he that believeth not, shall be damned.

provenance.other: “he that believeth and is baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “believeth not shall be damned” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Mark 16:16. The verse is reproduced entire and unaltered: seventeen consecutive words, with only the KJV's semicolon becoming a comma.
provenance.significance: This is the longest unbroken verbatim run in Mormon 9 and, at seventeen words, it clears the sixteen-word bar by which Skousen defines a King James quotation — a fact worth recording precisely because this catalogue does not adopt that threshold (CONVENTIONS §2) and can therefore state without special pleading that here it is met. The doctrinal weight is heavy for a text arguing about signs: the verse makes baptism a condition of salvation, and Moroni will spend 9:29 on receiving baptism and the sacrament worthily. And it belongs, like its neighbours, to Mark's longer ending — so the Book of Mormon's clearest statement that the unbeliever is damned rests on a passage the Greek manuscript tradition does not carry.

links.note: A whole KJV verse, seventeen words, word for word. There is nothing to adjudicate about the source and everything to notice about the frame: Moroni is quoting the risen Christ to prove that the gifts have not ceased, and the sentence he chooses is the one that makes belief the hinge — which is the same claim he made in his own voice at 9:20, that miracles stop where unbelief begins. Cited by Hardy as part of the 9:22-25 span; see the note at 9:22 on his keying.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 9.25 (Mark 16:15-18, cross-referenced at the end of the quoted span)
links.text: He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned.

pericopes.text: And these signs shall follow them that believe: In my name shall they cast out Devils; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover;

provenance.other: “these signs shall follow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does the shorter “signs shall follow”; “speak with new tongues” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. All three are Mark 16:17, and Mormon 9:24 reproduces the verse entire, twenty-two words, with the KJV's semicolon after 'believe' becoming a colon.
provenance.significance: The list Moroni quotes here is the answer to the list he put in his opponents' mouths at 9:7. There they deny 'gifts, nor healing, nor speaking with tongues, and the interpretation of tongues', which is Paul's inventory from 1 Corinthians 12:9-10; here he supplies Christ's own inventory from Mark 16:17-18, and the two overlap at tongues and at healing. That is the shape of the whole argument: a Pauline list is denied and a dominical list is produced against it, and the dominical one comes with a promise attached — 'these signs SHALL follow' — that the Pauline one, read through 1 Corinthians 13:10, was being used to cancel.

links.note: A whole KJV verse reproduced, containing three King James singletons. The 1830 capitalises 'Devils' where the King James does not, which is a compositor's habit rather than a reading. This verse and the next together carry the chapter's title claim — that the signs of Mark's longer ending are still on offer — and the run from 9:22 through the end of this verse is about fifty consecutive words of a passage that is absent from the oldest Greek witnesses to Mark. Part of the span Hardy cross-references at 9:25.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 9.25 (Mark 16:15-18, cross-referenced at the end of the quoted span)
links.text: And these signs shall follow them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues;

provenance.other: Four King James singletons in one verse. “take up serpents” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “deadly thing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “lay hands on the sick” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “and they shall recover” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. All four are Mark 16:18. Mormon 9:24 reproduces the verse entire, twenty-eight words, unaltered.
provenance.significance: Mark 16:18 is the most textually disputed sentence in the Gospel's most textually disputed paragraph, and it is reproduced here without a word out of place. Two of its four signs — serpent-handling and the harmless poison — have no other warrant anywhere in scripture and no counterpart in the Book of Mormon's own narrative; nothing in Nephite history involves either. They are here because the verse is here. That is an argument about mechanism rather than about doctrine, and it is why this row and its three neighbours are the chapter's centre of gravity: the borrowing includes material the borrower has no independent use for.

links.note: Twenty-eight consecutive words, four King James singletons, not a variant between the two texts. Catalogued as a separate row from Mark 16:17 because each is a whole verse quoted whole, and a reader looking up either should find the full source text against it; together they are one continuous quotation occupying the whole of Mormon 9:24. Part of the span Hardy cross-references at 9:25 with the observation that the wording exactly matches; the keying convention is discussed at 9:22.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Morm 9.25 (Mark 16:15-18, cross-referenced at the end of the quoted span)
links.text: They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover.

pericopes.text: and whosoever shall believe in my name, doubting nothing, unto him will I confirm all my words, even unto the ends of the earth.

And now behold, who can stand against the works of the Lord? Who can deny his sayings? Who will rise up against the almighty power of the Lord? Who will despise the works of the Lord? Who will despise the children of Christ? Behold, all ye that are despisers of the works of the Lord, for ye shall wonder and perish.

provenance.route: Habakkuk 1:5 → the Septuagint → Acts 13:41 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Habakkuk 1:5 — 'Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvelously: for I will work a work in your days which ye will not believe, though it be told you.'
provenance.lxx: Acts 13:41 quotes Habakkuk in its Greek form, which reads 'despisers' where the Hebrew has 'among the nations' (bogedim for baggoyim) and 'perish' (aphanisthete) where the Hebrew has 'wonder marvellously'. The KJV translates each from its own base, so the two English verses diverge exactly where the Greek and Hebrew do.
provenance.other: “wonder and perish” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 13:41; the Old Testament's corresponding phrase, “wonder marvelously”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Habakkuk 1:5. “despisers” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 13:41 and 2 Timothy 3:3. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points, both for Acts: the Book of Mormon has Acts's 'despisers', not Habakkuk's 'among the heathen and regard', and Acts's 'and perish', not Habakkuk's 'marvelously'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's cleanest mediation finding and one of the cleanest in the book, because the two candidate verses differ at precisely the two points Mormon 9:26 reproduces, and the Book of Mormon has the Greek side of both. The route is therefore not merely 'via the New Testament' in a loose sense: it runs through a Septuagint reading that the Hebrew does not support, which reaches English only because Paul quoted it at Antioch and the KJV translated Paul's Greek. A text presenting itself as an independent Israelite record has here the Septuagint's misreading of Habakkuk, in Luke's framing of it, in the King James's English. And the setting is apt to the point of comment: Acts 13:41 is the last sentence of Paul's first recorded sermon, the closing warning of a synagogue address that immediately precedes the turn to the Gentiles — which is the position Mormon 9:26-27 occupies at the close of Moroni's own last address to unbelievers.

links.note: 'Behold, all ye that are despisers of the works of the Lord, for ye shall wonder and perish.' Not a long run, but every word of it is the New Testament's rather than the Old Testament's at the two places where the Testaments disagree, and the next verse continues the engagement in Moroni's own voice — 'O then despise not, and wonder not' — taking up both of the borrowed verbs and negating them. That continuation is what raises this above a chance echo: the source's two distinctive words are used twice, once as accusation and once as counsel. Filed as quotation on the completeness of the reproduced clause and high rather than certain because the run is short.
links.text: Behold, ye despisers, and wonder, and perish: for I work a work in your days, a work which ye shall in no wise believe, though a man declare it unto you.

pericopes.text: O then despise not, and wonder not, but hearken unto the words of the Lord, and ask the Father in the name of Jesus for what things soever ye shall stand in need. Doubt not, but be believing, and begin as in times of old, and come unto the Lord with all your heart, and work out your own salvation with fear and trembling before him.

provenance.other: “work out your own salvation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Philippians 2:12; the trailing “with fear and trembling” occurs in exactly three, of which that is one, so the nine-word run as a whole is unique. The same verse's 'as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence' is the frame Moroni's own 9:30 will echo — 'I speak unto you as though I spake from the dead'.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is about what a congregation must do when its apostle is not there. Moroni's whole colophon is written from precisely that position and pressed to its limit: not absent but dead, addressing readers separated from him by centuries rather than by miles, who cannot ask him anything. Recover Philippians 2:12 and the borrowing supplies the reason the exhortation takes this form — 'not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence' is the premise of Mormon 9:30-31, where Moroni asks not to be condemned for imperfections no one can now correct. The nine borrowed words carry an argument about absence that Moroni never states.

links.note: 'And work out your own salvation with fear and trembling before him.' Nine consecutive words from a King James singleton, with 'before him' added. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold but a complete reproduced predicate, which is what decides the category under CONVENTIONS §2. The verse also returns to John 16:23 — 'ask the Father in the name of Jesus for what things soever ye shall stand in need' — already catalogued at 9:21, and its opening 'O then despise not, and wonder not' continues the Acts 13:41 borrowing catalogued at 9:26.
links.text: Wherefore, my beloved, as ye have always obeyed, not as in my presence only, but now much more in my absence, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.

pericopes.text: Be wise in the days of your probation; strip yourselves of all uncleanness; ask not, that ye may consume it on your lusts, but ask with a firmness unshaken, that ye will yield to no temptation, but that ye will serve the true and living God.

provenance.other: “consume it upon your lusts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:3, and the shorter “may consume it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one. The Book of Mormon reads 'consume it ON your lusts' for the KJV's 'upon', which is the only difference in six words.
provenance.significance: James 4:3 is the New Testament's one statement that a prayer can be answered with a refusal on grounds of motive — 'ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss'. Moroni has just issued, at 9:21, an unrestricted promise that whatever is asked of the Father in Christ's name will be granted, and at 9:27 has told his readers to ask for whatever they stand in need of. This verse is the qualification, and he takes it from the one verse in the Bible that qualifies exactly that promise. The pair is a small piece of pastoral engineering: the promise and its limit are both quoted, from John and from James, seven verses apart.

links.note: 'Ask not, that ye may consume it on your lusts, but ask with a firmness unshaken.' Six words from a King James singleton with one preposition changed, and the second half of the sentence answers James 1:6 ('let him ask in faith, nothing wavering') in Moroni's own vocabulary rather than the KJV's — 'a firmness unshaken' for 'nothing wavering', where the KJV's own figure is a wave driven by the wind. Filed as allusion rather than quotation because the borrowed words are a subordinate clause rather than a predicate.
links.text: Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.

pericopes.text: See that ye are not baptized unworthily; see that ye partake not of the sacrament of Christ unworthily; but see that ye do all things in worthiness, and do it in the name of Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God; and if ye do this, and endure to the end, ye will in no wise be cast out.—

provenance.other: “in no wise cast out” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 6:37, 'him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out'. The bare “in no wise” occurs in exactly eleven verses, so the phrase is identified by its verb. The 1830 prints 'in no wise' as two words where the modern edition has 'nowise', which preserves the King James spacing (CONVENTIONS §8). 'Endure to the end' is the Book of Mormon's standing form of Matthew 10:22's 'endureth to the end'; “endure unto the end” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13, and “endure to the end” occurs in no KJV verse at all.
provenance.significance: John 6:37 is a promise about admission, made in the discourse on the bread of life — the chapter in which Jesus identifies himself as the bread and says that whoever eats it has eternal life. Moroni's sentence is about the sacrament: 'see that ye partake not of the sacrament of Christ unworthily … and if ye do this, and endure to the end, ye will in no wise be cast out.' So the promise is taken from the one chapter of the Gospels where eating and being received are the same subject, and it is turned into the reassurance that follows a warning about eating unworthily. The warning itself is Paul's (1 Corinthians 11:27-29) and the reassurance is John's; Moroni does not name either.

links.note: Five words from a King James singleton, made passive — Christ's 'I will in no wise cast out' becomes 'ye will in no wise be cast out', which removes the speaker and leaves the guarantee. The conditional attached to it, 'if ye do this, and endure to the end', is the Book of Mormon's regular adaptation of Matthew 10:22 and is not itself a KJV phrase in that form.
links.text: All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.

pericopes.text: Behold, I speak unto you as though I spake from the dead: for I know that ye shall hear my words.

Condemn me not because of mine imperfection; neither my father, because of his imperfection; neither them which have written before him, but rather give thanks unto God that he hath made manifest unto you our imperfections, that ye may learn to be more wise than that which we have been.

And now behold, we have written this record according to our knowledge in the characters, which are called among us the reformed Egyptian, being handed down and altered by us, according to our manner of speech.

And if our plates had been sufficiently large, we should have written in the Hebrew; but the Hebrew hath been altered by us also; and if we could have written in the Hebrew, behold, ye would have had none imperfection in our record.

But the Lord knoweth the things which we have written, and also that none other people knoweth our language; and because that none other people knoweth our language, therefore he hath prepared means for the interpretation thereof.
And these things are written, that we may rid our garments of the blood of our brethren which have dwindled in unbelief.

provenance.route: Ezekiel 33:6 → Acts 18:6 and Acts 20:26 → KJV → Book of Mormon (2 Nephi 9:44, Jacob 2:2, Mosiah 2:28) → Mormon 9:35
provenance.other: “your blood be upon your own heads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 18:6, where Paul shakes his raiment at the synagogue at Corinth and says 'I am clean'; “pure from the blood” and “blood of all men” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:26, the farewell at Miletus. Neither KJV verse contains the Book of Mormon's actual phrase, which is 'rid our garments of the blood'; that formula is the Book of Mormon's own, and it occurs at 2 Nephi 9:44, Jacob 2:2, Mosiah 2:28 and here.
provenance.significance: This is the fifth and last link in a chain the catalogue has been following since 2 Nephi, and it is the one that closes the book. Jacob takes off his garments and shakes them (2 Nephi 9:44); Jacob comes to the temple to rid his garments of the people's sins (Jacob 2:2); Benjamin gathers his people to rid his garments of their blood before going down to his grave (Mosiah 2:28); Moroni writes to rid the garments of the record's authors — 'we', plural, his father and himself and those before them — of the blood of a people already destroyed. The proximate model is not the King James but Mosiah 2:28, a page Mormon himself abridged, and the difference in each recasting is what the gesture is performed against: Benjamin has an audience in front of him, Moroni has only a book. `mediation` is recorded as `direct-NT` because the enum has no value for a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon passage; the route field carries what the enum cannot, and this is flagged for the conventions rather than solved here (CONVENTIONS §7 provides OT-via-earlier-BoM only).

links.note: 'And these things are written, that we may rid our garments of the blood of our brethren which have dwindled in unbelief.' No King James words survive, which is why the type is conceptual: what survives is a gesture that the KJV performs once, at Acts 18:6, and a liability that it states once, at Acts 20:26, and behind both the watchman of Ezekiel 33:6 whose hand the blood is required at. The catalogue has filed Acts 18:6 at 2 Nephi 9:44, Jacob 2:2 and Mosiah 2:28 already; this row records the last occurrence and the fact that its immediate model is Nephite rather than biblical. The object of the gesture has changed one last time — Benjamin rids his garments of the blood of the living, Moroni of the blood of the dead.
links.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

pericopes.text: And behold, these things which we have desired concerning our brethren, yea, even their restoration to the knowledge of Christ, is according to the prayers of all the saints which have dwelt in the land.

provenance.other: “prayers of all saints” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 8:3, where an angel offers incense with them at the golden altar; the variant “prayers of the saints” occurs in exactly one, the following verse, and Revelation 5:8 has 'the prayers of saints' in the vials of the elders. Mormon 9:36 reads 'the prayers of all the saints which have dwelt in the land', which is Revelation 8:3's phrase with the article added.
provenance.significance: Revelation 8:3-4 is the moment the accumulated prayers of the whole church go up together and the seventh seal's silence ends; what follows immediately is fire cast on the earth. Moroni's last request before the book's closing benediction is that the restoration of his brethren should happen 'according to the prayers of all the saints which have dwelt in the land' — the prayers of the dead of a destroyed civilisation, gathered and still pending. Recover the context and the sentence acquires a mechanism: the prayers are not lost with the people who prayed them, because in the source they are held at an altar until they are offered. The chapter has already taken Revelation 22:11 at 9:14 and stands before John's throne at 9:2; this is consistent with the book's closing pages being written with the Apocalypse open.

links.note: Five words from a King James singleton, and no other contact with Revelation 8. Filed as an echo at moderate confidence because 'the prayers of the saints' is a phrase a devout writer might produce unprompted, and because the row rests entirely on rarity plus the Revelation stratum elsewhere in the chapter. It goes in under CONVENTIONS §0a as worth putting on the table: the significance, if the link holds, is that Moroni's last petition is made on the assumption that the prayers of his exterminated people are still in hand.
links.whyNot: Five words with no syntactic or contextual reproduction. The saints in Revelation 8 are the whole church at the end of history; Moroni's are the inhabitants of one land, and the KJV phrase without 'the' is close enough to ordinary devotional English that a writer could reach it by no route at all.
links.text: And another angel came and stood at the altar, having a golden censer; and there was given unto him much incense, that he should offer it with the prayers of all saints upon the golden altar which was before the throne.

pericopes.text: And may the Lord Jesus Christ grant that their prayers may be answered according to their faith; and may God the Father remember the covenant which he hath made with the house of Israel; and may he bless them forever, through faith on the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.

provenance.other: “remember the covenant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 26:45; Leviticus 26:42 has 'remember my covenant' three times over and 'I will remember the land'. Luke 1:72's “his holy covenant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is the New Testament's nearest form. Mormon 9:37's actual wording — 'remember the covenant which he hath made with the house of Israel' — is not any of these; it is Mormon 5:20's wording, 'then will the Lord remember the covenant which he made unto Abraham, and unto all the house of Israel', with Abraham dropped.
provenance.significance: The catalogue filed Leviticus 26:42 at Mormon 5:20, where Mormon states the promise after the scattering and before the restoration, exactly where Leviticus 26 places it. Mormon 9:37 is Moroni, finishing his father's book, closing it with his father's sentence in his father's order and one clause shorter. That is the small finding here and it is worth a row: the last verse of the book of Mormon is a benediction built out of the abridger's own formula, not out of the Bible directly, and `mediation` is `OT-via-earlier-BoM` on that account — the proximate model is a Book of Mormon page, and it happens to be a page by the man Moroni is burying.

links.note: 'And may God the Father remember the covenant which he hath made with the house of Israel.' No King James phrase survives intact — the covenant-remembering formula of Leviticus 26 is diffuse and the wording is Mormon 5:20's — so the row is filed as a conceptual echo and `kjvSpecific` as uncertain. It earns its place by the recurrence rather than by the vocabulary: the same clause, minus one member, from the same book, in the mouth of the son rather than the father, as the last petition of the last verse.
links.whyNot: Covenant-remembering language is spread across Leviticus, Psalms, Ezekiel and Luke, and a writer closing a book about Israel's restoration will reach for it without a source. The link to Mormon 5:20 is stronger than the link to Leviticus, and a reader who declines the Leviticus end of the chain will still have the internal repetition, which is the part that is actually demonstrable.
links.text: Then will I remember my covenant with Jacob, and also my covenant with Isaac, and also my covenant with Abraham will I remember; and I will remember the land.
